title: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha
excerpt: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.

inline.s: The Indian Tripitaka Master Kang Sengkai translated this sutra during the Cao Wei dynasty.
The commentary was composed by the monk Huiyuan of Jingying Temple in the capital city during the Sui dynasty.

blocks.text: Expository Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha, Fascicle One

inline.s: [Commentary]

The sacred teachings, in brief, are of only two kinds: the Sravaka Pitaka and the Bodhisattva Pitaka. That which teaches the Dharma to sravakas is the Sravaka Pitaka; that which teaches the Dharma to bodhisattvas is the Bodhisattva Pitaka. Within the Sravaka Pitaka there are two: sravakas who are sravakas, and pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. The former are persons who in the past sought the sravaka path, ever delighting to contemplate the four Noble Truths, thereby forming the nature of a sravaka; in their last body they met the Buddha, who taught them the four Truths, and they awakened to the Way. Being originally sravaka by nature and now again hearing the voice and awakening, they are called sravakas who are sravakas, that is, what the sutra calls 'for those who seek to be sravakas he spoke the four Truths.' The latter are persons who originally sought the pratyekabuddha path, ever delighting to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby forming the nature of a pratyekabuddha; in their last body they met the Buddha, who taught them the twelve links, and they awakened to the Way. Being originally pratyekabuddha by nature and having heard the voice and awakened in their last body, they are called pratyekabuddhas who are sravakas. Though the two attainments differ, both receive the Lesser Dharma and both awaken by hearing the voice in this present life; hence what is spoken to these two is the Sravaka Pitaka. Within the Bodhisattva Pitaka there are the gradual and the sudden. The gradual entrant studied the Great in the past, in the meanwhile practiced the Lesser and realized its fruit, and later returned to the Great, coming from the Lesser; hence 'gradual.' The sutra says, 'Except those who formerly studied the Lesser Vehicle, I shall also cause them to enter this Dharma.' The suddenly awakened are beings who have long cultivated good roots corresponding to the Great Vehicle, now first see the Buddha and are able to enter the Great, the Great not proceeding from the Lesser; hence 'sudden.' The sutra says, 'Or there are beings who, age after age, have always received my teaching; when first they see my body and hear my words, they at once believe and receive, entering the Tathagata's wisdom.' The gradual entrant relies on shallow stages and journeys far; the suddenly awakened understands the Great in a single leap. Though sudden and gradual differ, both receive the Great at the same time, so what is spoken to them is the Bodhisattva Pitaka. The sacred teachings, however many, do not pass beyond these two. Nagarjuna said that after the Buddha's nirvana Kasyapa and Ānanda compiled the Dharma-storehouse at Rajagrha as the Sravaka Pitaka, and Manjusri and Ānanda compiled the Mahayana on Iron-Circumference Mountain as the Bodhisattva Pitaka. The Bodhisattva-bhumi likewise says the Buddha spoke the sutras for sravakas and bodhisattvas practicing the way out of suffering, and the compilers gathered them into two Pitakas. The two are also called the Great and Lesser vehicles, the full and empty teachings; though the names are inverted, the meaning is not different. Now this sutra falls within the Bodhisattva Pitaka; it is the Dharma-wheel of sudden teaching for those of sharp and ripened faculties. We know it is sudden because it is precisely for ordinary beings who dread birth and death and seek right concentration, causing them to rouse the mind and be born in the Pure Land, not proceeding from the Lesser or the Great.
[Commentary]

Having distinguished the divisions, we next explain the title. 'The Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha' sets forth the particular name of the sutra. All sutras set the title first to show the Dharma they reveal; this sutra manifests the practice and attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the beings he gathers and transforms, and therefore first raises that name. The various sutras take their names differently: some only from the Dharma, as the Nirvana; some only from a person, as the Trapusa and Prince sutras; some only from an event, as the Withered Tree sutra; some only from a simile, as the Great Cloud and Jewelled Casket sutras; some from the time, as the sutra on right and wrong times; some from a place, as the Samgha sutra and the sutra of Gaya's Peak; some raise both person and Dharma, as the Vimalakirti and the Srimati sutras; some set forth both event and Dharma, as the Vaipulya Great Assembly sutra; some reveal both Dharma and simile, as the Avatamsaka and the Lotus sutras. Thus they are not of one pattern. This sutra is named from the person. In listing the person there are four: raising the person himself, as in Vimalakirti; raising the asker, as in Manjusri's questions; raising the person spoken of, as in the Prince sutra; raising the person to be transformed, as in the sutra of Sumati's daughter. The opening of this sutra generally raises both the speaker and the spoken of: 'the Buddha' raises the speaker, and 'Immeasurable Life' the spoken of. The occasions of preaching are five, as Nagarjuna says: the Buddha speaks himself; holy worthies speak; the gods speak; gods and immortals speak; and transformed persons speak. This sutra is spoken by the Buddha, and to set it apart from the other four the word 'Buddha' is raised. 'Buddha' is a foreign word translated 'the awakened.' 'Awakened' has two senses. First, awareness, directed at the affliction-obstacle: affliction harms, with an affair like a thief, and only sages are aware of it and are not harmed thereby; this sense is as explained in the Nirvana. Second, comprehension, directed at the wisdom-obstacle: ignorance lies asleep, its affair like sleep, and when sage-wisdom arises one awakens greatly, as one wakes from sleep. The ignorance that is its object is of two kinds: the nature-veiling ignorance that obscures the real nature, which being removed the false turns to the true, so that awakening to the real is called 'awakening'; and the unknowing within events, deluded about the characteristics of dharmas, which being removed one understands all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas. Therefore the Bodhisattva-bhumi says that in the categories of benefit-to-meaning, non-benefit-to-meaning, and neither-benefit-nor-non-benefit, he opens and awakens equally; hence he is called Buddha. Since he awakens himself and also awakens others, and the practice of awakening is fully carried out, he is called Buddha. Self-awakening sets him apart from ordinary beings, awakening others from the two vehicles, and the fully completed practice from the bodhisattvas; hence only he alone is called Buddha. Uttering with the mouth is 'speaking'; 'Immeasurable Life' is what is spoken. This sutra proclaims the practice and attainment of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and the beings he gathers and transforms. 'Practice' proclaims the vows he first made and the practice he first cultivated; 'attainment' speaks of the two fruits he now attains, the Dharma-body and the Pure Land; 'gathering' means he universally draws the connected beings of the ten directions to go together to that land, so that the benefit of the Dharma-transformation is called 'the gathered.' Moreover all bodhisattvas study his practice, obtain his attainment, and share his gathering; this too is 'the gathered.' The Buddha's name is of two kinds, common and particular: 'Thus-come One, Worthy of Offerings' are the common names; 'Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Immeasurable Life' are the particular designations. Among the particular names there are many: some from the lineage, as Śākyamuni and Kasyapa; some from the body, as the Honored Body Buddha; some from the voice, as the Wonderful Sound Buddha; some from the light, as the Universal Light Buddha; some from inner virtue, some from a simile. This Buddha is named from his lifespan. The lifespan has a true and an apparent one: the true is eternally abiding, its nature the same as empty space; the apparent lifespan is not fixed, sometimes long, sometimes short. What is discussed here is the apparent. Within the apparent lifespan this Buddha's life is long, and ordinary beings and the two vehicles cannot fathom its limit; hence 'immeasurable.' That this is apparent and not true we know because the Sutra of Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta says that though the life of this Buddha is long and far-reaching it too has an end, and after his nirvana the two bodhisattvas become Buddhas in succession. 'Sutra' is the foreign word 'sutra,' translated 'thread': the sayings of sages string all dharmas as a thread strings flowers. The thread strings flowers and the sutra maintains the lifespan, their functions being similar; hence 'sutra.' By the ordinary gloss 'sutra' means 'constant': people differ in past and present, but the teachings are an enduring norm; and any one Dharma passes through antiquity and reaches the present, always existing without interruption, which is its sense of 'constant.'

From beginning to end this sutra's text has but three divisions: the preface, the main teaching, and the transmission. From the beginning to 'he replied, 'I wish to hear them'' is the preface; from 'The Buddha told Ānanda, 'In the past, long ago...'' onward is the main teaching; from 'The Buddha told Maitreya, 'Those who shall hear that Buddha's name and rejoice''' onward is the transmission. Transformation must have a cause, so the preface is first set forth; since the preface has arisen, the main doctrine is next set forth; and the sages preach the Dharma for the benefit of beings and, having finished, praise its excellence, urge study, and entrust it for preservation, so third the transmission is distinguished.
[Commentary]

The preface's meaning and text, though many, have an essential meaning of only two: the initiating preface and the attesting-faith preface. About to teach, the Buddha first relies on time and place, uses supernatural power to gather the assembly, and raises the principle taught; this is 'initiating,' and as the cause of the teaching it is the initiating preface. After the Buddha finishes teaching, Ānanda receives the Dharma and, about to transmit it to later ages, first says to the assembly, 'Such is the Dharma, I heard it from the Buddha,' attesting it so as to be credible; this is the attesting-faith preface. Two prefaces are established because there are two sutras: the sutra spoken by the Tathagata and the sutra transmitted by Ānanda. Though the substance is one, measured by persons and times it is divided in two. The Tathagata's speech benefited that time; Ānanda's transmission reaches later ages. Facing the Tathagata's sutra the initiating preface is established, and facing Ānanda's transmitted sutra the attesting-faith preface is established. These two prefaces have further meanings, related elsewhere.

In the text the first words, 'Thus have I heard,' are the attesting-faith preface. From 'at one time' onward the meaning has two aspects: taken as the original event's arising, it is assigned to the initiating preface; and cited by Ānanda to attest the truth, it is the attesting-faith preface. Since the meaning has both aspects, one cannot take it one-sidedly.
I have heard thus.
In the attesting-faith preface there are three gates: explaining the reason for the words 'Thus have I heard'; clarifying the purpose of establishing them; and explaining their text.
[Commentary]

As to the reason, why does every sutra's opening bear the words 'Thus have I heard'? Because the Buddha directed them to be placed. Why did he direct it? Because of Ānanda's request. Why did Ānanda request? Because Aniruddha instructed him. Why did Aniruddha instruct? Because he saw Ānanda's mind grieved. Why was Ānanda grieved? Because he saw the Tathagata about to enter parinirvana. The Buddha was about to pass away, lying with head to the north between the twin sala trees; Ānanda, seeing this, wept and sobbed and could not contain himself. Aniruddha awakened him, saying, 'You are the transmitter of the Dharma; why do you not ask the Buddha about the affairs of the future world? Of what use is mere grief?' Ānanda replied, 'My mind has sunk in a sea of sorrow; what is there to ask?' Aniruddha then taught him to ask four matters: after the World-Honored One's nirvana, on what do the monks rely as teacher; on what do they abide; how to dwell with ill-natured monks; and what word to set at the head of all sutras. Instructed, Ānanda was somewhat awakened and asked, and the Buddha answered: they should rely on the Pratimoksa as teacher; if I were still in the world it would be no different. The Pratimoksa is the precepts the monks study. They should abide by the four foundations of mindfulness — the monk relying on the inner body to cultivate contemplation of the body, striving with diligence to remove worldly craving and love, and likewise with the outer body and the inner-outer body, and likewise with feelings, mind, and dharmas. The sutra says, 'If one abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, this is called one's own realm and one is not bound by Mara; if one abides in the five desires, that is Mara's realm and one is bound by him.' To dwell with ill-natured monks, govern them with the brahma-danda, the penalty of silence; if the mind is tamed, then speak of leaving the two extremes. At the head of all sutras set 'Thus have I heard, the Buddha dwelt in such a place,' among such an assembly, and the other six matters. Because the Buddha directed this, every sutra's opening is furnished with 'Thus have I heard.' Next, the purpose. The Buddha directed this phrase to produce faith in beings. As to 'thus,' Ānanda declares that he believed and obeyed the Buddha's words, saying the Buddha's speech was 'thus' and 'so,' causing other beings to join him in faith. As to 'I have heard,' Ānanda is himself an insufficient person; were he to say this Dharma was his own teaching, many would despise and slander it, but because he says it was heard from the Buddha, people all turn to faith. Faith is the first gate of entering the Dharma and the foremost in embracing it. The Avatamsaka says faith is the hand: a man with a hand, on reaching a place of treasures, takes what he wishes; a man without hands obtains nothing. Having the hand of faith, one takes the treasure of the Way at will. Therefore these words are set to produce faith. Next, the phrase itself. 'Thus' has two senses. By the Dharma: Ānanda says the Buddha's words are 'thus' with respect to dharmas — speaking principle as principle, events as events, cause as cause, fruit as fruit; hence 'thus'; and words that accord with the Dharma are correct in principle, hence 'so.' By the person: Ānanda says the present Śākyamuni spoke 'thus' like all the Buddhas of the past; hence 'thus.' The Nirvana sutra says, 'As the past Buddhas spoke, not changing, therefore called “Thus-come.”' To be contrary to the Buddhas' speech the words are not-so; to accord with them they are so. As to 'I have heard,' Ānanda, facing future beings, declares he received the teaching. Hearing is truly with the ear, yet he says 'I': the faculties differ but are all my instruments, and the speaker is set forth. In the Dharma there is no person, yet one speaks of the subject and says 'I,' because though the Dharma has no fixed subject it is not without a provisional name, as the Nirvana says: four armies combined form an army, and though there is no fixed commander one may still say 'my army is valiant.' One may ask why Ānanda, a sage who has attained the principle, uses 'I' like ordinary beings. There are three kinds of 'I': the 'I' of the view-mind, the ordinary beings who have not lost the view of self; the 'I' of the pride-mind, the trainees who though free of the view of self still have pride; and the 'I' of worldly convention, the sages beyond training whose view-impurities and pride are exhausted, who follow the worldly convention and provisionally say 'I.' Ānanda, when compiling the Dharma, was beyond training, his views and pride removed, and followed the worldly convention in saying 'I'; hence he is not the same as ordinary beings. But 'I' is a provisional name of worldly truth and no-self is the supreme truth, so why not take the supreme and proclaim no-self? Because the transformation of ordinary beings requires it: if one did not say 'I,' how could one distinguish this from that and cause people to know and recognize? Hence one must say 'I'; and even the Buddhas, when transforming, often say 'I,' and the wise find nothing strange.

From 'at one time' onward, though the meaning has both aspects, facing the foregoing which is entirely the attesting-faith preface, we explain it specifically as the initiating. Within it there are three: clarifying the Buddha as the transforming master; from 'with a great assembly of monks' onward, distinguishing his retinue; and from 'at that time the World-Honored One's faculties were serene' onward, the Tathagata manifests transformation as the initiation, and Ānanda makes the request.
At one time the Buddha was dwelling at Rajagrha, on Mount Grdhrakuta (Vulture Peak).
[Commentary]

'At one time' raises the Buddha's time of transformation; 'the Buddha' raises the transforming person; 'dwelling at Rajagrha' raises the place of transformation. As to 'one time,' people have various explanations, but here it means the season of transformation. Through the whole of the Buddha's lifetime the times of transformation are many, and 'one' distinguishes this from the others. The phrase abounds in the sutras: the Nirvana says, 'I at one time was at Rajagrha discussing worldly truth with the bodhisattva Maitreya'; 'I at one time was on the bank of the Ganges'; 'I at one time was in the cemetery of corpses.' 'The Buddha' is as explained before. 'Rajagrha' is a general raising by the city, so called because in ancient times many kings dwelt there. Mount Grdhrakuta is a separate designation of place: around Rajagrha there are five mountains, each with a monastery, so to distinguish it the mountain is named. It is translated 'Vulture Peak' because many spirit-immortals dwell there and vultures roost there; it is also called Vulture-Head Mountain, since many spirit-vultures live on its summit and the peak resembles a vulture's head. Within the place of roaming transformation, abiding is called 'dwelling.' The Dharma-body is equal and truly has no resting place, but the transformation is manifested in a direction, hence 'dwelling'; and to make the transforming teaching universal it must follow the transformation.
[Commentary]

In the second part, the assembly, the sravakas are first listed and then the bodhisattvas are revealed; so do the many sutras. Why? The explanation in general has four points. First, by near and far: the sravakas are mostly near the Tathagata, so after the Buddha is clarified they are listed first as near; the bodhisattvas are mostly not near the Buddha, so they are listed later. Why are the sravakas especially near? For two reasons: they have not practiced the Way long and, though they have attained the sage-fruit, in progress and deportment they always follow the Buddha's teaching, as the vinaya lays down that Aniruddha should not share lodging with women, that Svagata should not drink liquor, and that the seventeen youths should not play in the water — all arhats following the Buddha's rules; whereas the bodhisattvas, long familiar with the Dharma, do not rely on his teaching. Also, the sravakas are saved by the Buddha in this life, leaving the ordinary to become sages, and the grace being deep they always attend and serve him; the bodhisattvas, transforming beings according to conditions, are mostly not near him. Second, by deportment and form: the sravakas maintain their deportment, and their form resembles the Buddha, so the world reveres them and they are listed first; the bodhisattvas, transforming according to circumstances, have indeterminate form, as when Manjusri in a single summer dwelt in three places in retreat. Third, by the teaching: as Nagarjuna explains, the teaching is manifest or secret. According to the manifest teaching, the arhats and pratyekabuddhas, like the Buddha, have the outflows extinguished, so after the Buddha the sravakas are listed; the bodhisattvas manifest the various outflows and appear as ordinary beings, so to avoid startling people they are listed last. According to the secret teaching, the bodhisattvas' virtue is venerable and they should be first, as the Avatamsaka lists the bodhisattvas first and only in the assembly of the Jetavana Double-Gallery lists the sravakas. Fourth, by number: as the Nirvana says, the fewer are listed first and the greater later. Now, by the first two senses, the sravakas are listed first, then the bodhisattvas.
Within the sravaka assembly the text has four divisions: marking the distinction of the assembly; distinguishing its number; praising its virtue; and listing its names.
Together with a great assembly of monks.
[Commentary]

First this marks the assembly, and it is by reference to the Buddha that the assembly is made clear. Taking the body together with those others is 'together.' 'Great' is the foreign word 'maha,' translated with three senses: 'many,' as many people in the world are called a great assembly; 'surpassing,' for among those ninety-five kinds of paths this is most superior; and 'great,' for it broadly possesses elevated virtue and exceeds the recent learners. 'Bhiksu' is an Indian word translated with five senses: 'one who frightens Mara' — having left home, his roused mind is vast and causes Mara to fear, for Mara is jealous and mean, begrudging others surpassing himself, and fears that he will transform many beings out of birth and death, emptying his realm; 'alms-seeker' — having left home he stores up nothing and lives by begging; 'pure livelihood' — he seeks alms by a right livelihood apart from wrong livelihood; 'one who purely observes the precepts' — keeping the precepts purely with no transgression; and 'one who destroys evil' — by observing the precepts he leaves the fault of transgression. When there are many people it is called an assembly.
Twelve thousand people were gathered together.
[Commentary]
Second, distinguishing their number. Gathering together is called 'together.'
All the great sages, whose supernormal powers have already been attained.
[Commentary]

Third, praising their virtue. 'All the great sages' praises the eminence of the persons, raising one to imply the rest. Those whom the dull-rooted and recent learners cannot surpass are called 'great' — for high in stage, as those below from Ajnata Kaundinya onwards are all ultimate sages beyond training, and for surpassing virtue, as they are all sharp-rooted sravakas accomplishing surpassing virtue. Meeting the right is 'sage.' 'Supernormal powers already attained' praises the excellence of their virtue: what is done is spirit-wondrous, hence 'spirit'; without obstruction is 'through.' The superpowers are six: the bodily superpower, the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the extinction of outflows. These monks in the Lesser Vehicle have cultivated to the ultimate, hence 'already attained.' One may ask how Ānanda, who while the Buddha lived was in the stage of study and had not attained the extinction of outflows, is included. It is because, following the many, he is praised; and though his virtue was not complete he was the requester in this assembly and must be listed, and being of the highest sharp faculties he accomplished immeasurable sublime virtues in the stage of study, hence called 'great sage,' and comprehended the superpowers ultimately, hence also 'already attained.' Above is the praise of their virtue.

Their names are: the Venerable Ajnata Kaundinya, the Venerable Proper Vow, the Venerable Proper Speech, the Venerable Great Call, the Venerable Benevolent and Wise, the Venerable Free from Defilement, the Venerable Renowned, the Venerable Good and Real, the Venerable Complete, the Venerable Bull King, the Venerable Uruvilva Kasyapa, the Venerable Gaya Kasyapa, the Venerable Nadi Kasyapa, the Venerable Mahakasyapa, the Venerable Sariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Great Abiding, the Venerable Great Pure Will, the Venerable Maha Juna, the Venerable Full of Vows, the Venerable Free from Obstacles, the Venerable Conduit, the Venerable Firm and Subduing, the Venerable Face King, the Venerable Fruit Vehicle, the Venerable Benevolent Nature, the Venerable Joy and Bliss, the Venerable Good Coming, the Venerable Rahula, the Venerable Ānanda. All such as these are the elders at the head.
[Commentary]

Fourth, listing their names. 'Their names are' is the compiler's general raising, next the individual listing. These all have virtue and are venerable, hence 'Venerable.' Ajnata Kaundinya: Kaundinya is the surname, Ajnata the given name; 'a' means 'no' and 'jna' means 'wisdom,' so having realized the no and accomplished wisdom he is called 'no-wisdom.' 'No' is the original nature of all dharmas, called the original limit, and in this original limit he knows and sees clearly, hence 'Ajnata.' Of the twelve thousand, just thirty-two are listed, and 'all such as these are the elders at the head' concludes the praise generally.

Next are listed the assemblies of bodhisattvas, within which there are four: marking the distinction of the assembly; from 'Samantabhadra and the rest' listing their names; from 'possessing immeasurable virtues and practices' onward praising their virtue; and from 'such as these, beyond recounting' onward distinguishing the total number.
Together again with the great assembly of bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle.
[Commentary]

'Again' is a word of repetition; the sravakas having been listed, the bodhisattvas are now made clear. 'Together' has the same sense as before, distinguishing the Buddha and including those others. 'Great Vehicle' names the Dharma to distinguish the persons: 'vehicle' is the function of practice, which conveys and reaches; the vehicles are three, and the other two are not its equal, hence 'great.' 'An assembly of bodhisattvas' names the persons by the Dharma; not one is called an assembly. 'Bodhisattva' is a foreign word, fully 'bodhi-sattva,' abbreviated 'bodhisattva,' translated 'a being of the Way': 'bodhi' is the Way and 'sattva' is a being, for this person inwardly seeks the Way and fully possesses its practice, and is completed by the Way. One may ask why, since the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas also seek the Way and have its practice, only this one is called a being of the Way. The worthy and the sages have names both common and particular: by the common, all are included, as the Nirvana says the stream-enterer and the rest are also called bodhisattva because they seek the wisdom of the extinction of outflows and the knowledge of no-birth, and are also called Buddha because of the common and not-common right enlightenment. But to distinguish the worthy and the sages, the beings of the Great Vehicle are specifically named 'bodhisattva,' for three reasons. By the vow-mind toward the fruit: only these beings seek the great bodhi, hence only they are called beings of the Way, as the Bodhisattva-bhumi says, 'One who with fixed determination vows bodhi alone is called bodhisattva.' By the understanding-mind toward the principle: ordinary beings cling to being and the two vehicles abide in non-being, neither according with the middle Way, whereas only the bodhisattva lets go of being and non-being and accords with it. By the practice: in entering the Buddha-Dharma there are the teaching, the meaning, and the practice. The teaching is shallow, the meaning deep, and the practice most supreme. The sravakas, of dull faculties, are named from the teaching — 'sravaka' (the hearer) means hearing the voice and awakening. The pratyekabuddha, next superior, is established by the meaning — 'pratyeka' (dependent) means awakening on the conditions. The bodhisattva, most supreme, is named from the practice, being able to accomplish the Way of benefiting self, others, and both. Hence the Bodhisattva-bhumi says the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas can save only themselves, whereas the bodhisattva saves himself and others, so his Way is supreme. Gathering together is called 'together.'

Samantabhadra bodhisattva, Manjusri (Miaode) bodhisattva, Maitreya (Cishi) bodhisattva, and so forth, all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa (the Worthy Age). Moreover the sixteen worthies, headed by Bhadrapala: the bodhisattva Good Reflection, the bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Emptiness and No-thing, the bodhisattva Supernatural Flower, the bodhisattva Light and Radiance, the bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, the bodhisattva Wisdom Banner, the bodhisattva Serene Root, the bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, the bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the bodhisattva Jewel Radiance, the bodhisattva Dwelling in the Middle, the bodhisattva Regulating Conduct, the bodhisattva Liberation. All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra.
[Commentary]

Next the names are listed. First those bodhisattvas who will become Buddhas in the Bhadra-kalpa are listed, and then, under Bhadrapala and the rest, the bodhisattvas of the other kalpas. Within the Bhadra-kalpa, Samantabhadra, Manjusri, and Maitreya are listed separately. Manjusri is Wenshu; Maitreya is Cishi, his surname being compassionate, and his name is Ajita, which here means 'No-Superior.' 'And so forth' are the other bodhisattvas of the Bhadra-kalpa, and 'all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadra-kalpa' generally sums them by time. In the other kalpas, sixteen worthies are briefly raised, raising the beginning to include the rest, and 'Good Reflection and the rest' lists individually those among their equals. 'All these revere the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra' reveals what they studied, and may also be called distinguishing the lower from the higher.

Next is the praise of their virtue, within which there are two divisions: praising their twofold virtue of expedience and ultimate, and, from 'whose practice is pure' onward, praising their twofold virtue of self-benefit and benefiting others. Within the former there are three: from their own division briefly praising their virtue; from 'entering the Dharma-storehouse' onward, broadly praising their virtue in progressive advance; and from 'perfect and complete virtue, wondrous' onward, jointly concluding the praise.
Possessing the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, abiding in all the dharmas of virtue, roaming the ten directions, employing the skillful means of expedience.
[Commentary]

In the first brief praise, first the ultimate virtue is praised and from 'roaming' onward the expedient virtue. In the ultimate, 'possessing the immeasurable practices and vows' means the practices are complete and full — 'practice' meaning the six perfections and the four methods of gathering, 'vow' meaning the immeasurable bodhi practices and vows, as the Avatamsaka speaks. 'Abiding in all the dharmas of virtue' means the completed virtue is fully furnished and, being accomplished, never retreats. Having virtue it is accomplished, hence 'all.' 'Merit' (gong) means function, for all the practices benefit; this merit is the virtue of good practice, hence 'virtue' (de). The sutra's 'virtue and merit' has a common and a particular sense; in the common sense all practices are so, in the particular the practice of wisdom is called wisdom while the remaining precepts, giving, and so forth are called virtue; here the common is taken. The substance of virtue is called 'dharma.' In the expedient praise, 'roaming the ten directions' means the body is unobstructed, and 'employing the skillful means of expedience' means the transforming activity is skillfully appropriate, appearing variously according to the fitness of beings.
Above, their virtue was briefly praised according to their own division.

Below, their virtue is broadly praised according to the progressive advance. Within it, first the ultimate virtue is praised; from 'attaining Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds' onward, the expedient virtue is praised.
Entering the Dharma-storehouse of the Buddha, reaching in the ultimate the further shore.
[Commentary]

In the ultimate, first it says 'entering the Buddha's Dharma-storehouse'; to realize and attain is called 'entering.' 'The further shore reached in the ultimate' reveals the fruit as final; the further shore of nirvana, reached, is called 'ultimate.'
In immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary]

In praising the expedient virtue, 'in immeasurable worlds manifesting the accomplishment of right enlightenment' praises it in general, and as it praises the progressive advance it raises the attainment of Buddhahood as the expedient virtue.

From 'dwelling in Tushita' below it specifically reveals it. Within it, fully treated, there should be ten marks: ascending to the Tushita heaven; coming down and entering the womb; abiding in the womb; birth; the mark of the child; the mark of taking a consort; the mark of leaving home; the mark of accomplishing the Buddha-way; the mark of turning the Dharma-wheel; and the mark of parinirvana. In the present text one is missing, the abiding in the womb, leaving nine marks.
Dwelling in the Tushita heaven, widely proclaiming the correct Dharma.
[Commentary]

In the first mark, 'dwelling in the Tushita heaven' is the body ascending to Tushita. Tushita, one name variously transmitted, is translated 'splendid abundance,' also called 'contentment' — the fourth heaven of the desire-realm. Why is he born there? As the Nirvana explains, Tushita is supreme: the upper heavens are dark and dull and the lower heavens are indulgent, while this one has neither fault; and whereas giving and precepts obtain the upper and lower heavens, giving, precepts, and concentration obtain Tushita. Though Tushita is the distracted ground of the desire-realm, this is not the concentration of the eight meditations but rather, within the mind of thought-wisdom, the practice of the mindfulness of the Buddha samadhi, so one is born there in dependence on concentration. 'Widely proclaiming the correct Dharma' is the transformation by speech. This completes the first mark.
Leaving that heavenly palace, descending his spirit into the mother's womb.
[Commentary]

This is the second mark. He leaves the bliss of the highest heaven in order to cause the beings of Jambudvipa to all receive the Buddha's grace and produce a mind of reverence, thinking, 'The Buddha left heavenly bliss to be born in Jambudvipa out of compassion for us.' One may ask why of the four kinds of birth the Tathagata especially accepts womb-birth. Because egg-birth and moisture-birth have inferior retribution and transformation-birth, though supreme, has many senses; as the Nirvana says, in brief there are eight senses: at the beginning of the kalpa beings were born by transformation and their afflictions had not yet arisen, so there was no need for the Buddha to appear; when the Buddha appears in the world beings are womb-born, so to increase the power of co-born beings he accepts womb-birth; to be born in a superior clan showing forth the supremacy of the Dharma; to be born in a royal line to rely on it for protecting the Dharma; to teach people to respect the work of father and mother; to be born in a superior clan to still people's pride; to still slander — for if the Buddha were born by transformation many would say he is an apparition and not real; to leave a body and relics for the benefit of later ages — for a transformed birth would pass away as the lightning and leave nothing; and to be the same as all the Buddhas of the three times, who by the Dharma accept womb-birth. Possessing all these senses he accepts womb-birth. This is the second, finished.
According to the other sutras and treatises, here one is missing the mark of abiding in the womb. Since this is what is lacking, the third mark is hereby concluded.

Born from the right side, taking seven steps as he walked, his light shining brilliantly, universally illuminating the ten directions, immeasurable buddha-lands quaking in six ways, he raised his voice and declared, 'I shall be in this world the supreme honored one.' Sakra and Brahma attended him, and gods and men turned to him in reverence.
[Commentary]

This is the fourth mark, birth, within which there are three: the birth-place is extraordinary; what is manifested is extraordinary; and the gods and men revere and serve. In the first, the birth-place of worldly beings is impure, foul, and lowly, and the Buddha differs from them, hence he is born from the right side — and being born from the right side is as emerging from clouds and mist, the mother's body at ease, without effort and pain. Among the manifested wonders, first the wonder of the body is made clear, and from 'raised his voice' onward the wonder of speech. The body has three: in the ten directions he takes seven steps each, showing the heroic strength of a great man and standing forth alone without fear; the body-light universally illuminates, causing people to be aware; and the earth trembles, causing Mara to crouch in fear. The six kinds of quaking, as the Sutra of Stages says, are trembling, surging, shaking, quivering, roaring, and rising: quaking like a cart shaking, surging like a spring welling up or a pot boiling, shaking downward as worldly empty things fall when shaken, quivering causing the mind to be aware so that even beings in the sky know it, and roaring being the issuing of sound. From 'raised his voice' onward is the wonder of speech, self-proclaiming his honored title and causing people to come and take refuge. Finally, the Buddha's virtue being deep, he causes Sakra and Brahma to come and attend him and men and gods to turn to him in reverence. The fourth mark is finished.
He displayed skill in reckoning, letters, and archery. He broadly mastered the arts and techniques, and studied through the manifold scriptures.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the fifth youth. Within it there are two parts. First, his person was complete in every skill, meaning he displayed such matters as reckoning, letters, and the like. The Buddha had long known these, but conforming to the transformation he began to learn them, and so it is called "displayed." Second, from "broadly mastered" (bo zong) onward is the breadth of his knowledge and understanding. "Broadly mastered the arts and techniques": this is breadth in knowledge of affairs; "broad" means extensive, "master" means thorough practice. The secret arts of the immortals were all thoroughly learned by him, hence "broadly mastered the arts and techniques." "Studied through the manifold scriptures": this is breadth in knowledge of the teachings; "study through" means penetrating to the end, "studied" means fully mastered. The secular and heterodox classics are called the "manifold scriptures." Of all these he had complete knowledge, hence "studied through the manifold scriptures." This concludes the fifth.
He roamed in the rear garden, discoursing on martial skill and testing his arts. He dwelt within the palace, amid the sensations of form and flavor.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the sixth, the taking of a wife. Within it, first it says he roamed in the rear garden, discoursing on martial skill and testing his arts: these are matters antecedent to the taking of a wife, as related in the account of his origin. Reining the horse and exerting his sinews is called "discoursing on martial skill"; jointly shooting at the metal drum is spoken of as "testing his arts." "He dwelt within the palace, amid the sensations of form and flavor": these are matters subsequent to the taking of a wife. The Buddha was in truth free of attachment, but conforming to the transformation he displayed this dwelling, hence it is called "he dwelt." A question is asked: why did he display this mark, first receiving and then relinquishing it? To reveal that desire is to be loathed. This concludes the sixth.

Seeing old age, sickness, and death, he awakened to the impermanence of the world. He abandoned the kingdom, its wealth, and his station, and entered the mountains to study the Way. He mounted the white horse with jeweled crown and garland of pearls, then sent them back. He cast aside his precious and fine raiment and donned the robe of Dharma. He shaved off beard and hair, and sat upright beneath the Bodhi tree. Painfully he toiled for six years, doing what was fitting to be done.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the seventh, the going forth from home. Within it are six phrases, which combine into three pairs. The six phrases are: seeing old age, sickness, and death; awakening to the impermanence of the world; and abandoning the kingdom, its wealth, and his station. This is the first phrase, making clear what he relinquished. As related in the account of his origin, going out of the city to roam and observe, at the eastern gate he saw the aged, at the southern gate the sick, at the western gate the dead. Taking these as likened to himself, he awakened to the impermanence of his body, and so there arose loathing and renunciation; abandoning the kingdom, its wealth, and his station, he entered the mountains to study the Way. This is the second phrase, revealing what he undertook. At the northern gate he saw a wandering monk (shramana); through seeing the shramana he therefore sought to study the Way. The text omits this for brevity. These form one pair. "He mounted the white horse with jeweled crown and garland of pearls, then sent them back; he cast aside his precious and fine raiment": this is the third phrase, again making clear what he relinquished. "And donned the robe of Dharma": this is the fourth phrase, revealing what he received. These form the second pair. "He shaved off beard and hair": this is the fifth phrase, again making clear what he relinquished. "He sat upright beneath the Bodhi tree": this is the sixth phrase, making clear what he did, and also making clear what he cultivated. "Painfully he toiled for six years": first he shared in the heterodox practices; "doing what was fitting to be done." Turning away from heterodox learning, the right Way is what is fitting for him to cultivate and study, and he followed it in practice. These form the third pair. This concludes the seventh mark.

From here on is the eighth mark, the accomplishment of the Buddha-Way. Within it, following the events, there are five in sequence: first, bathing and washing away the stains of the body; second, from "the spirit birds" below, going to the place of the Way; third, from "auspicious" below, receiving the grass and sitting peacefully; fourth, from "he roused great" below, the spiritual power that subdues Mara; fifth, from "he attained the subtle" below, the manifest accomplishment of the Buddha-Way.

He appeared in the five defilements' world, conforming to the multitude of beings, and displayed the dust and grime [of the body]. He bathed in the golden stream; the devas pressed down the branches of the tree, and he gained their support to climb out of the pool.
[Commentary]

Within the first part there are three phrases. First, dwelling in the defiled world, he displayed the presence of dust and grime. As it speaks of the five defilements: the first is the defilement of life-span, in that the retribution of life is short and hasty; the second is the defilement of beings, in that people have no good conduct; the third is the defilement of afflictions, in that the various bonds grow ever stronger; the fourth is the defilement of views, in that false views burn fiercely; the fifth is the defilement of the age, in that famine, pestilence, and the weapons of war arise together. The impure world possesses these, and so it is called the five defilements' world. The Buddha appeared dwelling within it, conforming to the multitude of beings, and displayed the presence of dust and grime. Second, "he bathed in the golden stream": in the river of golden sand he bathed and washed away the stains and grime of the body; this is called "bathed in the golden stream." Third, "the devas pressed down the branches of the tree," and he climbed them to come out of the pool.
The spirit birds flew in attendance as he went to the place of the Way.
[Commentary]

Within the second passage, "the spirit birds flying in attendance, he went to the place of the Way" is as the scripture tells: five hundred bluebirds followed behind the Buddha. This is called "the birds flying in attendance." These are all spirit birds, so they are termed "spirit birds." The place where the Buddha attained the Way is called "the place of the Way" (bodhimaṇḍa), just as the place where wheat is dressed is called the wheat field, and the place where grain is dressed is spoken of as the grain field. And so with all things.
Auspiciousness came as a portent, manifesting the merit and blessing. He compassionately received the offered grass and spread it beneath the Bodhi tree, and sat cross-legged.
[Commentary]

Within the third passage, first he was moved by an auspicious sign which came as a portent. This auspicious one was the grass-cutter; in the scripture he is also named Jiana, for auspiciousness and peace are of the same meaning. As the Buddha was about to accomplish the Way, he was moved by the sight of this man as a portent, knowing that he was surely to accomplish the fruit of auspiciousness, and therefore it is named "auspicious portent." By this very man he manifested the merit and blessing of the fruit he was to accomplish, and so it is named "manifesting merit and blessing." Next, he received the grass: the Buddha's heart was compassionate, and his person received the grass, and so it is named "compassionately received the offered grass." Afterward he spread it and sat. Depending on the tree he attained Buddhahood, and so it is called "the Bodhi tree." Spreading it beneath this tree he sat cross-legged. Now, this is in accordance with the differing seeing and hearing of beings. If one discusses bodhisattvas, they see the Tathagata rising from the vajra-ground with the vajra-seat, going up to the place of the Way, and dwelling there to accomplish Buddhahood, as the Nirvana Sutra states. The common person and the two vehicles only see the Tathagata receive the grass of the auspicious one and spread it as a seat, as said in this text.
He roused forth the great radiance, making Mara aware of it. Mara led his retinue and came to press and test him. He subdued them by wisdom and power, causing them all to be vanquished.
[Commentary]

Within the fourth passage, first "he roused forth the great radiance, making Mara aware of it": "roused forth" (fen) is like releasing. Next, Mara came to press and test him; below, the Buddha subdued him. As to "by wisdom and power": this is the virtue of subduing Mara. Wisdom is the right wisdom, knowing that what is false is not to be followed; power is transcendent power, the spiritual power that subdues Mara. It may also be the power of compassion, the compassionate mind that subdues Mara, causing them all to be vanquished. This is the capacity to subdue Mara. Mara is a barbarian word; here it is translated "killer," because it harms the good of beings. Generally it is spoken of in four categories; the Nirvana Sutra speaks of eight. As to the four: the first is the Mara of afflictions, namely greed, hatred, and the like, which can harm good dharmas; the second is the Mara of the aggregates, namely the body of the five aggregates, mutually destroying one another; the third is the Mara of death, which can destroy the root of life; the fourth is the Mara of the heavens, for upon the sixth heaven of self-transformation there is another heaven of Mara, which is ever ruining the good of others. Of these four, the first is the cause of birth-and-death; the last, the heaven of Mara, is the condition of birth-and-death; the middle two, the aggregates and death, are the fruit of birth-and-death. These four categories are spoken of commonly by both great and small vehicles. As to the eight: upon the former four are added the four inverted minds of the unconditioned, which toward the Buddha's true virtue regard the eternal as impermanent, the happy as suffering, the self as no-self, and the pure as impure. With these four, in a near sense they destroy right understanding, and in a distant sense they obstruct true virtue, and so they are called Maras. These latter four are not regarded as afflictions in the small vehicle, and so it does not speak of them as Maras; in the great vehicle they are faults, and so it speaks of them as Maras. In general, discussing these eight, all must be subdued. Why is this so? The afflictions, aggregates, death, and the four inverted minds of the unconditioned obstruct one's own practice, and so they must be subdued. The modes of subduing differ. As to the Mara of afflictions, the small vehicle mostly uses contemplative contemplation to subdue it, and the great vehicle mostly uses the wisdom of emptiness to subdue it. As to the Maras of the aggregates and of death, the small vehicle mostly subdues them by the nirvana of no residue, because it achieves extinction, while the great vehicle mostly subdues them by the eternal Dharma-body. As to the four inverted minds of the unconditioned, within the great cause they are subdued by right understanding, and within the great fruit they are subdued by the true virtue of bodhi and nirvana. The single Mara of the heavens obstructs both one's own practice and the transformation of others, and so it must be subdued. The means used differ: within the cause of one's own practice it is subdued by right wisdom, for knowing that what is false is not to be followed, it retreats and disperses of itself; within the essential of one's own practice it is subdued by the ten powers, for the ten powers are firm and are not to be toppled by Mara and falsehood. Since one's own practice is thus, within the transformation of others the means are not fixed. If one is in the cause, subduing Mara oneself for the benefit of beings, one mostly uses transcendent power; when teaching others to subdue Mara, one mostly uses the divine mantra, for they have no spiritual power to subdue it. If one is in the fruit, subduing Mara oneself for the benefit of beings, one mostly uses the compassionate mind, and out of compassion for them they retreat and disperse; when teaching others to subdue Mara, one also uses the divine mantra, for they have no power of compassion to subdue it. What is discussed here is the specific subduing of the heaven of Mara. In violating one's own practice, right wisdom subdues it; in violating the benefit of others, transcendent power subdues it. Hence it is said "by wisdom and power he caused them all to be vanquished."
He attained the subtle Dharma and accomplished the highest right awakening.
[Commentary]

Within the fifth passage, "he attained the subtle Dharma and accomplished the highest right awakening": this is the manifest accomplishment of Buddhahood. The principle is the subtle Dharma; because he attained this Dharma he accomplished right awakening. This concludes the eighth mark.
From here on is the ninth mark, the turning of the Dharma-wheel. First, there is the request, and afterward the teaching.
Brahma and Indra prayed and urged, requesting that he turn the Dharma-wheel.
[Commentary]
This is the first, the request.

From here on, because of the request, he arose and taught. Within it there are two: first, the transformation arising through body and speech; second, from "with the Buddha's roaming tread, the Buddha's roar, he roared" below, and the radiance universally illuminating the countless lands, the body and speech that gather in and benefit.

With the Buddha's roaming tread he trod; with the Buddha's roar he roared. He beat the drum of Dharma, blew the conch of Dharma, wielded the sword of Dharma, raised the banner of Dharma, thundered the thunder of Dharma, flashed the lightning of Dharma, rained the rain of Dharma, and performed the gift of Dharma. Ever with the sound of Dharma he awakened all worlds.
[Commentary]

Within the former, first it says "with the Buddha's roaming tread he trod": this is the transformation arising through the body's action, displaying the Buddha's dignified deportment, roaming and transforming beings. It is called "the Buddha's roaming tread." From "the Buddha's roar he roared" onward is the transformation arising through speech action. Within it are ten phrases. The single phrase "with the Buddha's roar he roared" is the summary; all the sacred teachings are what the Buddha roars, and the bodhisattva uses them as a roar for beings. The eight phrases from "he beat the drum" onward are the particulars, using similes to reveal the Dharma. Of these, the first four are the four dharmas of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization. "He beat the drum of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of hearing, benefiting beings. A drum is solemnly beaten to warn the troops, so teaching by precept warns people. "He blew the conch of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of reflection, benefiting beings. The conch is blown in due season, so speaking the principle answers the occasion. "He wielded the sword of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of cultivation, benefiting beings. The sword can split apart, so cultivation can sever the bonds. "He raised the banner of Dharma": this openly proclaims the Dharma of realization; the Dharma of realization is lofty and surpassing, like a banner rising above. The last four are the four unobstructed knowledges, arising to teach and benefiting beings. "He thundered the thunder of Dharma": this is the Dharma-unobstructed wisdom transforming beings. Once the heavenly thunder moves, plants and grasses sprout; once the sound of Dharma is heard, the Way is quickly accomplished. "He flashed the lightning of Dharma": this is the meaning-unobstructed wisdom benefiting beings. Once the lightning flashes, creatures see it; once the meaning is proclaimed, all meanings are seen. "He rained the rain of Dharma": this is the expression-unobstructed wisdom transforming beings. Using expression to proclaim, like clouds sending down rain. "He performed the gift of Dharma": this is the joy-of-teaching unobstructed wisdom benefiting beings. According to what beings delight in, he proclaims and bestows, which is called "performed the gift of Dharma." These eight are the particulars. The single phrase "ever with the sound of Dharma he awakened all worlds" is the summary. Up to this point is the first, the transformation arising through body and speech.

From here on is the second, the gathering in and benefiting through body and speech. Within it there are four: first, the body's action subduing Mara, causing beings to abandon false livelihood; second, from "he rent and tore" below, the speech action destroying false views, causing beings to abandon afflictions. These form one pair. Third, from "entering the kingdom and begging" below, the body's action receiving offerings, producing the merit and good of beings; fourth, from "wishing to proclaim the Dharma" below, the speech action teaching the Dharma, causing beings to cultivate the path of transcendence. These form one pair.

The radiance universally illuminated the countless Buddha-lands, and all worlds trembled in six ways. He gathered in all the realm of Mara, moved the palace of Mara, and all the troops of Mara, seized with terror, had none who did not submit.
[Commentary]

Within the first part there are four: first, emitting radiance that universally illuminates the countless Buddha-lands; second, by spiritual power causing all worlds to tremble in six ways; third, because of the previous radiance, gathering in all the realm of Mara, causing them all to submit; fourth, because of the previous trembling, moving the palace of Mara and causing it fear and dread.

He rent and tore the net of falsehood, destroyed all the [false] views, scattered all the dust and toil, ruined all the moat of desire, guarded the city of Dharma, opened wide the gate of Dharma, washed away the stains and defilement, made manifest the pure and bright, let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine, and broadly flowed forth the right transformation.
[Commentary]

Within the second, the speech action, the text also has four. First, it is able to destroy the false: "he rent and tore the net of falsehood" is the breaking of false dharmas; "destroyed all the [false] views" teaches the severing of the false mind. These two remove the views. "He scattered all the dust and toil" is the destruction of the objects of desire; the objects of the five desires can be defiling dust that toils and disorders beings, and so they are called "dust and toil." He speaks emptiness to destroy and reject them, and this is termed "scattered." "He ruined all the moat of desire" teaches the relinquishing of the mind of desire. The mind of love and desire is deep and hard to cross, and so it is spoken of as a "moat"; teaching its severance is called "ruin." These two remove love. These four pairs together form the first, making clear he is able to destroy the false. Second, from "he guarded" onward makes clear he is able to open up the right. "He guarded the city of Dharma" wards off slander of it by people; the Dharma can guard and ward off, and so it is spoken of as a "city." Praising the good and stilling slander is called "guard" and "protect." "He opened wide the gate of Dharma": he proclaims the right teaching, and the total Dharma has the meaning of a path of entry and approach, and so it is called a "gate." Spreading and drawing beings in is called "open" and "wide." Third, from "he washed" below gathers up the previous first meaning of destroying the false: the afflictions of views and love are called "stains and defilement," and teaching their removal is called "washed." Fourth, from "he made manifest" below reveals the previous second meaning of opening up the right: "made manifest the pure and bright, let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine" reveals the previous phrase of "guarding the city of Dharma." Removing the false and revealing the right, so it is called "made manifest." The Dharma made manifest, transcending false slander, is called "pure and bright." Displaying the right Dharma, going forth from the false and depraved, is called "shine." Merging and ordering it to purity is called "let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine." "He broadly flowed forth the right transformation" reveals the previous phrase of "opening wide the gate of Dharma," broadly flowing to transform beings, and so it is called "opened wide." This concludes the first pair.
Entering the kingdom he begged for food, guarding the abundant meals. He stored up merit and revealed the field of blessing.
[Commentary]

Within the third, the body. "Entering the kingdom he begged for food": this is beginning the practice of begging. "Begging" (fen wei) is a barbarian word; here it is translated "begging for food." He obtained the abundant meals, for through begging he obtained food. From "he stored up merit" onward is the receiving and using that produces blessing. "Stored up" (chu) means to accumulate; storing and accumulating many meritorious virtues is called "stored up merit." Now he received offerings of things, hence it is named "revealed." It produces the merit and good of the world, and the field that produces things to the body is therefore called "field of blessing."

Wishing to proclaim the Dharma, he manifested a joyful smile. With all the medicines of Dharma he healed and saved the three sufferings. He manifested the meaning of the Way, the immeasurable merits, and bestowed the prediction [of Buddhahood] upon the bodhisattvas, causing them to accomplish the right awakening.
[Commentary]

Within the fourth, the speech. "Wishing to proclaim, he manifested a smile": this is the skillful means of beginning the teaching. Below is the correct teaching. Within it, first it says "with all the medicines of Dharma he healed and saved the three sufferings," causing beings to transcend birth-and-death. The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioning: these are the three sufferings. Their meaning is as in the separate chapter; this should be fully discussed. He bestows the teaching and instructs their severance, which is called "medicine and healing." From "he manifested" onward causes beings to enter the Way. Within it, first "he manifested the meaning of the Way" teaches beings to rouse the resolve, manifesting the aspiring mind of the Way which the bodhisattvas have roused, and causing beings to rouse it. "The immeasurable merits" teaches beings to practice. From "bestowing the prediction upon the bodhisattvas" onward finally causes them to attain the fruit. "Bestowing the prediction upon the bodhisattvas" is the means of attaining the fruit; practicing the cause and reaching the fruit is like the mind recording things, and so it is called a "prediction." The Sage's teaching showing it to beings is termed "bestowing." "Causing them to accomplish the right awakening" is the manifest accomplishment of Buddhahood. This concludes the ninth mark.
He displayed the passing into extinction, saving and delivering without limit, eradicating all the outflows, and planting the root of virtue.
[Commentary]

This is the tenth mark, the parinirvana. "He displayed the passing into extinction" is the manifest taking of extinction. Below is the benefit it reveals. "Saving and delivering without limit" reveals the broadness of the benefit. "Eradicating the outflows, etc." reveals the completeness of the benefit. Eradicating all the outflows: because of the manifest extinction, it causes beings to loathe existence and sever the cause of birth-and-death. Planting the root of virtue: because of the manifest extinction, it causes beings to rejoice in stillness and cultivate the cause of nirvana. This concludes the tenth mark.
The above broadly praises the two virtues, the provisional and the real.
Complete in virtue, subtle and hard to measure, he roamed in the various Buddha-lands and universally manifested the teaching of the Way.
[Commentary]

This is the third, the pair that gathers them up. "Complete in virtue, subtle and hard to measure" gathers up the previous real virtue. "He roamed in the various Buddha-lands and universally manifested the teaching of the Way" gathers up the previous provisional virtue. This is the provisional and real virtue.
The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll One, end.

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll Two

inline.s: From here on is the second, praising the merit of benefiting self and benefiting others. Practice that can benefit oneself is called "benefiting self"; practice that can also moisten others is called "benefiting others." The practice of the bodhisattva in essentials does not go beyond these, and so they are praised. Within it, first is a brief praise; from "the bodhisattvas' scriptures" onward is the broad praise.

Their cultivation was pure and without defilement, like a magician displaying many different forms, becoming male or female, with nothing he does not transform. Having clearly learned the original [arts], he does as he wills. These bodhisattvas are likewise: they study all dharmas, penetrating and thoroughly refining them; what they dwell in is peaceful and true, and there is nothing they do not influence. In countless Buddha-lands they are all universally present. Never were they proud or indulgent. Commiserating with beings, they are fully possessed of such dharmas.
[Commentary]

Within the brief [praise], first are the particulars, and afterward the summary. Within the particulars there are four: first, the purity of one's own practice; second, from "like a magician" below is the skillfulness of transformative practice, first with a simile and then the matching. Within the simile, first it says "like a magician": this is the simile for the one who rouses transformation. "Displaying many different forms, becoming male or female, etc." is the simile for the marks of the roused transformation. "Having clearly learned the original [arts], etc." is the simile for the virtue of the roused transformation. "Having clearly learned the original [arts]" is the simile for studying the dharmas of transformation; learning is the basis of transformation, hence it is called "original" (ben). In the Buddha's dharmas of transformation, mastering them well is called "clearly learned." "He does as he wills" means that when learning is accomplished, the function arises; the accomplishment lies in the mind, hence it is called "as he wills." Transforming at will is called "does." Below is the matching that reveals the Dharma. "These bodhisattvas are likewise" matches the previous magician. "They study all dharmas, etc." matches the virtue of the roused transformation. "They study all dharmas" matches the previous "clearly learned," meaning they study all the dharmas of transforming others. "Penetrating and thoroughly refining them" matches "clearly learned": penetrating, mastering, knowing the dharmas thoroughly and fully, hence "thoroughly refining." "What they dwell in is peaceful and true" matches "as he wills": in the dharmas in which they dwell they rest the mind in peace and true contemplation. "There is nothing they do not influence" matches "he does": "nothing" (mi) means there is no; "influence" (zhi) means to convey, so in every place there is nothing they do not convey in transformation. Also, "influence" is their moving the influence [of their teaching], causing all beings to have nothing they do not influence. "In countless Buddha-lands they are all universally present" matches the previous marks of transformation, matching "displaying many forms, becoming male or female, etc." This is the second, the skillfulness of transformative practice. Third, from "never were they proud" below reveals the previous first, the purity of one's own practice: because of what they attained, never were they high and proud in self-indulgence, so their practice is pure. Fourth, from "commiserating" below reveals the previous second, the skillfulness of transformative practice. "Commiserating" is compassion. Having a compassionate heart, commiserating with beings, they are therefore able to display various transformations for beings. The above is the particular praise. "Such dharmas, fully possessed" is the summary that gathers them up. The above is the brief praise.

Below is the broad praise. Within it there are four: first, relying on the bodhisattva dharmas to cultivate the practice belonging to one's own share; second, from "the immeasurable Buddhas altogether protect" below, relying on the Buddha dharmas to cultivate the surpassing advance; third, from "making offerings to the Buddhas" below, relying on the previous own-share to cultivate broadly and realize virtue; fourth, from "receiving and maintaining the Tathagata's deeply profound Dharma-treasury" below, relying on the previous surpassing advance to distinguish and realize virtue.
The bodhisattvas' scriptures: they deeply penetrated the essential and subtle. Their fame reached everywhere, and they guided and governed the ten directions.
[Commentary]

Within the first passage, first is the cultivation of benefiting self, and afterward the arising of benefiting others. "The bodhisattvas' scriptures they deeply penetrated the essential and subtle" is the benefiting of self. In the bodhisattva dharmas they thoroughly penetrated and were unobstructed, attaining their essential aim and knowing their subtle purport, and so it is called "deeply penetrated the essential and subtle." "Their fame reached everywhere and they guided and governed the ten directions" is the benefiting of others.

The immeasurable Buddhas altogether protected and kept them in mind. What the Buddha dwells in, they had all already attained. What the great Sages established, they had all established. The Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim; for the various bodhisattvas they became great teachers. With the profoundly deep meditation and wisdom they opened and guided beings; they penetrated the nature of all dharmas, reached the marks of beings, and were clear about the various lands.
[Commentary]

Within the second passage, it is also first the benefiting of self; from "the Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" below is the benefiting of others. Within the benefiting of self, "the immeasurable Buddhas protected them": the higher virtue draws in the lower; entering the Buddha's realm, they are therefore protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas together. Protecting keeps them from evil; keeping in mind causes them to increase in good. From "what the Buddha dwells in, etc." below is the lower practice following the higher. Within it, first "what the Buddha dwells in, they had all already attained": this is the realization of practice identical with the Buddha. What the Buddha dwells in as Dharma, the bodhisattvas dwell in alike; one may also say the various Buddhas dwell in the Thus-practice, and the bodhisattvas dwell in alike. "What the great Sages established, they had all established": this is the teaching-practice identical with the Buddha. "The great Sages" are the Buddhas; the perfections of the Dharma-realm are what the Buddhas established, and the bodhisattvas established them alike. Below, within the benefiting of others, first is the mark of benefiting others; from "they penetrated the various dharmas" below is the virtue of benefiting others. Within the mark of benefiting others, "the Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" and "became teachers for the bodhisattvas" is the teaching the Dharma benefiting people. "The Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" means their teaching of the Dharma was like the Buddha; "for the various bodhisattvas they became great teachers" means their benefitting people was like the Buddha. Now they practice the Buddha's transformation, and so they became great teachers for the bodhisattvas. Again, "with the profoundly deep meditation and wisdom they opened and guided beings": this is the realization of Dharma benefiting beings, for with the profound meditation and wisdom their transformative practice is like the Buddha. Meditation is stopping and wisdom is contemplation; although the realizations of practice are many, in essentials they do not go beyond these. "Opening and guiding beings" means benefitting people is like the Buddha. Below, within the virtue of benefiting others, it makes clear they possess the three kinds of sovereign-practice, and so they can transform beings. "They penetrated the nature of all dharmas" is the sovereign-practice of the knowledge of right awakening; it means they can penetrate the Dharma-nature of the two truths. "They reached the marks of beings" is the sovereign-practice of the world of beings. "Beings" (zhongsheng) — because of manifold deaths they are called "beings"; many dharmas complete their birth, and so they too are called "beings." Whether form or body, all sorts of marks, they know them all. "They were clear about the various lands" is the sovereign-practice of the world of vessels. The first phrase says "penetrated," the second "reached," the third "clear" — these are words [of the same sense] for left and right [variation]. These three are extensively as stated in other scriptures.

From here on is the third, relying on the previous own-share to cultivate broadly and realize virtue. Within it there are four: first, the skillful means of gathering and cultivating; second, from "also there is nothing done" below, realizing virtue through cultivation; third, from "dwelling in deep concentration" below, again making clear the arising of cultivation; fourth, from "surpassing all the things in the world" below, again making clear the realized fruit.

Within the first there are again four: first, cultivating the benefit of self; second, from "rent and tear" below, making clear the benefit of others; third, from "surpassing" below, again making clear the benefit of self; fourth, from "well establishing" below, again making clear the benefit of others. The first passage, benefiting self, makes clear the cultivation of the teaching-practice. The second, benefiting others, teaches beings to leave their faults. The third, benefiting self, makes clear the cultivation of the realization-practice. The fourth, benefiting others, teaches beings to cultivate good. So there are four distinctions.
Making offerings to the Buddhas, he manifested his body like a flash of lightning. He skillfully learned the net of fearlessness, and understood clearly the dharmas of illusion.
[Commentary]

Within the first, benefiting self: "Making offerings to the Buddhas, he manifested his body like a flash of lightning" makes clear the cultivation of the merit-practice. Making offerings to the Buddhas is a broad production of merit. Manifesting the body like lightning is swiftness in rising to practice; in a single thought the transformed body arrives everywhere, making offerings to the Buddhas. From "he skillfully learned" below makes clear the cultivation of the wisdom-practice. "He skillfully learned fearlessness" is the cultivation of the skillful means of wisdom; "understood clearly the dharmas of illusion" is the accomplishment of the wisdom-practice. Again, learning fearlessness, toward people he is undaunted; understanding clearly the dharmas of illusion, toward dharmas he can discern false from right and take the right, which is called "skillfully learned." Reaching the right and passing beyond the false, he is therefore fearless. With the fearless wisdom he gathers in all the dharmas, and so it is called a "net." One may also say that he learns this to use it to gather in people, and so it is said to be a "net." Seeing clearly that all dharmas are free of the nature of being and nonbeing, like illusion and neither existent nor nonexistent, is called "understood clearly the dharmas of illusion." If a dharma were fixedly existent, it could not be called illusorily existent; if a dharma were fixedly nonexistent, it could not be called illusorily nonexistent. The nonexistent taken as existent is what is called illusorily existent; the existent taken as nonexistent is what is called illusorily nonexistent. The nonexistent taken as existent, then the existent is not existent; the existent taken as nonexistent, then the nonexistent is not nonexistent. The illusory dharma is thus, and so it is taken as a simile; transformation is likewise. The scripture speaks of ten similes, all raising this one. The above is the self-benefit; this concludes the first passage.
He rent and tore the net of Mara, and released all the bonds and ties.
[Commentary]

Next, about benefiting others. "He rent and tore the net of Mara" causes beings to leave false livelihood. "He released all the bonds and ties" causes beings to leave afflictions. "Bonds" (chan) are the ten bonds: lack of shame, lack of remorse, sleepiness, regret, miserliness, jealousy, restlessness, hatred, anger, and concealment — these are its ten. Because they bind beings and bind the mind, they are called "bonds." "Ties" (fu) are the four ties: the tie of desire, the tie of existence, the tie of ignorance, and the tie of views — these are its four. The various bonds of the desire-realm, aside from ignorance and views, are called the tie of desire. In the upper two realms, all the afflictions aside from ignorance and views are called the tie of existence. The ignorance of the three realms is called the tie of ignorance. The views of the three realms are called the tie of views. Because they bind beings and bind the mind, they are called "ties." One may also say that all the various bonds of affliction are in general called bonds and ties. The bodhisattva teaches beings to sever and leave them, which is called "released." This concludes the two passages.
He transcended the ground of the voice-hearers and the pratyekabuddhas, and attained the samadhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
[Commentary]

From here on is the third, again making clear the benefit of self. "He transcended the ground of the voice-hearers and pratyekabuddhas" is the surpassing excellence of what was cultivated. Here it makes clear the name and meaning of "voice-hearer." Generally explained, there are three. First, the teachings spoken by the Tathagata are called "voice"; hearing the voice and awakening to the understanding, so called "voice-hearer." Second, what is called "self, beings, etc." has only a name and no reality, and so it is spoken of as "voice"; as the Shastra on the Stages says: contemplating this understanding, it is by meaning called "hearing." Third, what the Buddha speaks, the great-vehicle Dharma-sound, is called "voice"; with the Buddha-Way's sound he causes all beings to hear, so called "voice-hearer," as explained in the Lotus Sutra. The former two are small vehicle; the last is great vehicle. Now we discuss the small. Its name and meaning being thus, what are its essence and marks? There are two: one is "voice-hearer among voice-hearers," two is "voice-hearer among pratyekabuddhas"; the meaning is as explained above. As to "pratyekabuddha" (solitary awake), its name and meaning are three: first, the twelve-conditioned dharmas are called "conditions" (yuan); contemplating these he awakens, hence "condition-awakened" (pratyekabuddha), as the Sutra of the Twelve Nidanas says. Second, the events of the present world and their interrelated conditions are called "conditions"; by relying on these he awakens, hence "condition-awakened," as the Sutra of the Pratyekabuddha's Attainment of the Way says. Third, the Dharmarealm of the Tathagata-treasury's dependent-arising is called "conditions"; within it awakening from delusion, hence "condition-awakened." Of the three, the former two are small vehicle; the last is great vehicle. Now we discuss the small. Its name and meaning being thus, what are its aspects? There are two: one is "pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas," two is "pratyekabuddha among voice-hearers." The pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas is one who originally sought the Way of pratyekabuddhas, ever delighting in contemplating the twelve-conditioned dharmas, accomplished in the nature of pratyekabuddha; in his last body, not encountering a Buddha's world, he relies on the conditions of present matters and attains the awakening of the Way, and so he is called "pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas."
