If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, coming to be born in my land, do not surely reach the stage of one more birth — apart from their own vows, at liberty to transform themselves freely, for the sake of sentient beings, clad in the armor of the great vows, accumulating roots of virtue, delivering all beings, roaming through the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva practices, making offerings to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions, teaching and transforming countless sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, establishing them in the supreme, right, true Way, surpassing the common course of the stages of practice, and present in practice perfecting the virtue of Samantabhadra — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-third vow: making offerings to the Buddhas.

If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, relying on the Buddha's power, make offerings to the Buddhas — in the space of a single meal not able to go everywhere to immeasurable, countless koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-fourth vow: offerings at will.

If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, before the Buddhas, manifesting the roots of their virtue, find that the offerings they wish to present are not as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-fifth vow: proclaiming the wondrous wisdom.
If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land cannot set forth all-knowledge, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-sixth vow: the nārāyaṇa body.
If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land do not gain the vajra nārāyaṇa body, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-seventh vow: all things adorned and pure.

If I attain buddhahood, and the gods and humans of my land, and all things, are not adorned, pure, and resplendent — of extraordinary form and color, reaching the subtlest and most wondrous, beyond all measure — and if the sentient beings there, even down to gaining the divine eye, can clearly discern and declare their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-eighth vow: the bodhi tree, tall and resplendent.

If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, even those of merely lesser merit, cannot know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi-mandala tree, four hundred million leagues tall, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-ninth vow: reciting the scriptures, gaining wisdom.

If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, receiving and studying the teachings, reciting and upholding and expounding them, do not gain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirtieth vow: eloquence and wisdom without limit.
If I attain buddhahood, and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas of my land could be limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

[Commentary] In the fifth part: the first three vows gather in sentient beings of other lands; the next one gathers in sentient beings of his own land; the next one again gathers in sentient beings of other lands; the last eight again gather in sentient beings of his own land.
The thirty-first vow: reflecting the ten directions.

If I attain buddhahood, and my land, pure and clean, does not reflect all the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as a bright mirror shows one his own face — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-second vow: jeweled fragrance, wondrously adorned.

If I attain buddhahood, and from the ground upward to the sky — palaces, towers, and pavilions; ponds, streams, flowers, and trees; all things of the land — are not entirely formed of immeasurable manifold treasures and a hundred thousand kinds of fragrance, adorned and wondrous, surpassing gods and humans, their fragrance perfuming the worlds of the ten directions, so that bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the Buddha-practice — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
[Commentary] In the sixth part [the vows] gather in the pure land; the text is clear.
The thirty-third vow: receiving light, becoming soft.

If I attain buddhahood, and the sentient beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, touched by my light, are not made soft and gentle in body and mind, surpassing gods and humans — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-fourth vow: hearing the name, gaining forbearance.

If I attain buddhahood, and the sentient beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, do not gain the bodhisattva's patience with the unborn and the deep dhāraṇīs, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-fifth vow: release from the female body.

If I attain buddhahood, and in the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions there are women who, hearing my name, rejoice in faith, rouse the bodhi mind, and loathe the female body, yet at the end of their lives are again born in female form — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-sixth vow: ever cultivating the pure practice.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, do not, after the end of their lives, always cultivate the pure practice until the attainment of the Buddha-way — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-seventh vow: gods and humans pay reverence.

If I attain buddhahood, and the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, prostrate with all five members, bow in reverence, rejoice in faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva practices — yet the gods and humans of the worlds do not all pay them reverence — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-eighth vow: robes as thought.

If I attain buddhahood, and the gods and humans of my land, wishing for robes, have them come at the moment of thought, the Dharma-attired robes praised by the Buddha naturally upon their bodies — if there is any need of sewing, dyeing, washing, or rinsing — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-ninth vow: bliss like that of the destruction of the outflows.
If I attain buddhahood, and the bliss received by the gods and humans of my land is not like that of a monk whose outflows are destroyed, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The fortieth vow: Buddha-lands revealed in the trees.

If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, wishing at will to see the immeasurable, adorned, pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, do not see them all at once, as a bright mirror shows one his own face, within the jeweled trees — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-first vow: all faculties complete.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, are not, even down to the attainment of buddhahood, in faculties unimpaired and entire — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-second vow: pure and liberated.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not all gain the pure liberation samādhi — abiding in that samādhi, in a single arising of thought, offering to immeasurable, inconceivable Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, yet without losing the concentrated mind — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-third vow: hearing the name, gaining merit.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not, at the end of their lives, be born in families of noble rank — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-fourth vow: practicing and perfecting virtue.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not rejoice and leap, cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and perfect the roots of virtue — if it is not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-fifth vow: universal samādhi.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not all gain the universal samādhi — abiding in that samādhi until the attainment of buddhahood, ever seeing the immeasurable, inconceivable, all Buddhas — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-sixth vow: hearing the Dharma according to one's kind.
If I attain buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of my land, according to their vows and wishes, do not naturally hear the Dharma they desire to hear — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-seventh vow: hearing the name, never regressing.
If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not straightway attain non-regression — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-eighth vow: gaining the three dharma-forbearances.

If I attain buddhahood, and the multitudes of bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands of other directions, hearing my name, do not straightway attain the first forbearance, the second and third dharma-forbearances, and do not straightway attain non-regression with respect to the Dharmas of the Buddhas — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

[Commentary] In the seventh part: the first five gather in sentient beings of other lands; three gather in sentient beings of his own land; the next five again gather in sentient beings of other lands; the next one again gathers in sentient beings of his own land; the last two again gather in sentient beings of other lands.
This third part is complete.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "At that time, when the monk Dharmākara had proclaimed these vows, he uttered verses."

From here down is the fourth [part]: in accordance with the vows made above he pledges himself. Within it there are eleven verses in all. The first ten verses make the pledge to himself; the last one requests attestation. Among the first ten, the first three pledge themselves; the last seven seek in accord.
I establish the vow that surpasses the world
to surely reach the supreme Way. If this vow is not fulfilled, I swear not to attain perfect enlightenment.
I for immeasurable kalpas
will be the great giver, universally rescuing all the poor and distressed. If I do not, I swear not to attain perfect enlightenment.
When I attain the Buddha-way
my fame shall surpass the ten directions; if in the end there are those who do not hear it, I swear not to attain perfect enlightenment.

[Commentary] Within the first pledge of self, the first verse pledges himself in the Buddha's own virtue. In what was vowed above, seeking the Dharma-body vow and seeking the pure-land vow is called "the vow that surpasses the world." To rouse the mind is called to establish. The fruit is assured, hence "surely reach the supreme Way"; this is spoken in accord. "If this vow is not fulfilled, I swear not to attain [enlightenment]" is the pledge to himself. The last two verses pledge himself in the virtue of converting beings. The first of these sets forth the Buddha's teaching and yielding benefit and pledges himself; the last sets forth the Buddha's universal fame and pledges himself in the virtue of universal conversion. "Not" is like "none." When I become Buddha my name shall be heard in the ten directions; if there are any who to the end never hear my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Free from desire, deep in right mindfulness, with pure wisdom practicing the pure life,
seeking the supreme, most honored one, to be the teacher of gods and humans.
With divine power setting forth great light,
universally illumining the boundless lands, dispelling the darkness of the three stains, brightly rescuing all from distress.
Opening the eye of wisdom for them,
extinguishing this blindness of darkness, closing off the evil paths, and opening the gate of the happy course.
The merit of merit grows to fullness,
majesty and light shining through the ten directions; the sun and moon gather in their radiance, and the light of heaven withdraws and shows not.
Opening the treasury of Dharma for the multitudes,
widely bestowing the treasure of merit; ever amid the great assemblies, preaching the Dharma with a lion's roar.
Making offerings to all the Buddhas,
perfecting all the roots of virtue; vow and wisdom both fulfilled, I will be the hero of the three realms.
Like the Buddha's immeasurable wisdom,
that reaches all things and illumines all — may my merit and power equal this most supreme, honored one.

[Commentary] Within the seeking in accord, the first verse is an abbreviation. "Free from desire, deep in right mindfulness, with pure wisdom practicing the pure life" sets forth his own good causes; below, by it he seeks the fruit — seeking the supreme Way, seeking the Buddha's own virtue; "to be the teacher of gods and humans" seeks the virtue of benefiting others. The remaining six verses are the fuller exposition. Within it the first five and a half verses broadly set forth the Buddha's virtue; the last half verse makes the vow to be like it. Among the virtue set forth above, the first two verses set forth the Buddha's virtue of conversion; the next one verse sets forth the Buddha's own virtue; the next one verse again sets forth the virtue of conversion; the last one and a half verses again set forth his own virtue. Within the two verses of the virtue of conversion, "with divine power setting forth great light, universally illumining the boundless lands" is the conversion through the body; from "dispelling" onward is the conversion through speech. "Dispelling the three stains, rescuing from distress" is the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, converting to sever the three poisons — hence called dispelling the three stains. "Opening the eye of wisdom, extinguishing the blind darkness" is the conversion of the Greater Vehicle. "Closing off the evil paths, opening the gate of the happy course" is the conversion of gods and humans. The verse on merit sets forth the Buddha's own virtue: "The merit of merit grows to fullness" is the fullness and vastness of the Buddha's virtue — the fruits of merit and blessing all come to fullness. "Majesty and light shining" and the rest are the function of the Buddha's virtue, and he briefly mentions the function of light, leaving the rest unspoken. "Shining through the ten directions" is the breadth of the light; "the sun and moon gather in their radiance, the light of heaven shows not" is the excellence of the light — the Buddha's light eclipses them, and sun and moon draw in their light, unable to shine outward, hence "gathering in their radiance." The verse on the multitudes again sets forth the virtue of conversion; the text is clear. The last one and a half verses again set forth his own virtue. The first verse shows the Buddha's causes fulfilled and the fruit attained: "Making offerings to all the Buddhas, perfecting all the roots of virtue" shows the cause of merit fulfilled; "vow and wisdom all fulfilled" shows the cause of wisdom fulfilled; "to be the hero of the three realms" shows the cause attaining the fruit. Below, half a verse reveals the freedom of function: the Buddha's unimpeded wisdom reaches and illumines everything. The section above broadly sets forth the Buddha's virtue. "May my merit and wisdom equal this supreme one" makes the vow to be like it. "Merit" is the cause of blessing; "wisdom" is the cause of knowledge. "May I, by the power of this merit and wisdom, equal the Buddha Tathāgata, the most supreme, honored one." The ten verses above pledge themselves.
If this vow yields its fruit,
let the great-thousand world be moved; let the gods in the sky rain down rare, exquisite flowers.
[Commentary] This one verse requests the auspicious sign of attestation: if the fruit is surely attained, the great-thousand world should move and the sky rain down exquisite flowers.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "When the monk Dharmākara had delivered this verse, at once the whole earth shook in six kinds of motion, heaven rained down exquisite flowers, scattering them above him, and music sounded of itself. A voice in the sky praised, saying, “Surely he will attain supreme, right enlightenment.”"

[Commentary] In the fifth [part], as the vow is made the token appears: when Dharmākara had spoken, at once the earth moved, responding to the pledge asked for above; the rain of flowers scattered above responded to the later pledge; from "of itself" onward a voice emerged recording the praise.
Thereupon the monk Dharmākara fully cultivated and fulfilled such great vows, truly and without falsehood, surpassing the world, deeply delighting in the stilling of all conditioning.
[Commentary] The sixth [part] sums up with praise. First he concludes; from "surpassing" onward he praises.
Above, the vows have been set forth.

Next, the practice is set forth. Within it there are two: first, the full cultivation; second, from "according to the place of birth" onward, the surpassing excellence of the retribution. Within the first there are again two: first, the practice of the pure land; second, from "not giving rise to the thought of desire" onward, the practice of the Dharma body.

Ānanda, the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of that Buddha, amid the assemblies of gods, māras, brahmās, dragons, spirits, and the eight classes, made this great vow. Having established this vow, he single-mindedly applied himself to adorning the wonderful land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was vast and broad, surpassing and alone in its excellence, established abiding from the beginning, without decay or change, and in inconceivable, immeasurable eons he planted the immeasurable virtues of a bodhisattva.

[Commentary] Within the practice of the pure land: "that monk, in the presence of that Buddha, amid the assemblies, made this great vow, having established this vow" ties up the preceding and gives rise to the following — it takes up the vow-mind above and gives rise to the practice below. Dragons, spirits, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so on are the eight classes. "He made this great vow" takes up the forty-eight vows made above and gives rise to what follows. "Having established this vow" takes up "I establish the vow that surpasses the world" and the rest and gives rise to what follows. Below he sets forth the practice: "single-mindedly applying himself to adorning the wonderful land" is the general description of taking up the practice. From "the Buddha-land he cultivated" onward he sets forth the practice specifically. Within the specific exposition he first points to the fruit of the pure land, then from "inconceivable" onward he cultivates the cause in response to it. In pointing to the fruit above, "the Buddha-land he cultivated, vast and broad" shows the breadth of the land; "surpassing and alone in its excellence" shows its excellence; "established abiding from the beginning, without decay or change" shows its constancy. The cultivation of the cause is likewise understood.

Within the practice of the Dharma body: first the separate parts, then the general. Within the separate parts there are four: first, leaving the afflictions; second, from "fearless" onward, cultivating the wholesome Dharmas; third, from "far from" onward, leaving the evil deeds; fourth, from "abandoning the kingdom" onward, again cultivating the wholesome.

He gave rise to no thoughts of desire, no thoughts of anger, no thoughts of harm. He did not arouse perceptions of desire, perceptions of anger, perceptions of harm. He was unattached to forms, sounds, odors, flavors, tangibles, and mental objects. The power of patience was perfected in him. He took no account of the many sufferings. He was of few desires and content. He was free of defilement, anger, and delusion. His samadhi was ever still. His wisdom was unobstructed. He had no mind of falsity, flattery, or crookedness. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he anticipated others' thoughts and asked after them.

[Commentary] In the [section on] freedom from affliction, first, with respect to practice for his own benefit, it explains freedom from affliction; from “He had no falsity...” onward, with respect to practice for the benefit of others, it explains freedom from affliction. In the former, practice for his own benefit, the text has four turns. First, it explains the causes and conditions of affliction. Second, from “the power of patience” onward, it explains the cultivation of antidotes. Third, from “free of defilement” onward, it [sets forth] the very substance of freedom from affliction. Fourth, from “his samadhi” onward, it again explains cultivation as remedy. In the first passage, first [it shows] freedom from the causes of delusion; “unattached to forms” and the rest explains freedom from the conditions of delusion. In the former, freedom from causes, “he gave rise to no thoughts of desire, anger, or harm” directly explains what is abandoned. There are eight kinds of “thought,” as the Sutra of the Bodhisattva Stages explains. The first is the thought of desire: thinking of wealth and thinking of sensual form. The second is the thought of anger, also called the thought of ire: thinking of what one desires and being angry at others. The third is the thought of harm, also called the thought of vexation: intending to injure others. The fourth is the thought of kin: recalling one's relatives. The fifth is the thought of country: thinking of the world's safety or peril. The sixth is the thought of deathlessness: that the body will not die, and so amassing possessions widely. The seventh is the thought of clan: thinking of the high or low standing of families. The eighth is the thought of contempt: thinking of lording it over others. Among these eight, the first three are the gravest faults, and so they alone are singled out; “he did not arouse perceptions of desire or anger” again displays them. Not arousing the perception of desire is called freedom from the thought of desire; not arousing the perception of anger is called freedom from the thought of anger; not arousing the perception of harm is called freedom from the thought of harm. One may also say that the former words, “he did not give rise to the three thoughts,” reveal abandonment at the outset, while “he did not arouse the perceptions of desire, anger, and harm” makes clear abandonment at the end. Before one faces an object, evil thinking arising in advance is called a “thought”; when the mind arises in response to conditions, it is called the three “perceptions.” All of these he abandoned. Next, freedom from the conditions of delusion: “unattached to forms, sounds, odors, flavors, tangibles, and so on.” Here the first passage is finished. Next it explains cultivation as remedy: “the power of patience was perfected; he took no account of the many sufferings.” Because he could patiently endure adverse conditions, he was free of the three thoughts and did not arouse the three perceptions; “of few desires and content,” he could patiently endure favorable conditions, and so was free of forms, sounds, odors, flavors, tangibles, and so on. These two passages are finished. Next, the substance of freedom from delusion: “free of defilement, anger, and delusion” — “defilement” is the same as greed. These three passages are finished. Below, cultivation as remedy again: “his samadhi was ever still” shows the practice of calming to be profound; “his wisdom was unobstructed” shows the practice of insight to be supreme. The above four passages together form the practice for his own benefit. Below, with respect to benefiting others, it explains freedom from affliction. “He had no mind of falsity, flattery, or crookedness” explains freedom from faults of mind; “with a gentle countenance” explains freedom from faults of body; “loving words” and “asking after them” explain freedom from faults of speech. Because he was free of affliction, no fault arose in body, speech, or mind. The above is the first, explaining freedom from affliction.

He was brave and diligent, and his aspiration and vow never wearied. He sought single-mindedly the pure Dharma, that he might benefit the multitudes of beings with kindness. He reverently served the Three Jewels and honored and served his teachers. With great adornment he fulfilled all practices, causing all beings to perfect their merits. He dwelt in the Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in non-activity and non-arising, contemplating all dharmas as magical illusions.

[Commentary] The second explains his cultivation of good. Within it there are three: first, the arousing of the vow-mind; second, from “reverently” onward, engaging in practice in reliance on the vow; third, from “he dwelt in emptiness” onward, the practice accomplished and entering realization. In the first, the arousing of the vow, “brave and diligent, his aspiration and vow never wearied, seeking the pure Dharma” is the vow for his own benefit; “benefiting the multitudes of beings with kindness” is the vow for the benefit of others. In the second, on practice, first it explains his own benefit and afterward the benefit of others. In the former, “reverently serving the Three Jewels and honoring and serving his teachers” are the expedients that gather in practice: revering the Three Jewels is the expedient that gathers merit, and serving teachers is the expedient that gathers wisdom. “With great adornment” and so on reveals the accomplishment of practice. “With great adornment” means that he adorned himself with the two adornments of merit and wisdom. “Fulfilling all practices” distinguishes them one by one: that is, fulfilling all practices, beginning with giving and the rest. Below it explains benefiting others: by practice he taught others, and so caused beings to perfect their merits. In the third, on realization, “he dwelt in the Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in non-activity and non-arising.” That all dharmas are non-existent, that persons and dharmas have no own-nature, is called emptiness. That the marks of the provisional person and the provisional dharma likewise do not exist is called signlessness. Within these two, to have no mind of seeking, longing, or delighting is called wishlessness; to be free of false thinking is likewise called wishlessness. Within these three, to have no fruit to be produced is called non-activity. Hence the Vimalakirti [Sutra] says: “Though he practices non-activity, he manifests the receiving of a body.” Thus we know that non-activity is discussed with respect to the fruit. Within the former three, to have no cause to be produced is called non-arising. Hence the Vimalakirti [Sutra] says: “Though he practices non-arising, he performs good practices.” Thus we know that non-arising is stated with respect to the cause. Yet among the sutras the exposition of principle is not fixed. Some speak of one emptiness, such as the “solitary emptiness” spoken of in the Great Perfection of Wisdom [Sutra]: since it sets forth one and not many, it is called solitary. Some speak of two kinds, namely the two kinds of non-self. Some speak of three: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Some speak of four, as the Vimalakirti says: emptiness, non-activity, signlessness, and non-arising. The Great Perfection of Wisdom also speaks of the emptiness of existent dharmas, the emptiness of non-existent dharmas, the emptiness of own dharmas, and the emptiness of transformed dharmas; these too are four, and they are explained at length in a separate chapter. Some speak of five, as here: emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-activity, and non-arising, fully as explained above. Some speak of seven emptinesses, as the Great Perfection of Wisdom says. Some speak of nine emptinesses, as the Abhidharma says. Some speak of eleven, as the Nirvana [Sutra] says. Some speak of fourteen, as the Great Perfection of Wisdom says. Some speak of eighteen, as the Great Perfection of Wisdom says. Some speak of twenty-five emptinesses, as the Nirvana [Sutra] says. Broadly there are measureless [divisions], but now, taking one approach, only five are stated. To realize this principle and Dharma and be united with it is called “contemplating all dharmas as magical illusions”; the realized Dharma is not nothing. Here the second is finished.
He kept far from coarse speech, which harms oneself, harms others, and harms both together; he cultivated good speech, which benefits oneself, benefits others, and benefits both self and others.

[Commentary] The third explains freedom from evil karma. Within it, first it explains freedom from faults, and from “cultivating good speech” onward it reveals the remedies that gather them in. In the former, freedom from faults, “keeping far from coarse speech” explains freedom from the evil of speech, and “keeping far from harming oneself, harming others, and harming both” explains freedom from the evil of the body. In the remedies below, “cultivating good speech” remedies the former evil of speech, and “benefiting oneself and benefiting others, benefiting both others and oneself” remedies the former evil of the body. Here the third is finished.
He abandoned his kingdom and gave up the throne, cut off wealth and sensual desire, practiced the six paramitas himself, and taught others to practice them.

[Commentary] The fourth again explains the cultivation of good. Within it, first it explains his own benefit: “he abandoned his kingdom and gave up the throne, cut off wealth and sensual desire” shows what he renounced, and “he practiced the six paramitas himself” reveals what he cultivated. Below it explains benefiting others: with the former six paramitas he taught others to practice them.
The above four passages separately explain the causes of the body.
For countless kalpas he accumulated merit and gathered virtue.
This gathers it up in conclusion. The above is the first [section], explaining the completeness of his cultivation.

Wherever he was born, according to the wish of his mind, measureless treasuries of jewels spontaneously appeared in response. He taught, converted, and established countless beings in the unsurpassed, true, and right Way. Sometimes he was a wealthy elder, a householder, or one of noble and honored lineage; sometimes a kshatriya king or a holy wheel-turning sovereign; sometimes the lord of the six heavens of desire, or even a Brahma king. Always with the four offerings he made offerings to and reverenced all Buddhas. Such merits cannot be told. The breath of his mouth was fragrant and pure as the utpala flower; from every pore of his body came the scent of sandalwood, and that fragrance perfumed measureless worlds. His countenance was upright and fair, his marks and features surpassing and wondrous. From his hands ever issued inexhaustible treasures: clothing and food, precious and wondrous flowers and incense, silk canopies, banners, and pennants, and all the implements of adornment. Such things as these surpassed those of all devas and humans. In all dharmas he attained sovereign freedom.

[Commentary] The second shows the excellence of his reward. Within it there are two: first, with respect to the causes of the Pure Land that he cultivated above, it explains the excellence of the reward obtained, that is, the excellent dependent fruit; second, from “Sometimes he was a wealthy elder or householder” onward, with respect to the causes of the dharma-body that he cultivated above, it explains the excellence of the reward obtained, the excellent direct fruit. In the former, the first words, “wherever he was born, according to the wish of his mind, measureless treasuries of jewels spontaneously appeared in response,” show that he himself obtained excellent wealth; “being” here means “at liberty.” “He taught, converted, and established [beings] in the right Way”: by wealth he gathered others in and caused them to take refuge in the true Dharma. In the latter, first it explains the fruit of merit, and then “in all dharmas he attained sovereign freedom” explains the fruit of wisdom. In the fruit of merit, first the particulars and afterward the conclusion. In the particulars there are four: first, the reward of his body is exalted; second, from “always with the four offerings he made offerings” onward, relying on the body he engaged in practice; third, from “the breath of his mouth” onward, the reward of his body is subtle and wondrous, in which there are three phrases whose sense is evident from the text; fourth, from “from his hands issued” onward, relying on the body he engaged in the functions of practice, his hands issuing offerings with which he made offerings to all Buddhas. The above particulars are finished. “Such things as these surpassed all devas and humans” concludes and praises it in general. The fruit of wisdom is evident.
The above explains what he practiced.
The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, Fascicle Three, End.

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, Fascicle Four

inline.s: From here the second [part] explains what he accomplished, namely the accomplishment of the fruits of the dharma-body and the Pure Land. Yet this accomplishment corresponds to the forty-eight great vows above and should be matched to them one by one; this is evident from the text. Within the text there are two: first, a brief explanation of what was accomplished; second, from “The Buddha told Ānanda: The majestic spirit of Amitabha Buddha...” onward, a broad explanation of what was accomplished.

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Has the bodhisattva Dharmakara already attained Buddhahood and passed into extinction, or has he not yet attained Buddhahood, or is he now present?” The Buddha told Ānanda: “The bodhisattva Dharmakara has now attained Buddhahood. He is present in the west, a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands away from here, and his Buddha-world is named the Land of Peace and Bliss.” Ānanda asked again: “How long has it been since that Buddha attained the Way?” The Buddha said: “Since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed in all. The land of that Buddha is naturally of the seven treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, mother-of-pearl, and carnelian — combined to form its ground. It is vast and boundless, beyond all limit, all intermingled and mutually alternating, blazing and radiant, subtle and wondrously beautiful, pure and adorned, surpassing the finest of all the treasures in the worlds of the ten directions; those treasures are like the treasures of the sixth heaven. Moreover, in that land there is no Mount Sumeru, nor any of the encircling adamantine mountains, nor great seas, small seas, streams, channels, wells, or valleys. By the Buddha's spiritual power, they are seen when he wishes them to be seen. There are no difficult destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals. There are no four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter; it is neither cold nor hot, but always gentle and agreeable.” At that time Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if that land has no Mount Sumeru, on what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trayastrimsa heaven rely to dwell?” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “On what do the third heaven, the Yama, and even the Akanishtha heaven rely to dwell?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “The karmic reward of their actions is inconceivable.” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The karmic reward of actions is inconceivable, and the Buddha-worlds are likewise inconceivable. The merit and power of goodness of those beings dwell on the ground of their actions, and so it is thus.” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “I do not doubt this Dharma, but for the sake of beings in the future, wishing to remove their doubts, I asked this meaning.”

[Commentary] Within the brief [explanation] there are four. First, Ānanda asks with respect to the body whether he has already attained Buddhahood, and the Tathagata answers fully. Second, from “his Buddha-world” onward, it takes up the body to explain the land. Third, from “he asked again” onward, Ānanda again asks with respect to the body how long it has been since he attained [Buddhahood], and the Tathagata answers fully. Fourth, from “the land of that Buddha is naturally of the seven treasures” onward, it takes that up to explain the land. In the first passage, Ānanda first asks whether the bhiksu Dharmakara has already attained Buddhahood, has not yet, or is now present: he asks with respect to the distinction of the three times. The Buddha's answer is evident. In the second passage, it directly sets out the name of that Buddha-land but does not yet explain its characteristics. In the third passage, first the question and then the answer; the text makes both evident. In the fourth passage, first it explains what exists; from “moreover, in that land there is no Mount Sumeru” onward, it reveals what does not exist. In explaining what exists, “naturally formed of treasures” explains its substance, “vast and boundless” explains its measure, and “all intermingled” and so on explains its adornments. In explaining what does not exist, first it directly sets it forth, and from “Ānanda said” onward question and answer reveal it again. In the former direct statement, first there are no mountains and so on, next no four [evil] destinies, and last no distinction of the four seasons, spring and autumn and the rest. In the latter re-revelation, the text has three parts: first Ānanda asks, “If there is no Mount Sumeru, on what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the rest rely to dwell?” and the Tathagata questions him in return; second, Ānanda answers directly, and the Tathagata takes that up to reveal that matter; third, Ānanda makes clear that he asked for others' sake, not from his own ignorance. The above brief [explanation] is finished.

In the broad [explanation] below, the text has four parts: first, it explains the Buddha's body; second, taking up the body, it explains his followers; third, it explains the land; fourth, taking up the land, it explains its people.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The majestic spiritual light of Amitabha Buddha is supreme and foremost; the light of no other Buddha can match it. Some Buddhas' light illumines a hundred Buddha-worlds, some a thousand Buddha-worlds; to speak concisely, it illumines Buddha-lands in the east as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it is likewise so. Some Buddhas' light shines for seven feet, some for one yojana, two, three, four, or five yojanas, and so doubling onward, until it illumines one Buddha-land. Therefore Amitabha Buddha is named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Peerless Light, the Buddha of the Blazing King of Light, the Buddha of Pure Light, the Buddha of Joyful Light, the Buddha of the Light of Wisdom, the Buddha of Uninterrupted Light, the Buddha of Inconceivable Light, the Buddha of Ineffable Light, and the Buddha of Light Outshining the Sun and Moon. Whatever beings encounter this light have their three defilements extinguished; body and mind become gentle; they rejoice and leap for joy, and a good mind arises in them. If they are in the three evil paths, in places of utmost suffering, and see this light, they all find repose and are free of affliction. After the end of life they all attain deliverance. The light of Amitabha Buddha is bright and glorious, shining upon the ten directions, and there is no Buddha-land where it is not heard of. Not only do I now praise his light; all Buddhas, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and hosts of bodhisattvas likewise together praise it in the same way. If any beings hear of the majestic virtue of his light and day and night proclaim it with an undivided mind, then according to their wish they will be born in that land, and will be together praised by the hosts of bodhisattvas and sravakas, who will acclaim their merits. When they afterward attain the Buddha Way, they will universally be praised for their light by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, even as [Amitabha is] now.” The Buddha said: “If I were to speak of the majestic light of Amitabha Buddha, so lofty and wondrous, for a day and night throughout a kalpa, I still could not exhaust it.” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Moreover, the lifespan of Amitabha Buddha is long and beyond reckoning. Do you know? Suppose that measureless beings in the worlds of the ten directions all obtained human bodies and were all made into sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, and all gathered together in one assembly, meditating with single minds; exhausting their powers of intellect, for a hundred thousand million kalpas they all together calculated and reckoned the length of that lifespan: they could not exhaust it or know its limit.”

[Commentary] In the first passage, one should first explain the meaning of the three bodies of a Buddha and then explain the text; the meaning is as in a separate chapter. In the text, first it explains the marks of the Buddha's light and afterward reveals his lifespan. In the former, on the light, it marvels and praises in order to reveal it: first the particulars and then the conclusion. In the particulars there are four: first, Śākyamuni's own praise; second, from “whatever beings encounter this light” onward, it explains the benefit of seeing and hearing for beings; third, from “the light of Amitabha is bright and glorious” onward, the holy ones praise it together; fourth, from “if any beings hear of his light” onward, it again explains the benefit of seeing and hearing for beings. In the first there are three: first, it distinguishes the surpassing from the inferior, that the light of Amitabha Buddha is foremost; second, from “the light of no other Buddha can match it” onward, it raises the inferior to reveal the surpassing — the Buddhas' light is in truth equal, and it is so only in accordance with their teaching activity; third, from “therefore” onward, it praises and reveals his supremacy. There are twelve phrases. First, Immeasurable Light, Boundless, and Unobstructed: these three praise him by his own characteristics. Immeasurable means much, boundless means vast, unobstructed means free. Peerless and Blazing King: these two convey his supremacy — since no other light can match it, he is called Peerless Light, and since this light surpasses all others, he is called the Blazing King of Light. Pure, Joyful, Wisdom, and Uninterrupted: these four praise him by his own characteristics. Freedom from defilement is called pure; being able to make those who see him delight in their minds is called joyful; shining well upon the Dharma is called the Light of Wisdom; shining without cease is called Uninterrupted Light. Inconceivable, Ineffable, and Outshining the Sun and Moon: these three convey his supremacy by contrast. Because it transcends the mind's conceptions of the world, it is called inconceivable; because it transcends the world's words, it is called ineffable; because it transcends the world's forms, it is called outshining the sun and moon. The above is the first, Śākyamuni's own praise. From here the second, the benefit of seeing and hearing: first, “those who encounter it have their three defilements extinguished” explains the benefit of removing obstructions — the three poisons are here called the three defilements. “Body and mind become gentle” and so on explains the benefit of producing good. From “if they are in the three [evil paths]” onward, it explains the benefit of extinguishing suffering; from “after the end of life” onward, it explains the benefit of obtaining bliss. The third, the common praise, is evident from the text. In the fourth, which again explains the benefit, first it explains proclaiming it and being reborn according to one's wish; next, being together praised by all the holy ones; last, it explains that when one attains Buddhahood all [Buddhas] praise one together. The above is the separate praise. From “The Buddha said: If I were to speak of the light of Amitabha Buddha” onward, it concludes the praise in general. The above explains the light; below it explains the Buddha's lifespan, which is evident from the text. The above is the first, explaining his Buddha-body.

The host of sravakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans: the length of their lifespans is likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning or simile. Moreover, the sravakas and bodhisattvas are so numerous that they cannot be measured or told; their spiritual wisdom penetrates all, and their majestic power is sovereign: they can hold all worlds in the palm of the hand. The Buddha said to Ānanda: “At that Buddha's first assembly, the number of sravakas could not be counted, and of bodhisattvas likewise. Were there those like Mahamaudgalyayana, a hundred thousand million billion, measureless and countless, who for asamkhya nayuta kalpas, until [the Buddha's] extinction, all together calculated and reckoned, they could not determine how many there were. Suppose the great sea, deep and vast and measureless. If someone were to split one of its hairs into a hundred parts, and with one part of a hair dip up a single drop, what do you think? Is the water he dips up, compared with that great sea, which is more?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “The water he dips up, compared with the great sea: the measure of how much it is, is not something that clever reckoning, calculation, words, or similes can know.” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Those like Maudgalyayana, for a hundred thousand million nayuta kalpas, reckoning the sravakas and bodhisattvas of that first assembly: the number they know is only like a single drop, and what they do not know is like the water of the great sea.”

[Commentary] The second, taking up the body, explains the multitude. Within it there are four: first, it explains that the people of that land have long lifespans, like [that of] Amitabha; second, from “moreover, the sravakas” onward, it explains their great number; third, from “their spiritual wisdom penetrates” onward, it reveals the excellence of their virtues; fourth, it again reveals their great number, and for the moment reveals the marks of their multitude only in the first assembly, the rest being beyond discussion. The marks of their number cannot be fully described, and so it is revealed through Maudgalyayana's not knowing. Within this, first it explains Maudgalyayana's not knowing; from “Suppose the great sea” onward, it borrows a matter to reveal it: the Buddha first sets up a simile and questions Ānanda in return, next Ānanda answers, and then the Buddha takes that up to reveal how much Maudgalyayana knows and how much he does not.

[Commentary] From here the third explains the land. In this one should first understand the meaning of the Pure Land and then explain the text; the meaning is as in a separate chapter. In the text it speaks generally: there are three adornments. The first is the adornment of things: forms, fragrances, flavors, and the other five desires are exquisite and supreme. The second is the adornment of Dharma: it treats purely of the wondrous Dharma. The third is the adornment of persons: excellent and good beings dwell therein. In what is explained here, within the excellence of the land, there are the adornment of things and the adornment of Dharma; the fourth section below, on the excellence of the people, is the adornment of persons. Yet the wondrous adornments of that land cannot be fully described, and so in this text four matters are briefly raised: first, it explains the jeweled trees; second, it explains the music; third, it explains the lecture halls, palaces, and the like; fourth, it explains the jeweled pools.

Moreover, in that land there are trees of the seven treasures, filling the world all around: trees of gold, trees of silver, trees of lapis lazuli, trees of beryl, trees of coral, trees of carnelian, and trees of mother-of-pearl. Some are made of two treasures, three treasures, or up to seven treasures, combined together in turn. Some golden trees have silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; some silver trees have leaves, flowers, and fruits of gold. Some lapis lazuli trees have beryl for leaves, and flowers and fruits likewise; some beryl trees have lapis lazuli for leaves, and flowers and fruits likewise; some coral trees have carnelian for leaves, and flowers and fruits likewise; some carnelian trees have lapis lazuli for leaves, and flowers and fruits likewise; some mother-of-pearl trees have all treasures for leaves, and flowers and fruits likewise. Some jeweled trees have purple gold for root, white silver for stem, lapis lazuli for branches, crystal for twigs, coral for leaves, carnelian for flowers, and mother-of-pearl for fruit. Some jeweled trees have white silver for root, lapis lazuli for stem, crystal for branches, coral for twigs, carnelian for leaves, mother-of-pearl for flowers, and purple gold for fruit. Some jeweled trees have lapis lazuli for root, crystal for stem, coral for branches, carnelian for twigs, mother-of-pearl for leaves, purple gold for flowers, and white silver for fruit. Some jeweled trees have crystal for root, coral for stem, carnelian for branches, mother-of-pearl for twigs, purple gold for leaves, white silver for flowers, and lapis lazuli for fruit. Some jeweled trees have coral for root, carnelian for stem, mother-of-pearl for branches, purple gold for twigs, white silver for leaves, lapis lazuli for flowers, and crystal for fruit. Some jeweled trees have carnelian for root, mother-of-pearl for stem, purple gold for branches, white silver for twigs, lapis lazuli for leaves, crystal for flowers, and coral for fruit. Some jeweled trees have mother-of-pearl for root, purple gold for stem, white silver for branches, lapis lazuli for twigs, crystal for leaves, coral for flowers, and carnelian for fruit. Row matches row, stem faces stem, branch aligns with branch, leaf turns to leaf, flower follows flower, fruit meets fruit. Their purple radiance dazzles the eye beyond bearing. When a pure breeze rises, it gives forth the five tones, and subtly the notes gong and shang harmonize of themselves. Moreover, the tree of the place of enlightenment of Amitabha Buddha is four million li tall; its trunk is five thousand yojanas around, and its branches and leaves spread out for two hundred thousand li. It is naturally formed of all precious treasures, and is adorned with the moon-light mani and the sea-holding wheel-jewel, king of all treasures. Around it, among the twigs, hang jeweled garlands; a hundred thousand million colors, manifold and ever-changing; measureless light and flame shine without limit; exquisite jeweled nets spread over it, and all adornments appear according to what is fitting. A gentle breeze slowly stirs and blows upon the jeweled trees, giving forth measureless wondrous sounds of Dharma. These sounds spread abroad throughout all Buddha-lands. Those who hear them attain the deep acceptance of the Dharma and dwell in non-retrogression until they attain the Buddha Way; their ear-faculties are clear and pure, and they meet with no affliction. Eyes see its color, nose knows its fragrance, mouth tastes its flavor, body touches its light, and mind takes the Dharma as its object: all attain the profoundly deep acceptance of the Dharma, dwell in non-retrogression until they attain the Buddha Way, their six faculties clear and pure, free of all afflictions. Ānanda, if the devas and humans of that land see these trees, they attain three acceptances of the Dharma: the first is the acceptance of sound; the second is the acceptance of gentle compliance; the third is the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. All this is by the power of the majestic spirit of Amitabha Buddha, by the power of his original vows: his fulfilled vows, his clear vows, his firm vows, his ultimate vows. The Buddha told Ānanda: “The kings of the world have a hundred thousand kinds of music; from the holy wheel-turning king up to the sixth heaven, the sounds of their music surpass one another by a thousand million billion times. Yet the ten thousand kinds of music in the sixth heaven do not equal a single sound from one of the seven-jeweled trees of the land of Immeasurable Life by a thousand million times.”

[Commentary] Within [the section on] trees, first it generally explains the trees; second it separately explains the tree of the place of enlightenment; third it compares them all together to reveal their excellence. In the former general explanation, first it lists the trees and afterward explains their issuing of sounds. In listing the trees, “the jeweled trees of that land fill the world all around” states it in general; “trees of gold and silver” and so on explains trees of pure treasure; from “some are made of two treasures” onward, it explains trees of mixed treasures. As for the sounds they issue, “giving forth the five tones” means the five tones known as gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu. In the second, on the tree of the place of enlightenment, first it explains the tree's characteristics, next it explains its issuing of sound, and below it explains the benefit of seeing and hearing for beings. In the former, on the tree, first it explains its measure, that it is four million li tall; “naturally formed of all precious treasures” explains its substance; “with the moon-light mani” and so on explains its adornment. The issuing of sound is evident. In explaining the benefit of seeing and hearing, first it explains that the six faculties, in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, all obtain benefit; below it explains the differences among the acceptances attained. The devas and humans of that land all attain the three acceptances: this states it in general. When the wisdom-mind settles upon the Dharma, this is called acceptance; acceptance is divided into three according to depth. Next it lists the three names: following the sound and awakening to understanding, knowing sound to be like an echo, is called the acceptance of sound, [for those] up to and including the third ground; abandoning verbal exposition and tending to the real is called the acceptance of gentle compliance, the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds; realizing the real and transcending marks is called the acceptance of non-arising, from the seventh ground upward. Below it explains the cause by which beings attain these acceptances. “All by the majestic spirit of Amitabha” means that by the present majestic power of that Tathagata they obtain the three acceptances; “the power of his original vows” and so on means that by the power of his past original vows they obtain the three acceptances. The original vow is the general; the other four are the particulars. “Fulfilled vows” means his vow-mind was complete; “clear vows” means his seeking mind was manifest; “firm vows” means conditions could not destroy them; “ultimate vows” means in the end he accomplished non-retrogression. By these vows, those born in that land all attain the three acceptances. Previously it explained the trees, next it separately explained the tree of the place of enlightenment, and below it comprehensively measures them to reveal their excellence, particularly revealing the excellence of the sounds among the trees. The text makes this evident. The above explains the trees.

There is also music of ten thousand kinds, arising of itself; and its sounds are none but Dharma-sounds — clear and flowing, plaintive and bright, subtle and harmonious. Among all the sounds of the worlds of the ten directions, it is foremost.

[Commentary] The second explains the music. “There is also music of ten thousand kinds, arising of itself” states it in general; “and its sounds are none but Dharma...” reveals the wondrousness of its sounds; “among the ten directions” and so on reveals the supremacy of its sounds, that it surpasses all sounds of the worlds of the ten directions.

Their lecture halls, retreats, palaces, and towers are all adorned with the seven treasures and spontaneously transformed into being; and they are draped and covered over with nettings of true pearls, moon-bright mani, and many other jewels.

[Commentary] The third explains the lecture halls, palaces, and the like. That the lecture halls, retreats, palaces, and towers are all made of the seven treasures explains their substance; “and with true pearls” and so on explains their adornment.

Within and without, to left and right, there are bathing pools, some ten yojanas, some twenty or thirty, and even a hundred thousand yojanas, in length, breadth, and depth each of one measure. The water of eight excellent qualities is still and brimming, pure, fragrant, and clean, its taste like nectar. Pools of gold have bottoms of silver sand; pools of silver have bottoms of gold sand; pools of crystal have bottoms of lapis lazuli sand; pools of lapis lazuli have bottoms of crystal sand; pools of coral have bottoms of amber sand; pools of amber have bottoms of coral sand; pools of mother-of-pearl have bottoms of carnelian sand; pools of carnelian have bottoms of mother-of-pearl sand; pools of white jade have bottoms of purple gold sand; pools of purple gold have bottoms of white jade sand. Some are made of two treasures, three treasures, or up to seven treasures, combined together in turn. On the banks of these pools are sandalwood trees, whose flowers and leaves hang down and spread, their fragrance perfuming all around. Heavenly utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and pundarika flowers, of variegated color and lush radiance, completely cover the water. When those bodhisattvas and the host of sravakas enter the jeweled pools, if they wish the water to cover their feet, the water covers their feet; if they wish it to reach their knees, it reaches their knees; if they wish it to reach their waists, the water reaches their waists; if they wish it to reach their necks, the water reaches their necks; if they wish it to bathe their bodies, it bathes their bodies of itself; if they wish it to recede, the water at once recedes. It tempers cold and warmth of itself according to their wish. It opens the spirit and gladdens the body, washing away the stains of the mind. Clear and limpid, so pure it seems formless, the jeweled sands shine through it, and nothing is so deep that it is not illumined. Gentle ripples swirl and flow, pouring into one another, moving gently and slowly onward, neither slow nor swift. The waves raise measureless spontaneously arising wondrous sounds, and each hears according to what suits him, none failing to hear: some hear the sound of the Buddha, some the sound of the Dharma, some the sound of the Sangha; some the sound of stillness, the sound of emptiness and non-self, the sound of great compassion, the sound of the paramitas; some the sound of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the dharmas unique [to the Buddhas], the sound of the penetrations and wisdoms, the sound of non-activity, the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing, the sound of the acceptance of non-arising, and even the nectar-anointment and all the wondrous Dharma-sounds. According to what they hear, their joy is measureless. They accord with the meaning of purity, freedom from desire, quiescence, and reality; they accord with the Three Jewels and with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique dharmas; they accord with the path practiced by bodhisattvas and sravakas of penetrating wisdom. There is not even the name of the suffering of the three evil paths, but only the sounds of spontaneous joy. Therefore that land is named the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Commentary] The fourth explains the characteristics of the pools. Within it, first it sets forth the characteristics of the pools and afterward explains their issuing of sounds. In setting forth the pool characteristics, the text has four turns. First, it explains their measure: the pools of that land are ten yojanas, twenty or thirty, and even a hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Second, it explains the water's characteristics: it possesses the eight excellent qualities, namely clear, odorless, light, cold, soft, sweet, agreeable when drunk, and causing no harm after drinking. “Clear” belongs to the field of form; “odorless” to the field of smell; “light, cold, and soft,” these five belong to the field of touch; “sweet” belongs to the field of taste; “agreeable when drunk” and “causing no harm after drinking,” these two belong to the field of mental objects. These eight are the functions belonging to water, and so they are called functions; they are the virtues of water, and so they are called qualities. In the text, first, “the water of eight excellent qualities is still and brimming” states it in general. “Pure” is the purity among the eight; “fragrant and clean” is the fragrance among the eight; “its taste like nectar” is the sweetness among the eight. Third, from “pools of gold” onward, it explains the adornments of the various treasures. Fourth, from “when those bodhisattvas and sravakas enter” onward, it reveals the marks of their unobstructed enjoyment. Within this there are five phrases: first, no obstruction as to shallowness or depth; second, cold and warmth are just right; third, it opens the spirit and removes stains; fourth, it is pure and without blemish; fifth, the flowing back and mutual pouring, slow and swift each in its proper measure. The above explains the pools; below it explains their issuing of sounds. Within this there are four. First, “it sends forth measureless spontaneously arising wondrous sounds” directly explains the issuing of sounds. Second, from “according to what suits” onward, it shows that it responds to beings with many kinds of hearing: within this, first a general statement, next the particulars, and last the conclusion. Third, from “they accord with purity, freedom from desire” onward, it explains that these sounds can give rise to good: “according with the meaning of purity, freedom from desire, quiescence, and reality” accords with nirvana; “according with the Three Jewels, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so on” accords with bodhi. These two accord with the fruit. “According with the path practiced by bodhisattvas and sravakas of penetrating wisdom” accords with its cause. Fourth, from “no three evil paths” onward, it explains that they can produce joy: “no three evil paths” and so on shows that there is no suffering; “but only the sounds of spontaneous...” shows that there is joy. From “therefore” onward, it concludes and praises, revealing its excellence.
The above four passages together form the third, explaining the land.

From here the fourth explains its people. Within it there are four: first, it explains that the direct reward of those newly born there from other directions is subtle and wondrous; second, from “the palaces in which they dwell” onward, their dependent reward is excellent; third, from “those sravakas and bodhisattvas” onward, it explains that the direct reward of the long-dwelling ones is subtle and wondrous; fourth, from “the clothing of those devas and humans” onward, their dependent reward is excellent.
Ānanda, those who are born in that Buddha-land are fully endowed with such pure bodily form, with all wondrous voices, and with spiritual powers and virtues.

[Commentary] In the first, “fully endowed with pure bodily form” shows the excellence of the body; “all wondrous voices” shows the excellence of speech; “spiritual powers and virtues” shows the excellence of mind.

The palaces in which they dwell, their clothing, food and drink, all the wondrous flowers and incense, and their adornments are like the spontaneously appearing things of the sixth heaven. When they wish to eat, seven-jeweled bowls appear before them: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, carnelian, coral, amber, moon-bright pearl, and true pearl — such bowls come according to their wish. Food and drink of a hundred flavors fill them of themselves. Yet though such food appears, there is in truth no one who eats; they merely see its color and smell its fragrance, and with the mind take it as food, and are naturally satisfied. Body and mind are gentle, with no attachment to flavor. When the meal is done it vanishes; when the time comes it appears again. That Buddha-land is pure and peaceful, subtly wondrous and blissful, next to the Way of unconditioned nirvana.

[Commentary] In the second passage, that the palaces, clothing, and other things they dwell in are like those of the sixth heaven shows the excellence of their provisions; from “when they wish to eat” onward, the excellence of their use, and this is spoken with reference to food alone. “That Buddha-land is pure and peaceful...” and so on praises it in general, revealing its excellence. “Next to the Way of unconditioned nirvana”: “niyuan” and “nirvana” are originally one name, differing only in the transmitted sound.

Those sravakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans are lofty and brilliant in wisdom and penetrating in spiritual powers; all are of one kind, with no difference in appearance. Only because they conform to other lands are they given the names of devas and humans. Their countenances are upright and fair, surpassing the world and rarely seen; their complexion is subtle and wondrous, neither deva nor human. All receive a spontaneously appearing body of emptiness, a form without limit. The Buddha told Ānanda: “Suppose a poor beggar of the world stood beside a king: could his appearance and countenance be compared?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Even if this person stood beside a king, he would be so wretched, mean, and ugly that no simile could describe it, a hundred thousand million times beyond reckoning. Why is this? The poor beggar is at the very bottom of the scale: his clothes do not cover his body, his food barely sustains his life; hunger and cold oppress him, and all human decency is nearly gone. All this because in former lives he planted no root of virtue: he hoarded wealth and gave nothing, and the richer he grew the stingier he became; he wished only to gain without effort, greedy and insatiable; he did not believe in cultivating good, and his transgressions piled up like a mountain. When such a one's life ends, his wealth and jewels scatter; his suffering body accumulates [karma], and he grieves over it, yet it profits him nothing — it merely belongs to others. With no good to rely on and no virtue to depend on, he falls at death into the evil paths and endures this long suffering. When his offense is finished he emerges and is born lowly and base, foolish and mean to the utmost, appearing in the likeness of humans. In the same way the kings of the world, alone honored among men, owe it entirely to virtue accumulated in former lives. Kind and generous in giving, benevolent and helpful to all, truthful in conduct and cultivating good, quarreling with no one: therefore at the end of life their merit answers and they rise to the good paths, are born in the heavens above, and enjoy such blessings and bliss. With accumulated good and its lingering blessings, they now obtain human birth and are born into a royal house, naturally honored, their bearing and countenance fair, revered and served by all, with wondrous clothing and rare delicacies worn and enjoyed as they wish — the merit of former lives follows them, and so they can attain this.” The Buddha told Ānanda: “What you say is so. Consider: though a king is honored among men and fair in form, compared with a holy wheel-turning king he is most base and mean, like that beggar beside the king. The holy wheel-turning king's majestic marks are wondrous, foremost in the world; yet compared with the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven he is again ugly and vile, not to be compared even by ten thousand million times. Even if the lord of the heavens were compared with the lord of the sixth heaven, they would not be of the same kind by a hundred thousand million times. And if the lord of the sixth heaven were compared with the bodhisattvas and sravakas of the land of Amitabha Buddha, his light, countenance, and complexion would not reach them by a hundred thousand million incalculable times.”

[Commentary] In the third, on the excellence of the long-dwelling beings, “those sravakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans are lofty and brilliant in wisdom and penetrating in spiritual powers” shows the excellence of their virtues; from “all are of one kind” onward it reveals the excellence of their bodies. In this, the first words, “all are of one kind, with no difference in appearance; only because they conform to other lands are they given the names of devas and humans,” show that their bodies are equal. From “their countenances are upright” onward, it shows the surpassing excellence of their bodies: “their countenances are upright and fair, surpassing the world and rarely seen” distinguishes their excellence by their characteristics. From “The Buddha told Ānanda” onward, it compares them to reveal their excellence. In the comparison there are five: first, comparing the poor man with a minor king; second, comparing a minor king with a holy wheel-turning king; third, comparing the wheel-turning king with the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven; fourth, comparing the lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven with the lord of the heaven of the enjoyment of others' transformations; fifth, comparing the lord of the heaven of the enjoyment of others' transformations with all the devas and humans of Immeasurable Life, whom in the end he does not reach. In the first comparison the text has three turns: first, the Buddha sets the poor man against a minor king and questions Ānanda in return; second, Ānanda answers directly, “even if this person stood beside a king, no simile could describe it, a hundred thousand million times beyond reckoning,” directly showing that the poor man does not match the king, and from “Why is this?” onward it explains the reason for his falling short, namely that in former lives he had no good; from “In the same way the kings of the world” onward it explains the reason for the king's surpassing, namely that in former lives he cultivated good. The text is evident. Third, the Tathagata approves. The remaining four comparisons are evident and easily understood.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “In the land of Immeasurable Life, the clothing, food and drink, flowers and incense, jeweled garlands, silk canopies, banners and pennants, subtle wondrous sounds, and the dwellings, houses, palaces, and pavilions of those devas and humans accord with their bodily form and color, their height and size; whether of one treasure, of two treasures, or up to measureless many treasures, they come at a thought, according to their wish. Moreover, wondrous garments of many treasures are spread over all the ground, and all the devas and humans walk upon them. Measureless jeweled nets completely cover the Buddha-land, all adorned and embellished with gold threads, true pearls, and hundreds of thousands of assorted treasures, wonderful and rare, and all around on every side hang jeweled bells, their light and color blazing, utterly magnificent. A spontaneously arising breeze of virtue rises gently and stirs softly; the wind is harmonious, neither cold nor hot, temperate, cool, and soft, neither slow nor swift. It blows upon the nets and the jeweled trees, sending forth measureless subtle and wondrous Dharma-sounds and diffusing ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant fragrance of virtue. For those who hear it, the dust of affliction and the stains of habit do not arise of themselves; when the wind touches their bodies, they all obtain bliss, like a bhiksu who has attained the samadhi of extinction. Again the wind blows and scatters flowers that fill the Buddha-land, arranged in order by color without confusion, soft and lustrous, richly fragrant. When the foot treads on them, they sink four inches; when the foot is lifted, they return as before. When the flowers' purpose is done, the earth opens and they vanish in order, leaving no trace, pure and clean. According to the season the wind blows and scatters flowers, and thus six times over. Moreover, lotus flowers of many treasures fill the world all around; each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand million petals, and the light of these flowers is of measureless kinds of color: blue flowers with blue light, white flowers with white light; dark, yellow, crimson, and purple, their light and color brilliant, blazing and radiant, outshining the sun and moon. From each flower issue thirty-six hundred thousand million rays of light; from each ray issue thirty-six hundred thousand million Buddhas, their bodies the color of purple gold, their marks and features extraordinary. Each of these Buddhas again emits a hundred thousand rays of light and universally teaches the wondrous Dharma for the ten directions. Thus each Buddha establishes measureless beings in the right path to Buddhahood.”

[Commentary] In the fourth, which again reveals the excellence of the reward, first it explains that all the clothing, food, and other things in that land accord with their bodies. From “whether of one treasure” onward, it separately reveals their excellence. Within this there are five: first, it explains that the various treasures appear before them according to their minds; second, jeweled garments spread over the ground; third, jeweled nets spread over all; fourth, from “spontaneous” onward, the breeze of virtue blows and stirs; fifth, from “moreover” onward, jeweled flowers fill all. In the fourth, on the wind, “a spontaneously arising breeze of virtue rises gently and stirs softly” states it in general; below it is shown separately. In the particulars there are four: first, the wind's substance is harmonious, slow and swift each in its proper measure; second, it blows on the nets and stirs the trees, emitting subtle wondrous sounds; third, touching the body it produces bliss; fourth, it blows and scatters the many flowers throughout that land. In the fifth, on the flowers, there are four phrases: first, it explains that the jeweled flowers fill the world all around; second, it explains that each flower has many petals; third, it explains that each flower issues many rays of light; fourth, from “from each flower issue thirty-six” onward, it explains that from each flower many Buddhas issue, in which there are again four: first, it makes clear that from each single ray many rays issue, “thirty-six hundred thousand million rays of light”; second, it makes clear that from each single flower many Buddhas issue, “thirty-six hundred thousand million Buddhas”; third, it makes clear that each of those Buddhas emits many rays of light; fourth, it makes clear that each of those Buddhas universally teaches the wondrous Dharma for the ten directions. Within this, first it explains what they teach, and from “thus each Buddha” onward it reveals the benefit of the teaching.

From here, the third, makes clear what it draws in. It draws in the sentient beings of the ten directions who have karmic affinity, to be reborn together in that land, transforming and benefiting them through the Dharma. Yet what is drawn in below answers the forty-eight great vows made above, each one separately corresponding, and their mutual relationship can be understood. The text has four divisions: first, it draws in those below to be born together in that land; second, from “the majestic virtue of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit” onward, it draws in those above to go and be reborn in that land; third, from “the bodhisattvas of that land shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth” onward, it again draws in those below to be born together in that land; fourth, from “Maitreya asked the Buddha how many bodhisattvas of this world would be born there” onward, it again draws in those above to be born together in that land. What is the difference between the first and the third? In the earlier first division the birth-karma is fully explained and rebirth is taught; in the third division gain and loss are set forth to encourage people to be reborn there. Since the meaning differs in this way, they must be distinguished. What is the difference between the second and the fourth? In the earlier second, those above are drawn in to go there together; in the fourth, they are drawn in to be born there together. Since there is this difference, they must be spoken of separately. That it draws in those below makes clear the benefit conferred; that it draws in those above reveals that land's superiority and increases people's yearning for it.

The first has three parts. First, it shows that those born there dwell in the right concentration, leading people to long for it. Second, from “the Buddhas of the ten directions all praise together” onward, it cites those who hear the Name, that they all attain rebirth, increasing people's resolve to go. Third, from “The Buddha told Ānanda” onward, it properly distinguishes the birth-karma and teaches the practice of rebirth.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The sentient beings born in that land all dwell in the gathering of right concentration. Why is that? In that Buddha-land there are no gatherings of the erroneous or of the indeterminate.”

[Commentary] In the first division, that those born in that land all dwell in right concentration makes clear what is drawn in. People have three gatherings: first, erroneous concentration; second, right concentration; third, indeterminate. In the Lesser Vehicle the treatises differ. According to the Abhidharma, the ordinary person who is always sinking is called erroneous concentration; the five-stopping contemplation, the general and particular mindfulness, and the two minds of soft and top are called indeterminate, and because these can regress they are called indeterminate; from the mind of endurance onward, firm and unregressing, is called right concentration. According to the Satyasiddhi, the ordinary person who is always sinking is called erroneous concentration; the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection, whose practice can regress, are spoken of as capable of regression; the five-stopping contemplation is called the wisdom of hearing, the general and particular mindfulness the wisdom of reflection, and from soft and top onward is called the wisdom of cultivation; seeing directly that dharmas are empty and never regressing, all of it is right concentration. In the Great Vehicle, before the stage of good destiny is called erroneous concentration; within the stage of good destiny, advancing and retreating many times, is called indeterminate; from the stage of the seed of practice onward, the stage does not regress, and is called right concentration. Whether the sentient beings of the Great Vehicle or of the Lesser Vehicle, those born in that land all dwell in right concentration. Below it explains why: there is no erroneous concentration nor the indeterminate gathering, so all are right.

The Tathagatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the majestic spiritual power and merit of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life as inconceivable.
