All sentient beings who hear his Name, with faith and joy, even in a single thought, with a sincere heart turn their merit and vow to be born in that land, immediately attain rebirth, and dwell in non-retrogression — except only those who commit the five heinous wrongs and slander the true Dharma.

[Commentary] In the second division, first it shows that the Tathagatas of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all together praise the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; next it shows that sentient beings who hear the Name, have faith, and turn their merit and make vows all attain rebirth; below it reveals the differentiation: excepting only the five heinous wrongs and those who slander the true Dharma, all others are born there. As for the five heinous wrongs: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, breaking the harmony of the sangha, and causing blood to flow from a Buddha's body — these are the five. These five all go against kindness and violate the field of blessing, so they are called heinous. The first two are acts against kindness; the latter three violate the field of blessing. To uphold the false and destroy the right is called slandering the Dharma. Because these obstructions are heavy, they are excluded. Someone asks: In the Contemplation Sutra it is said that even those who commit such wrongs can attain rebirth, yet this sutra says they cannot be born there. How is this explained? There are two meanings. First, distinguishing by person: people are of two kinds. One kind, who long ago aroused the Great Vehicle mind, encounter circumstances and commit the wrongs, like King Ajatashatru and others; though they commit the wrongs, they must have deep repentance, and, arousing the mind, seek to escape, which can extinguish the heavy offenses — hence they attain rebirth, and the Contemplation Sutra is based on this. The other kind, who previously did not arouse the great mind and now commit the heinous offenses, mostly lack deep repentance and cannot resolutely arouse bodhicitta — hence they are not born there, and this sutra is based on this. Second, distinguishing by practice: practice has concentration and scattering. Though some commit the heinous wrongs, they can cultivate the sixteen contemplations of true goodness and deeply contemplate the Buddha's virtue, which extinguishes the heavy offenses, and so attain rebirth — the Contemplation Sutra is based on this. If a person commits the wrongs and cannot cultivate the Buddha-contemplation samadhi, though he does other good it cannot extinguish the offenses, so he is not reborn there — this sutra is based on this.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “The gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land are of three grades.”

[Commentary] The third properly distinguishes the birth-karma and teaches the practice of rebirth. Within it, first it says that the gods and humans of the ten directions who wish to be born in that land are of three grades, giving a general statement. As in the Contemplation Sutra, roughly divided into three, finely into nine. Roughly divided into three, they are the upper, middle, and lower. Among persons of the Great Vehicle, from the stage of the seed of practice onward is called the upper grade; among persons of the Lesser Vehicle, the ordinary person who keeps the precepts, up to the once-returner, are the middle grade; among persons of the Great Vehicle, the ordinary person of the stage of good destiny is called the lower grade. Finely divided into nine, within the upper grade it is further divided into three: the upper-upper, upper-middle, and upper-lower. From the fourth ground onward is called upper-upper, for born there one immediately attains the patient acceptance of non-arising; the first, second, and third grounds are called upper-middle, for born there, after one small eon one attains the patient acceptance of non-arising — the days of that land are long, so within one small eon one attains it, whereas in this world it takes immeasurable eons. The lineage and the stage of understanding and practice are called upper-lower; born there, after three small eons one attains the hundred Dharma-doors and dwells on the first ground. Thus we know that before the ground, too, because the days of that land are long, it takes three small eons to reach the first ground, whereas in this world it takes immeasurable eons.

(Here the stages are judged too high, and do not accord with the intent of drawing in those below. Examining the text on the upper grade in the Contemplation Sutra, it is also ordinary beings of great mind who, relying on their vows, are reborn. One should accord with the Perfect Teaching, and at the fullness of the ten stages of faith, be born in the upper-upper grade, and at that time enter the first stage of abiding — as the Avatamsaka Sutra says, proving all is proven, that is, at the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment. This alone accords with the subtle meaning of this sutra. The commentator, following the Gradual Teaching, judged it as the stages of the grounds for the upper grade, fearing this might cause later people to doubt and think ordinary beings have no share; therefore I briefly discuss it.)

The middle-grade persons are also divided into three: the middle-upper, middle-middle, and middle-lower. From the seeing of the path onward is called middle-upper, for born there one immediately attains the arhat fruit. The inner ordinary person is called middle-middle, for born there one immediately attains the stream-enterer fruit. The four minds from “warm” onward are called the inner ordinary; the outer ordinary person who keeps the precepts is called middle-lower, for born there, after one small eon one attains the arhat. The lower-grade persons are also divided into three: the lower-upper, lower-middle, and lower-lower. There they are divided by the lightness or heaviness of the offenses done, not by their stages. The nine grades there are here combined into three: the three persons of the upper grade combine into the upper class, the three of the middle grade into the middle class, and the three of the lower grade into the lower class. Though the pursuits of these three classes differ, when it comes to wishing to be born there, all must arouse the mind and seek great bodhi, single-mindedly think of that Buddha, turn their merit and make vows, and only then attain rebirth; hence this is discussed. A question: Vasubandhu, in composing the verses on rebirth, says that women, those with deficient faculties, and those of the two-vehicle seeds all cannot be born there; yet the Contemplation Sutra declares that beings of the Lesser Vehicle also attain rebirth. How is this explained? The explanation: that statement that women and those with deficient faculties cannot be born there is spoken from the standpoint of receiving the retribution within that land, for there are no women there nor those with deficient faculties. The statement that those of the two-vehicle seed cannot be born there is spoken from the standpoint of going from this land; Lesser Vehicle beings, though they previously studied the Lesser Vehicle, when about to depart must arouse the great mind to attain rebirth; if with the small mind they seek birth in that land, there is no principle of going. Hence Vasubandhu says the two-vehicle seed cannot attain rebirth. A question: if the departure uses the great mind, why upon arrival do they realize the small fruit? The explanation: because of their long habituation to the Lesser Vehicle; originally here they studied much the contemplation of suffering and impermanence, and upon arrival, hearing of suffering and impermanence, they immediately awaken and understand, and so realize the small fruit. Because in the end they aroused the great mind to seek birth there, having attained the arhat there they immediately seek the great. Above was the general statement; below it is shown separately.

As for the upper class: they abandon the home and put aside desire, becoming monastics; they arouse bodhicitta; they single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; they cultivate various merits; and they vow to be born in that land. When these beings approach the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with the great assembly, appears before them; they then follow that Buddha and are born in his land, and in the seven-jeweled lotus they are spontaneously transformed and born; they dwell in non-retrogression, with wisdom brave and fierce, and spiritual powers effortless. Therefore, Ānanda, whatever beings wish to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life in this present life should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, cultivate merit and virtue, and vow to be born in that land.

[Commentary] Within the upper class, first it states, then distinguishes, then concludes with praise. In the distinguishing there are three: first it sets forth their cultivation of the causal practice; second, from “these beings” onward, they together accomplish rebirth; third, from “dwelling in non-retrogression” onward, the benefit they gain in that land. In the initial cause of cultivation there are five clauses: first, leaving the world and the home; second, arousing bodhicitta; third, single-mindedly thinking of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; fourth, cultivating various merits; fifth, using the aforementioned goodness to vow birth in that land. In the rebirth, first that Buddha welcomes them, then from “they follow” onward, this going to and being born in that land; in the benefit, dwelling in non-retrogression — the stage is firm; wisdom brave, and so on — the accomplished virtue is supreme. Above was the statement, next the distinguishing, and from “therefore” onward the concluding praise of the practice.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “As for the middle class: the gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land — though they cannot act as monastics or greatly cultivate merit, they should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and in some measure cultivate goodness: receive and observe the precepts and the pure fasts, erect stupas and images, feed monastics, hang pennants and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense; and turning this merit, vow to be born in that land. When such a person approaches the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life manifests his body, in light and marks and appearance fully like the true Buddha, and together with the great assembly appears before him; he then follows the transformed Buddha and is born in that land, dwelling in non-retrogression, with merit and wisdom next to those of the upper class.”

[Commentary] Within the middle class, first it states, then distinguishes. In distinguishing, again first it sets forth their causal practice, next the rebirth, then reveals the benefit. In the first statement of the cause: the gods and humans of the ten directions who with sincere heart wish birth in that land — a general statement. “Though they cannot act as monastics, etc.” distinguishes them from the upper class. According to the Contemplation Sutra, these are Lesser Vehicle persons, and so they cannot greatly cultivate merit there. From “they should arouse” onward it properly distinguishes their cause, with four clauses: first, arouse bodhicitta; second, single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; third, cultivate a little merit and goodness; fourth, turn the merit and vow birth. Though such a person previously studied the Lesser Vehicle, when truly wishing to be born there he must cultivate these four practices, and only then attains rebirth. In the rebirth, first that Buddha welcomes him, then he is born there; the benefit can be understood.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “As for the lower class: the gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land — even if they cannot do various merits, they should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, single-mindedly direct their attention, and even to ten thoughts, think on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and vow to be born in his land. If they hear the profound Dharma and rejoice with faith and joy, giving rise to no doubt, and even in a single thought think on that Buddha, and with a most sincere heart vow to be born in that land, then at the end of life, dreaming of that Buddha, they too attain rebirth, with merit and wisdom next to those of the middle class.”

[Commentary] Within the lower class, first it states, then distinguishes. In distinguishing, again first it sets forth their causal practice, next the rebirth, then reveals the benefit. In the first statement of the cause: the gods and humans of the ten directions who with sincere heart wish birth in that land — a general statement. “Even if they cannot do various merits” distinguishes them from the middle class. As in the Contemplation Sutra, the offenses are cited to distinguish; here it is briefly omitted. From “they should arouse” onward it properly distinguishes their cause, with four names: first, arouse bodhicitta; second, single-mindedly think of that Buddha of Immeasurable Life, even to ten thoughts, and vow birth in that land; third, hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice with faith and joy, giving rise to no doubt; fourth, with a most sincere heart, even in a single thought think on that Buddha, and vow birth in that land — they too attain rebirth. In the rebirth, it shows that dreaming of that Buddha at the end of life, one also attains rebirth; the benefit can be understood.
Above, the first division set forth drawing in those below.

From here, the second division sets forth drawing in those above to be reborn together in that land. It is cited to reveal the superiority of Amitabha's land and to increase the resolve of the lower people to seek rebirth. Within it, first the prose briefly explains, then the verses expand the discussion.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The majestic spiritual power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless and inconceivable, all without exception praise him. In the east, in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the immeasurable and countless assemblies of bodhisattvas all go to the place of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and respectfully make offerings, together with the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas, hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, and proclaiming the teaching of the Way. So likewise in the south, west, and north, in the four directions and above and below.”

[Commentary] In the earlier prose there are two divisions: first, the Buddhas all praise together; second, from “in the east” onward, the bodhisattvas together go and are born. The later verses separately praise them; one should carefully note this. In the earlier Buddha-praise: first the Buddha told Ānanda that the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit — Śākyamuni praising himself; from “the ten directions” onward, the other Buddhas praise together. Below, these are separately sung; one should also note it. In the going-together below, first the east is listed, then the other directions are analogized. In listing the east: in the eastern Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges the countless bodhisattvas all go to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life — this is the beginning. Respectfully making offerings, together with the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas — this is the next. Hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, and proclaiming the teaching of the Way — this is the end. Since the east is thus, the other directions are also so. This beginning, middle, and end are separately sung in the verses below; one should also note it. The verses below sing it.
At that time the World-Honored One spoke verses, saying:

The World-Honored One spoke verses — the sutra's compiler sets this out. Below is the actual singing. There are thirty verses. The first fifteen sing of the earlier latter division, the bodhisattvas going together; the last fifteen sing of the earlier first division, the Buddhas praising together.

Of the first fifteen, the first two verses sing of the going together above; then five verses sing of the respectful making of offerings in the earlier text; below, eight verses sing of the earlier hearing of the Dharma and proclaiming of the teaching.
In eastern Buddha-lands,
as many as Ganges' sands, the bodhisattvas of those realms all go to see the Immeasurable One.
South, west, and north, the four,
above and below likewise: the bodhisattva hosts of those lands all go to see the Immeasurable One.

[Commentary] Of the first two verses, the first sings of the earlier going-together in the east, and the latter sings of the going-together in the remaining directions. Arriving there, they respectfully greet the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; hence it is called “beholding the Immeasurable Enlightened One.”
All the bodhisattvas,
each bearing heavenly wondrous flowers, precious incense and priceless garments, make offerings to the Immeasurable One.
Together they sound celestial music,
pouring forth gentle and harmonious tones, singing praise of the most supreme One, making offering to the Immeasurable One.
Having reached the depths of spiritual powers and wisdom,
they roam into the deep gates of Dharma, complete in the treasury of merit, with wondrous wisdom without peer.
The sun of wisdom illumines the world,
dispelling the clouds of birth and death; in reverence they circle three times and bow before the supreme One.
They see that land, adorned and pure,
subtle and wonderful beyond thought, and so arouse the measureless resolve: “may my land be likewise.”

[Commentary] Of the next five verses, the first four speak of seeing the Buddha and making offerings, and the last one of seeing the land and forming the wish. Of the first four, the first two speak of outer offerings to things, and the latter two of inner offerings. In the outer offerings: each bearing wondrous flowers is an offering; the precious is an offering of treasure; the incense is an offering of incense; the priceless garments are an offering by clothing; the sounding of celestial music and so forth is an offering of music; and within the tones of music they sing praise of the Buddha's virtue. In the inner offerings, the first verse and a half speak of the offering of praise by speech, and the latter half verse of reverent offering by the body. In the praise by speech, the first verse praises the Buddha's own virtue, and the latter half verse praises the Buddha's benefiting of others. In praising his own virtue: reaching the depths of spiritual powers and wisdom and roaming into the deep Dharma praises the Buddha's two virtues of wisdom and spiritual powers. Wisdom is the root of spiritual powers, and spiritual powers are the function of wisdom; the two are mutually dependent, so both are praised. The perfection of the spiritual powers and wisdom is called “reaching the depths”; being wholly complete is called “utter,” and being thorough is called “attaining.” These spiritual powers and wisdom both arise in accordance with the Dharma, so again it shows the roaming into the deep Dharma: to dwell in contemplation is called “roaming,” and to exhaust the source is called “entering”; realizing the realm of Dharma of the dependent-rising gate, one can manifest supreme spiritual powers, and realizing the realm of Dharma of the wisdom gate, one can raise up supreme wisdom. Complete in the treasury of merit with wondrous wisdom without peer praises the Buddha's two practices of fortune and wisdom. Fortune is the support of wisdom, and wisdom is the guide of fortune; the two are mutually dependent, so both are praised. The practice of fortune fully complete is called “endowed with the treasury of merit,” and the wisdom-practice supreme is called “wisdom without peer.” “Peer” means a match; there is no match for the Buddha, so it is called “without peer.” In the latter benefiting of others: the sun of wisdom illumining the world transforms people and gives rise to wisdom; wisdom can awaken and illumine like the sun, teaching people to gain understanding, so it is called “ilumining the world.” Dispelling birth and death transforms people and removes obstructions; birth and death cover and obstruct, and from a metaphor it is spoken of as “clouds.” The reverent bowing by the body is understood. The four verses above speak of seeing the Buddha and making offerings; the verse below speaks of seeing the land and forming the wish; the text is clear and can be understood.
Then the Immeasurable One,
his countenance moved, issued a joyful smile; from his mouth countless lights streamed, illumining the lands of the ten directions.
Turning back the light to encircle his body,
three times it circled and entered the crown; all the hosts of gods and humans, leaping, rejoiced with joy.
The great being, Guanyin,
arranging his robes and bowing, asked: “Tell me, O Buddha, what cause of this smile? We beg you, we wish you to explain the meaning.”
His Brahma-sound like thunder's roll,
the eight tones pouring out wondrous sound: “I shall bestow the bodhisattva's prophecy; now hear it, O virtuous ones, and listen well.”
The true sages come from the ten directions;
I know all their vows: seeking to adorn a pure land, they receive the prophecy and shall become Buddhas.
Awake to all dharmas,
as dream, illusion, and echo, fulfilling all the wondrous vows, they shall surely attain such a land.
Knowing dharmas as lightning and shadows,
they carry the bodhisattva-way to its end; with their root of merit and virtue, they receive the prophecy and shall become Buddhas.
Penetrating the nature of all dharmas,
all empty and without self, seeking the pure Buddha-land with compassion, they shall surely attain such a land.

[Commentary] These eight verses sing of the earlier hearing of the Dharma and proclaiming of the teaching. In this text, the first two verses show the Tathagata Amitabha manifesting a sign to initiate; then one verse has Guanyin ask in wonder; and the last five verses have that Buddha answer fully. “The Brahma-sound like thunder” and “the eight tones pouring out wondrous sound” answer in praise of the wondrousness of the sound. The eight Brahma-tones, as the Brahma-deva-parable Sutra explains: first the most wondrous sound, whose tone is sorrowful and beautiful; second the easily-understood sound, whose words are clearly distinguished; third the harmonious sound, whose loud and soft are measured; fourth the gentle sound, whose tone is gentle; fifth the unerring sound, whose words have no error; sixth the unwomanish sound, whose tone is virile and resounding; seventh the honored-and-wise sound, whose words have dignity and awe, like the sound of a respected and wise person in the world; eighth the deep and far sound, whose tone is deep and far like the rolling of thunder. With this wondrous sound he answers Guanyin: “I shall bestow the bodhisattva's prophecy; now hear it, O virtuous ones, and listen well” — commanding them to listen and permitting the explanation. The words of the prophecy are as explained above. “Now I shall speak this; do you, virtuous ones, listen well.” From here, four verses set forth what is actually said. In them, the first verse raises their vow-mind and prophesies certain Buddhahood. The second verse raises their wisdom and vow and prophesies certain attainment of the land: “awake to all as dream and illusion, etc.” raises their wisdom; “fulfilling all the wondrous vows” raises their vow; “shall attain such a land” prophesies the attainment. The third verse raises their wisdom and practice, prophesying certain Buddhahood: “knowing dharmas as lightning” raises their wisdom; “carrying the bodhisattva-way to its end and having all the roots of virtue” raises their practice; “receiving the prophecy and becoming Buddha” prophesies the attainment. The fourth verse raises their wisdom and vow, prophesying certain attainment of the land: “penetrating the nature of all dharmas and all empty and without self” raises their wisdom — the earlier “awake to all as dream and illusion, etc.” is the wisdom of worldly truth, while this “penetrating the nature of all dharmas and all empty without self” is the wisdom of ultimate truth; “seeking the pure land with compassion” raises their vow; “shall attain such a land” prophesies the attainment.

The last fifteen verses sing of the Buddhas' praising together in the earlier text. The first five sing of the earlier Buddhas of the ten directions all praising together; the last ten sing of the earlier Śākyamuni praising himself.
The Buddhas announce to the bodhisattvas:
“Now go and behold the Buddha of Peaceful Nurture; hearing the Dharma, rejoice and receive and practice, and quickly attain the pure abode.”
Arriving at that land, adorned and pure,
they quickly attain spiritual powers, and surely from the Immeasurable One receive the prophecy and become enlightened ones.
The power of that Buddha's original vows:
hearing the Name and wishing to be reborn, all reach that land, and are settled in non-retrogression.
The bodhisattvas rouse surpassing vows:
may their own land be no different; with universal thought they save all, and their names fill the ten directions.
Serving countless Tathagatas,
flying and transforming through all lands, respectfully and joyfully departing, they return to the land of Peaceful Nurture.

[Commentary] Of the first five verses, the Buddhas announce to the bodhisattvas, commanding them to behold the land of Peaceful Nurture — this is the direct exhortation to go. “Hearing the Dharma and receiving and practicing” shows what is done upon going. “Quickly attaining” and below shows the benefit of doing so: “quickly attaining the pure abode” shows the benefit of the earlier hearing of the Dharma, receiving, and practicing; in the future getting a wondrous pure land is called “attaining the pure abode.” The four verses below reveal the benefit of the earlier going to behold the land of Peaceful Nurture; the benefit has five kinds. First, the benefit of attaining spiritual powers there — the first half verse. Second, the benefit of receiving the prophecy there — the next half verse; previously it was said that that Buddha prophesies to the bodhisattvas, which is just this matter. Third, the benefit of attaining non-retrogression there — the next verse; previously it was said that being born there one dwells in the right concentration, which is just this matter. Fourth, the benefit of rousing vows there — the next verse; “the bodhisattvas rouse surpassing vows” is the general statement, and below it is separately praised. In the separate praise, “may their own land be no different” is the vow of seeking a pure land, the vow to attain a land like Amitabha's, called “no different”; “with universal thought saving all” is the vow of transforming sentient beings; “their names fill the ten directions” is the vow of seeking the Buddha-body, the vow that when they become Buddhas their names reach the ten directions. Fifth, the benefit of broadly serving many Buddhas and rousing practice there — the last verse.

From here, ten verses have Śākyamuni praising himself, to lead people to go together. Within it there are three parts: the first three verses raise the difficulty of hearing the sutra and the joy of practicing; the next four verses praise the Buddha Amitabha's giving of prophecy to the bodhisattvas, that is, the supreme excellence of his Buddha-wisdom, leading people to turn and take refuge; and the last three verses exhort by principle.
If a person has no mind of goodness,
he cannot hear this sutra; those pure in precepts may gain the hearing of true Dharma.
One who has seen the World-Honored One before,
can then trust in this matter; with humility and respect he hears, receives, and practices, leaping with great joy.
The arrogant and the evil, the indolent,
can hardly trust this Dharma; those who in former lives saw the Buddhas delight to hear such teaching.

[Commentary] Of the first three verses, the first half verse raises the person without goodness who does not hear this sutra, revealing the profundity and weight of the sutra; then a verse and a half raises the person with goodness who at last gains the hearing, showing the subtlety of the sutra. Within it, first it shows that the person with goodness gains the hearing of this sutra; from “one who has seen” onward it shows that the one who has seen the Buddha can then believe, revere, rejoice, and practice. The next half verse raises the person with evil who does not believe this Dharma, revealing its depth and weight. The half verse below raises the one with goodness who delights to hear this teaching, showing its subtlety. Raising the evil who do not hear leads people to reject and distance themselves; raising the good who gain the hearing leads people to long to practice. Moreover, this text reveals the depth and weight of the sutra to dispel people's light disrespect, and shows its subtlety to give rise to people's faith and reverence.
Whether shravaka or bodhisattva,
none can fathom the sage's mind; it is like one born blind who would go and be a guide to others.
The Buddha's sea of wisdom,
deep and vast without bottom or shore; the two vehicles cannot measure it; only the Buddha alone knows it clearly.
Suppose all people,
fully attained the Way, their pure wisdom like the original emptiness, pondering the Buddha's wisdom for a billion eons,
exhausting their strength in utmost discourse,
even to the end of life they would not know it; the Buddha's wisdom is without bound, and thus brings them to purity.

[Commentary] These four verses praise the supreme excellence of the Buddha Amitabha's wisdom and virtue, leading people to turn and take refuge. Within them, the first seven sentences show that the shravakas and bodhisattvas cannot measure it: first the principle, next the simile, then the combining, as can be understood. Then one sentence shows that the Buddha alone knows it. Then six sentences show that all people, having attained the holy Way, together think upon it and know it not: “suppose all people” shows the many; “fully attaining the Way” shows the excellence of their conduct and virtue; “pure wisdom reaching the root” shows the depth of the empty understanding; “pondering the Buddha's wisdom for a billion eons” shows the long contemplation; “exhausting strength in utmost discourse” shows the uttermost of words; yet even so, “to the end of life they would not know it.” The half verse below concludes and praises its superiority: “the Buddha's wisdom without bound” praises the breadth of the Buddha's wisdom; “thus bringing them to purity” praises the purity of the Buddha's virtue. “Bringing” means arriving; reaching to the purity of the Dharma-nature and nirvana, so it is hard to measure and know.
Life is very hard to gain; a Buddha's world also is hard to encounter. The mind of faith and wisdom is hard; if one hears this, one should strive with diligence.
Hearing the Dharma, one does not forget; seeing and revering, one gains the great rejoicing. Then one is my good friend and benefactor; therefore one should rouse the resolve.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma; one shall surely accomplish the Buddha-way and broadly save the stream of birth and death.

[Commentary] These three verses exhort by principle. Of them, the first verse raises the three difficulties and urges people to seek diligently: life being hard to gain is the first difficulty; a Buddha's world being hard to encounter is the second; having the mind of faith and wisdom being hard is the third. These three difficulties one has now gained, so having heard this sutra one should diligently seek. The next verse raises the benefit from seeing and hearing, urging people to arouse the mind: hearing without forgetting means hearing the Dharma without forgetting at the place of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; seeing and revering means seeing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and giving rise to profound reverence; gaining the great rejoicing means the good benefit of the earlier hearing the Dharma, seeing the Buddha, and revering him; gaining the good and being joyful is called gaining the great rejoicing. “Then one is my good friend” means being taken in by the Buddha; practicing in accord with Śākyamuni is called being my good friend; “therefore one should rouse” is the concluding exhortation to arouse the resolve. The last verse teaches the resolute going: “though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma” shows the resolute decision to go; “one shall surely accomplish Buddhahood and broadly save the stream of birth and death” shows what one goes for: to surely accomplish Buddhahood is to seek the fruit of self-benefit, and to broadly save the stream of birth and death is to seek the fruit of benefiting others.
The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Scroll Four, End

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Scroll Five

inline.s: From here, the third, again draws in those below to be born together in that land. Within it there are three: first, it broadly raises the supremely wonderful affairs of the land of Immeasurable Life to make people wish for it; second, from “the worldly people of shallow customs” onward, it reveals the Saha world to be full of defilement and evil, making people weary and abandon it; third, from “broadly reverencing the Immeasurable” onward, taking the land of Amitabha it distinguishes gain and loss, leading people to cultivate and to abandon.

Within the first there are two: first, it broadly raises the affairs of supreme joy in the land of Immeasurable Life; second, from “the Buddha told Maitreya and the gods and humans” onward, it urges people to be reborn there. In the former there are eight: first, it shows that the life in that land is long; second, it shows the supreme marvelousness of their light; third, it shows that their bodies and marks are complete; fourth, it shows the supreme excellence of their wisdom and virtue; fifth, it shows that those born there forever leave the evil destinies; sixth, it shows that they offer many things in that land; seventh, it shows that their hearing of the Dharma is uninterrupted; eighth, it shows that the practice and virtue of the bodhisattvas there are fully complete.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The bodhisattvas of that land shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth, excepting those whose original vows, for the sake of sentient beings, adorn themselves with the merit of the great vow and universally desire to deliver all sentient beings.”

[Commentary] In the first division, it shows that those bodhisattvas shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth, revealing the long life with no untimely death, excepting those who, for the sake of beings, receive bodies in other lands.

“Ānanda, in that Buddha-land the assemblies of shravakas have a body-light of a fathom, and the bodhisattvas' light illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and supreme, whose majestic spiritual light universally illumines the three-thousand great-thousand world. Ānanda said to the Buddha: ‘What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?’ The Buddha said: ‘One is called Guanyin, the other Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas, in this land, cultivated the bodhisattva-way, and at the end of life, transformed, were born in that Buddha-land.’”

[Commentary] In the second division, first it shows that the shravakas of that land have a body-light of a fathom; next it shows that the other bodhisattvas there illumine a hundred yojanas — one yojana is forty li, so a hundred yojanas is four thousand li; and third, it reveals that Guanyin and Mahasthamaprapta illumine the three-thousand great-thousand world. Within it, first it distinguishes, then from “Ānanda said to the Buddha” it distinguishes their names; and from “these two bodhisattvas, in this land” onward it shows that they were born from this land.
“Ānanda, the sentient beings born in that land all possess the thirty-two marks in full.”
[Commentary] In the third division, it shows that the bodies and marks of those born there are complete, all possessing the thirty-two marks, as extensively set forth in the sutra.

“Their wisdom is complete and fulfilled; they penetrate deeply into all dharmas, exhaust and express the essential mysterious meaning; their spiritual powers are without obstruction; their faculties are all bright and sharp. Those of dull faculties attain the two kinds of patient acceptance; those of sharp faculties attain the incalculable patient acceptance of non-arising.”

[Commentary] In the fourth division, it shows the supreme excellence of the wisdom and virtue of those born there. The sentences are four: first, wisdom complete and fulfilled, penetrating deeply into all dharmas, realizing the Dharma-nature, exhausting and expressing the essential mysterious meaning, reaching the marrow of the teaching; second, spiritual powers without obstruction; third, all faculties bright and sharp; fourth, the patient acceptance differs: those of dull faculties accomplish two kinds of patient acceptance, namely the patient acceptance of sound and the patient acceptance of compliance; those of sharp faculties, up to and including the attainment of Buddhahood, attain the asamkhya patient acceptance of non-arising.

“Moreover, those bodhisattvas, up to the attainment of Buddhahood, do not receive the evil destinies; they have spiritual powers at ease and always know their former lives, excepting when, to transform beings, they are born in other pure lands of the five turbidities of the evil world, manifesting in harmony with those lands, as in my land.”

[Commentary] In the fifth division, it shows that those born there forever leave the evil destinies. Within it, first it shows that those born in that land, up to and including the attainment of Buddhahood, no longer fall into the evil destinies, having spiritual powers at ease and always knowing their former lives; later, excepting when, for the sake of beings, they are born in other lands, Śākyamuni says this himself, as with the bodhisattvas of his own land.

The Buddha spoke to Ānanda: “Those bodhisattvas of that land, relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, in the space of one meal, go to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and respectfully make offerings to the Buddha World-Honored Ones. According to what the mind thinks, flowers and incense, music, canopies, umbrellas, banners, and countless immeasurable offerings are spontaneously transformed and produced, responding to the thought and arriving. Wondrous and precious, supremely special, not what the world has, they scatter them over all the Buddhas and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas. In the sky they transform into flower-canopies, their light and color shining brilliantly, their fragrance pervading all. The flowers, four hundred li around and so on, doubling and trebling, spread over the three-thousand great-thousand world. Following their order, they transform and vanish in turn. Those bodhisattvas, all together joyful, in the sky jointly play celestial music, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing praise of the Buddha's virtue. Hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, their joy is measureless. Having made offering to the Buddha, before eating, suddenly lightly lifting, they return to their own land.”

[Commentary] In the sixth division, it shows that those born there can offer extensive offerings. Within it, first it shows their going to the ten directions to offer extensively to many Buddhas; next, from the receiving of the Dharma, and later it shows that while the meal is not yet eaten they return to their own land. In the former there are four clauses: first, it shows that those bodhisattvas of that land, within the space of one meal, go to the ten directions and offer to all the Buddhas; second, from “according to the mind” onward, it shows the offerings transforming in accord with the mind; third, from “in the sky” onward, it shows them transforming into flower-canopies in the sky; fourth, from “those bodhisattvas” onward, it shows the bodhisattvas jointly playing celestial music and singing praise of the Buddha's virtue. “All” means all; all rejoicing and leaping is called “all joyful.” And having made offering to the Buddha, before the meal is eaten, they return to their own land.

The Buddha spoke to Ānanda: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, for the shravakas, bodhisattvas, gods, and humans, proclaims the Dharma, they all assemble in the seven-jeweled hall; widely proclaiming the teaching of the Way, and expounding the wonderful Dharma, none but rejoice, the mind attaining understanding and the Way. At that time, from the four directions a wind naturally arises, blowing the seven-jeweled trees, which give forth the five kinds of sound; measureless wonderful flowers, drifting with the wind and scattering in the four directions, naturally make offering, without ceasing. All the gods bring hundreds and thousands of celestial flowers and incense, and ten thousand kinds of music, to offer to that Buddha and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas. Universally scattering flowers and incense, they play all the music; coming and going, each giving way to the other. At that time, peacefully joyful, the happiness cannot be told.”

[Commentary] In the seventh division, it shows that the hearing of the Dharma by those born there is uninterrupted. Within it, first when the Dharma is spoken, the assembly gathers in the hall and the Tathagata preaches; from “none but” onward it shows the benefit of the preaching: the mind attaining understanding and the Way. From “at that time” onward it sets up the offering to the Buddha; within it, first the wind shakes the trees to give sound, next it blows the wonderful flowers, and later the gods and so forth hold flowers and incense and music, offering and presenting, with entertainment without end.

From here, the eighth shows that the practice and virtue of those bodhisattvas are fully complete. Within it, first the particulars, later the general conclusion. In the particulars there are seven: first, the practice cultivating away from transgression; second, from “fully endowed” onward, the accomplished virtue fully complete; third, from “equal contemplation of the three worlds as empty and non-existent” onward, the practice is fully accomplished; fourth, from “thoroughly the One Vehicle” onward, the accomplished virtue is supremely excellent; fifth, from “destroying jealousy” onward, the practice advances; sixth, from “the power of causes” onward, all powers are complete; seventh, from “the marks and good qualities of the body” onward, taking all the virtues together it generally praises and reveals their superiority.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The bodhisattvas born in that Buddha-land, whatever they expound, always proclaim the true Dharma, following wisdom, without transgression and without loss. Toward all things of that land, they have no mind of self-possession, no mind of attachment; going, coming, advancing, stopping, their feelings have no clinging; at ease and free, no preference and no aversion, no self and no other, no contention and no litigation. Toward all sentient beings they gain the mind of great compassion and benefit, gentle and subdued, without a mind of anger and hatred; free of the coverings, pure and clean, without a mind of weariness and neglect; with the equal mind, the superior mind, the deep mind, the concentrated mind, and the mind that loves the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, and rejoices in the Dharma. They extinguish all afflictions, and have the mind that leaves the evil destinies; thorough in all that the bodhisattva practices.”

[Commentary] In the first [section], the divisions are set out first and the summary follows. Within the divisions, the opening words — “what may be expounded,” “constantly proclaiming what is right,” and so on — speak of transforming practice and freedom from faults. From “in that land” onward, it shows that one's own conduct is without fault. Within that, first, from “grasping the antidotes” through “extinguishing the afflictions,” it makes clear the freedom from all faults. In the former, on grasping the antidotes, it shows the cultivation of the six perfections as antidotes. First the practice of giving is cultivated. Giving is dana. “Toward all the myriad things in that land, with no thought of mine” makes clear freedom from views; “with no mind of defilement or attachment” reveals freedom from craving. Removing and renouncing these two is called the practice of giving. Next the practice of the precepts is cultivated: “coming and going, advancing and stopping, with the mind unfettered, at ease and following its own will” makes clear freedom from bodily fault. “Without partiality, without this or that, without other or self” makes clear freedom from mental fault. Toward living beings, having no close attachment of favoritism and no distant estrangement is called “without partiality.” “Without contention, without dispute” makes clear freedom from verbal fault. Next the practice of patience is cultivated: “toward all living beings, gaining a heart of great compassion and benefit, gentle and tamed” properly shows the capacity to endure; “without anger or resentment” and the rest removes the obstacle to patience. Next vigor is cultivated: “seeking the good without cease” is called freedom from weariness and sloth. Cultivating all practices in equal measure is therefore called the equal mind; what is cultivated being supreme is called the supreme mind; the seeking mind being earnest and weighty is therefore called the profound mind. Next the practice of meditation is cultivated: being far removed from a scattered mind is therefore called the concentrated mind. Below, the practice of wisdom is cultivated: “attaining love and attachment for the Dharma” is called loving the Dharma — this is with reference to the end; “at the time of hearing, the joy of nectar” is called delighting in the Dharma — this is with reference to the middle; “at the time of seeking, the mind rejoices” is called rejoicing in the Dharma — this is with reference to the beginning. The above is the cultivation of the antidotes; below it makes clear the freedom from faults. “Extinguishing all afflictions” is freedom from affliction; “removing the mind that inclines to evil destinies” is the removal of evil karma. The above completes the divisions; “perfecting all the practices of bodhisattvas” concludes them in summary. The above is the first, the practice of conduct and freedom from faults.

They are fully accomplished in immeasurable merit and virtue. They attain profound meditative concentration, the spiritual penetrations, the illuminations, and wisdom. They roam in aspiration through the seven limbs of enlightenment and cultivate the Buddha-Dharma in the mind. Their fleshly eye is pure and clear, so that nothing is not distinctly seen. Their heavenly eye is penetrating and unobstructed, immeasurable and boundless. Their Dharma eye observes and fathoms all paths. Their wisdom eye sees the truth and can cross to the other shore. Their Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the Dharma-nature. With unobstructed wisdom they expound for others.

[Commentary] The second [section] makes clear the perfection of accomplished virtue. “Fully accomplished in immeasurable virtue” gives a general statement; below it is revealed in detail. Within the detail, first the merit of self-benefit is made clear; from “with unobstructed” onward, the virtue of benefiting others is made clear. In the former, “they attain profound meditative concentration, the spiritual penetrations, the illuminations, and wisdom; they roam in aspiration through the seven limbs of enlightenment” is the merit of one's own portion. “Meditation” means the four dhyanas; “concentration” means the four formless concentrations and the like; “the penetrations” are the six spiritual penetrations; “the illuminations” are the three illuminations — the knowledge of past lives, the heavenly eye, and the extinction of outflows; “wisdom” means the three wisdoms, of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. As for the seven limbs of enlightenment, they are mindfulness, wisdom, vigor, pliancy, joy, concentration, and equanimity — these are the seven. From “cultivate the Buddha-Dharma in the mind” onward is the virtue of superior progress: cultivating the Buddha's virtue in the mind, seeking the Buddha's virtue above. From “the fleshly eye” onward, the accomplished virtue is immeasurable; here the meaning of the five eyes is raised in brief, and it is set forth fully in separate chapters, so it should be discussed in full. Now the text is simply explained. “The fleshly eye is pure and clear, so that nothing is not distinctly seen” — the fleshly eye is supreme. Form and skin are called flesh; the faculty of pure flesh is able to illumine and observe, and this is called an eye. In that land, by the retribution of fleshly eye one sees clearly the affairs of countless worlds — this is called pure and clear; what is seen is bright and exact, hence nothing is not understood. This illumines and observes present visible forms, and is called the fleshly eye. “The heavenly eye is penetrating and unobstructed, immeasurable and boundless” — the heavenly eye is supreme. All meditative concentrations are called the dwelling of heaven; relying on heaven one obtains the eye, hence it is called the heavenly eye. It can see living beings dying here and being born there; what is seen is broad and much, hence “immeasurable”; what is seen is long and far, hence “boundless.” “The Dharma eye observes and fathoms all paths” — the Dharma eye is supreme. Wisdom illumines dharmas, hence it is called the Dharma eye. It can see the faculties, desires, natures, and minds of all living beings, and it knows all the methods of transforming living beings. What is known reaches the utmost, and is called “fathoming”; clearly knowing the differences among the paths and dharmas of the three vehicles is called “fathoming all paths.” “The wisdom eye sees the truth and can cross to the other shore” — the wisdom eye is supreme. The true wisdom that illumines emptiness, seeing the principle, is called an eye; it can see true emptiness, hence “sees the truth”; casting off all marks of existence, it reaches the other shore of equality and no-marks, and is called “crossing to the other shore.” “The Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the Dharma-nature” — the Buddha eye is supreme. The former four are particular; the Buddha eye is universal. The sphere it sees is all-encompassing, hence “complete.” Moreover, the Buddha eye can see the non-empty true nature within the true Tathagata-garbha, and is called “awakening to the Dharma-nature.” The above is one's own virtue; “with unobstructed wisdom he expounds for others” is the virtue of benefiting others. This second [section] is finished.

They regard the three realms with equanimity, as empty and without anything whatsoever. They aspire to seek the Buddha-Dharma and are complete in all eloquence. They remove and extinguish the affliction-plagues of living beings. Born from the Tathagata, they understand the Dharma as thusness. They are skilled in knowing the methods of the sounds of gathering and cessation. They take no delight in worldly speech, but rejoice in right discourse. They cultivate all roots of goodness and aspire to the Buddha's Way. They know that all dharmas are utterly still and extinguished. The body born of birth and the afflictions — both remnants are wholly exhausted. Hearing the profound Dharma, their minds are free of doubt and fear, and they can constantly practice it. As for their great compassion, it is deep, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous, and there is nothing it does not cover and bear.

[Commentary] The third makes clear the completeness of cultivation. Within it there are two pairs, of self-benefit and benefit of others. The first pair concerns the beginning of cultivation; the latter pair concerns the end of cultivation. From the beginning through “removing and extinguishing the afflictions,” all of this is the first pair; from “born from the Tathagata” onward is the latter pair. In the former, the opening words, “they regard the three realms with equanimity, as empty and without anything whatsoever; they aspire to seek the Buddha-Dharma,” are self-benefit. Regarding the three realms with equanimity as empty and without anything is the practice that leaves birth-and-death behind; aspiring to seek the Buddha-Dharma is the practice that tends toward bodhi. From “complete in all eloquence” onward, the benefit of others is made clear: “complete in all eloquence” makes clear the virtue of transforming others; “removing and extinguishing the affliction-plagues of living beings” makes clear the benefit of transforming others. In the latter pair, first self-benefit is made clear; from “as for their great compassion” onward, the benefit of others is made clear. Within self-benefit the text has four parts: first, the understanding of one's own portion; second, from “they cultivate all roots of goodness” onward, the practice of one's own portion; third, from “hearing the profound Dharma” onward, the understanding of superior progress; fourth, from “they can constantly practice” onward, the practice of superior progress. In the understanding of one's own portion, “born from the Tathagata, they understand the Dharma as thusness” is the understanding of principle: their understanding is born and brought forth by the Tathagata's teaching and transformation, and therefore it is said to be “born from the Tathagata.” Emptiness and sameness are called “thus”; understanding and knowing that all myriad dharmas are all thus is called understanding thusness. “They are skilled in knowing the methods of the sounds of gathering and cessation” is the understanding of the teaching: the teaching that cultivates the good is called the sound of gathering; the teaching that extinguishes evil is called the sound of cessation. The bodhisattva is able to understand all of this well, and therefore is called “skilled in knowing”; within this he knows with skill, and therefore it is called “method.” Because he is able to know the sacred teaching well, “they take no delight in worldly speech, but rejoice in right discourse.” In the practice of one's own portion: “they cultivate all roots of goodness and aspire to the Buddha's Way” is the practice that tends toward bodhi; “they know that all dharmas are utterly still and extinguished; the body born of birth and the afflictions — both remnants are wholly exhausted” is the practice that extinguishes birth-and-death. Knowing all dharmas to be utterly still and extinguished is the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness; that the two remnants of the body born of birth and the afflictions are wholly exhausted is the accomplishment of cultivation and freedom from obstruction. The body born of birth is the painful retribution; the afflictions are the cause of delusion; these two remnants are all utterly extinguished. In the understanding of superior progress, “hearing the profound Dharma, their minds are free of doubt and fear”: because they can understand the profound, they do not doubt; because they can enter the profound, they do not fear. In the practice of superior progress, “they can constantly practice it” means that in regard to the Buddha's profound Dharma their practice never ceases. The above is self-benefit; next the benefit of others is made clear. “As for their great compassion” gives a general statement; below it is revealed in detail. “Deep, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous” means the compassionate mind is profound; “there is nothing it does not cover and bear” means compassion for living beings is vast. This third [section] is finished.

They reach the ultimate One Vehicle and arrive at the other shore. They cut through the net of doubt; wisdom issues from the mind. Toward the Buddha's teaching they encompass all, nothing outside. Their wisdom is like the great sea; their samadhi is like the king of mountains. The light of their wisdom is pure and bright, surpassing sun and moon. The dharmas of purity and whiteness are fully complete. They are like a mountain of clouds, for they illumine all virtues as one purity. They are like the great earth, for toward the pure and the foul, the fair and the ugly, they have no divided mind. They are like pure water, for they wash away all the dust and defilement of weariness. They are like the king of fire, for they burn up all the firewood of affliction. They are like a great wind, for they move through all worlds without obstruction. They are like empty space, for toward all forms of existence they are unattached. They are like the lotus flower, for in all the world they are unstained. They are like the great vehicle, for they carry the multitudes forth from birth-and-death. They are like heavy clouds, for they sound the great Dharma-thunder and awaken the unawakened. They are like a great rain, for they rain the Dharma of nectar and moisten living beings. They are like the adamantine mountain, for all demons and outsiders cannot move them. They are like Brahma, king of gods, for among all good dharmas they are foremost. They are like the nyagrodha tree, for they cover all alike. They are like the udumbara flower, for they are rare and hard to encounter. They are like the golden-winged bird, for they awe and subdue the outsiders. They are like the flocks of wandering birds, for they hoard and store up nothing. They are like the king of bulls, for none can overcome them. They are like the king of elephants, for they are well tamed. They are like the lion king, for they are without fear. Vast as empty space, for their great compassion is equal toward all.

[Commentary] The fourth makes clear the supremacy of accomplished virtue. Within it, first the virtue of self-benefit is made clear; from “like the great vehicle” onward, the virtue of benefiting others is made clear. In one's own virtue, first the supremacy of gathering the good; from “illumine all virtues” onward, the supremacy of freedom from faults. In the supremacy of gathering the good, “the ultimate One Vehicle” is the perfection of the virtue of bodhi. “Vehicle” means the functioning of practice; practice can carry and convey, and therefore it is called a vehicle. In accord with transforming [beings] there are many vehicles; as to reality they are not different, and therefore it is spoken of as one. The meaning of “one” is not uniform; broadly explained, there are four. First, “one” as distinguishing and separating: the Tathagata, in that teaching of the three baskets, divided [the Dharma] into three in accord with his transforming [beings]. For those seeking the hearer's [vehicle] he taught the four noble truths; for those seeking the solitary-buddha [vehicle] he taught causation; for those seeking the great vehicle he taught the six perfections, proclaiming that the bodhisattva, through three asamkhyeya kalpas, cultivates the six perfections that are still subject to outflows, and in the last life, within a single body, severs the fetters and attains buddhahood. Distinguishing and separating those three, therefore it is spoken of as one. Second, “one” as refuting separateness: the Tathagata, in accord with transforming [beings], proclaimed the three vehicles, and people of the world obstinately grasped them as real; to refute and set aside those three, therefore it is spoken of as one. Hence the sutra says: “Only the one is real; all the rest are not true — like an illusory city, not a true place of rest.” Third, “one” as gathering the separate: the Tathagata's root, divided into three and then gathered back to the root, therefore is spoken of as one, as the Srimala [Sutra] says. Fourth, “one” as without separateness: as to reality, speaking of reality, from the first there has been no distinction, and therefore it is called one. In this One Vehicle, reaching the end is called “ultimate”; “arriving at the other shore” is the ultimate fruit of nirvana. These two form one pair. “They cut through the net of doubt; wisdom issues from the mind” is their knowledge by realization: removing the false and revealing the true is called cutting the net of doubt; the true understanding issuing from within is called wisdom issuing from the mind. “Toward the Buddha's teaching they encompass all, nothing outside” is their knowledge of the teaching: understanding to the utmost without remainder is called encompassing all, nothing outside. This realization and this teaching together form one pair. “Their wisdom is like the great sea” makes clear that wisdom is deep and broad; “their samadhi is like a mountain” reveals that concentration is lofty and supreme; “the light of their wisdom is pure and bright, surpassing sun and moon” reveals the brightness of their wisdom; “the dharmas of purity and whiteness are fully complete, like a snowy mountain” shows the purity of their concentration. This concentration and wisdom again form one pair. The above is gathering the good; below the freedom from faults is revealed. “They illumine all virtues as one purity” is the direct statement: all virtues are pure, and this is called equal, one purity. Below it is revealed by similes; the similes are six in number, and the text and similes may be understood. The above is self-benefit; below the benefit of others is made clear, in thirteen clauses, all revealed through similes. “Like the great vehicle, for they carry the multitudes”: a great cart of the world is called a great vehicle; the virtue of benefiting others of those bodhisattvas is like a great cart of the world, and is called the great vehicle that carries the multitudes forth from birth-and-death. The rest may be understood. This fourth [section] is finished.

They crush and extinguish the mind of envy, for they do not begrudge others' superiority. They delight solely in seeking the Dharma, and their minds are never satiated. They constantly wish to expound it widely, and their resolve never wearies. They beat the Dharma-drum, raise the Dharma-banner, shine the sun of wisdom, and dispel the darkness of delusion. They cultivate the six harmonies and reverence, and constantly practice the giving of Dharma. Their resolve is brave and vigorous, and their minds never retreat or grow weak. They are a lamp for the world and the supreme field of blessing. They are constantly a teacher and guide, equal toward all, without hatred or love. They delight only in the right path, with no other joy or sorrow. They draw out the thorns of desire to bring peace to living beings. Their merit and virtue are supreme, and none fail to revere them. They extinguish the three defilements and their obstructions, and range through all spiritual penetrations.

[Commentary] The fifth [section] concerns the advance of practice. Within it there are five pairs, each beginning with benefiting others and then making clear self-benefit. What distinguishes the five pairs? The first two are one's own portion; the latter three are superior progress. In one's own portion, the first pair is the method that initiates cultivation. “They crush and extinguish the mind of envy, for they do not begrudge others' superiority” is the method of benefiting others: one whose mind is envious and begrudging cannot benefit others, and therefore this must be removed and extinguished. “They delight solely in seeking the Dharma, and their minds are never satiated” is the method of self-benefit. The next pair is proper cultivation. “They constantly wish to expound it widely, and their resolve never wearies” properly makes clear the benefit of others: constantly wishing to expound widely and their resolve never wearying is the supremacy of the mind that undertakes to speak. “They beat the Dharma-drum” and the rest is the supremacy of the Dharma that is spoken. To speak of beating the Dharma-drum is a simile for the Dharma of the wisdom of hearing: the sound of the teaching spreads far, and is called beating the Dharma-drum. “They raise the Dharma-banner” is a simile for the Dharma of the wisdom of reflection: establishing the meaning is called raising, and the meaning going forth is called a banner. “They shine the sun of wisdom and dispel the darkness of delusion” means that by teaching the Dharma of the wisdom of cultivation they open up living beings. “They cultivate the six harmonies and reverence” properly makes clear self-benefit: their practice accomplished, they are one with others, and their minds hold no discord or difference — this is called the six harmonies and reverence. Sameness of body, speech, and mind are the three harmonies; sameness of precepts, sameness of giving, and sameness of view make six in all. These six being harmonious, they come to be close and reverent toward one another, and this is called the six harmonies and reverence. Below, in superior progress, the first pair is the beginning of cultivation, the second the middle of cultivation, the third the accomplishment of cultivation. In the first pair, “they constantly practice the giving of Dharma” is the beginning of benefiting others; “their resolve is brave and vigorous, and their minds never retreat or grow weak” is the beginning of one's own practice. In the second pair, “they are a lamp for the world and the supreme field” and the rest is the middle of benefiting others. “They are a lamp for the world and the supreme field of blessing” makes clear the supremacy of the virtue of transformation: possessing wisdom themselves, they can produce understanding in living beings, and are called a lamp for the world; possessing merit themselves, they can produce goodness in living beings, and are called the supreme field of blessing. “They are constantly a teacher and guide, equal toward all, without hatred or love” makes clear the supremacy of the benefit of transformation: opening people by wisdom is called being a teacher and guide; benefiting and moistening them with blessed goodness is why there is no hatred or love. “They delight only in the right path, with no other joy or sorrow” is the middle of one's own practice: delighting in the Way and cultivating the good is “delighting only”; having nothing else is freedom from faults. In the third pair, “they draw out the thorns of desire” and the rest is the accomplishment of benefiting others: drawing out the thorns of desire to bring peace to living beings transforms people to leave faults behind; “their merit and wisdom are supreme, and none fail to revere them” transforms people to follow the good. “They extinguish the three defilements” and the rest is the accomplishment of one's own practice: extinguishing the three defilements and their obstructions accomplishes the virtue of severance — greed, hatred, and delusion are the three defilements and obstructions; “they range through all spiritual penetrations” accomplishes the virtue of practice. This fifth [section] is finished.

The power of cause, the power of conditions, the power of intention, the power of vows, the power of skillful means; the power of constancy, the power of goodness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom; the power of much hearing; the powers of giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom; the power of right mindfulness and of calm and insight; the powers of the spiritual penetrations and illuminations; the power of the Tathagata's taming and disciplining; the power of [transforming] all living beings. Powers such as these are all complete.

[Commentary] The sixth [section] concerns the completeness of the powers. First the divisions, then the conclusion. Within the divisions, first the completeness of one's own powers is made clear; from “the Tathagata's taming and disciplining” onward, the powers of transforming others are complete. Within one's own, following one another they make seven gates. The power of cause and the power of conditions form the first gate, the basis on which cultivation arises: all the good practices cultivated in the past can produce present goodness, and are called the power of cause; drawing near to good teachers and hearing the right Dharma is called the power of conditions. The power of intention and the power of vows form the second gate, the method by which cultivation arises: the mind that seeks the Buddha is called the power of intention; the vow that arouses practice is called the power of vows. The power of skillful means, the power of constancy, and the power of goodness form the third gate, preparatory practice and proper cultivation: cultivating with skill in accord with the Dharma is called the power of skillful means; cultivating constantly in accord with the Dharma is called the power of constancy; cultivating rightly in accord with the Dharma is called the power of goodness. The power of concentration and the power of wisdom form the fourth gate, the accomplishment of cultivating the mind: the accomplishment of cultivating calm is called the power of concentration; the accomplishment of cultivating insight is called the power of wisdom. These first four gates are distinguished with respect to cultivation. The power of much hearing forms the fifth gate, the understanding that gives rise to practice. The powers of giving, precepts, patience, vigor, concentration, and wisdom form the sixth gate: it makes clear the practice that is produced, and that practice is the six perfections. These two gates are distinguished with respect to practice. The power of right mindfulness and right contemplation, and the powers of the spiritual penetrations and illuminations, form the seventh gate, the virtue accomplished by relying on practice: casting off marks and entering reality is called right mindfulness; leaving delusion and seeing the Dharma is spoken of as right contemplation. Relying on these two, one accomplishes the six spiritual penetrations and attains the three illuminations, and this is called the power of penetrations and illuminations. This last gate is distinguished with respect to virtue. The above is self-benefit; “in accord with the Dharma he accomplishes the power of [transforming] all living beings” makes clear the benefit of others. The above completes the divisions; “powers such as these are all complete” concludes them in summary. This sixth [section] is finished.

His body, countenance, and marks, his merit and eloquence, are fully adorned, and none is equal to him. He reverently makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, and is constantly praised together by all the Buddhas. He perfects all the bodhisattva perfections and cultivates the samadhis of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness, and the samadhi-doors of non-arising and non-ceasing. He is far removed from the grounds of the hearers and the solitary Buddhas.

[Commentary] The seventh takes all the virtues together and praises them in summary, revealing their supremacy. Within it there are four: first, one's own virtue is supreme; second, one is praised together by the Buddhas; third, the great vehicle is perfected; fourth, the lesser vehicles are surpassed. In the first, “his body, countenance, and marks, his merit and eloquence, are fully adorned, and none is equal to him” is what is accomplished by one's own portion. That his body, countenance, and marks have no equal makes clear the supremacy of his body; that his merit and eloquence have no equal makes clear the supremacy of his virtue; the words “fully” make clear that virtue is complete; the word “adorned” makes clear that the body is adorned. “He reverently makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas” is what superior progress brings forth. The second, the praise of the Buddhas, is evident. In the third part, “he perfects all the bodhisattva perfections” is the fulfillment of the practice of the teaching; “he cultivates the samadhis of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness, and of non-arising and non-ceasing” is the fulfillment of the practice of realization. In the fourth part, he surpasses the two vehicles — the text is evident. The above is the separate praise.

Ānanda, those bodhisattvas accomplish immeasurable merit and virtue such as this. I have but spoken of it to you in brief; were I to speak of it fully, a hundred thousand million kalpas could not exhaust it.
[Commentary] Here it concludes with a summary of praise.
The above eight sections together form the first, setting forth the supremely blissful matters of Amitabha's land.

The Buddha told the bodhisattva Maitreya, the gods and humans, and all the rest: In the land of Immeasurable Life the hearers and the bodhisattvas — their merit, virtue, and wisdom are beyond all reckoning, and that land itself is subtle, wondrous, blissful, and pure as this. Why do you not strive with all your strength to do good, and set your minds upon the Way that comes of itself? Dwell neither above nor below; penetrate to the boundless edge. Each of you should diligently advance, and strive to seek it for yourselves: you will surely pass beyond and go, reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, their courses are closed of themselves; you rise upon the Way that knows no end. Easy it is to go, and yet there are none who go; that land turns none away, for nature itself draws them on. Why not cast the world's affairs aside, and diligently practice, seeking the Way and its virtue? Thus may you attain the utmost of long life, with lifespan and bliss that have no end.

[Commentary] The second [section] urges people to seek rebirth. “The Buddha told Maitreya” indicates whom he addressed; “the gods and humans and all the rest” names those for whom it was spoken. “In the land of Immeasurable Life the merit, virtue, and wisdom of the hearers and bodhisattvas cannot be told” takes up what was distinguished above: the merit, virtue, and wisdom of the hearers and bodhisattvas cannot be told — this takes up the persons distinguished in the preceding text. “And that land itself is subtle, wondrous, blissful, and pure as this” takes up the land distinguished in the preceding text. From “why do you not strive” onward, it properly urges rebirth. Within that there are three: first, it properly urges rebirth; second, from “easy it is to go” onward, the Tathagata grieves and laments; third, from “why not cast aside” onward, it again urges rebirth. In the first, “why do you not strive with all your strength to do good” properly urges the cultivation of the cause: why do you not exert yourselves to do good and seek rebirth — this is called striving for good. From “set your minds upon the Way” onward, the benefit of cultivation is made clear: one who sets his mind on the Way is naturally reborn there, and this is called thinking upon the Way that comes of itself. Simply being able to think upon the Way, one's practice and virtue become manifest, and without distinction of high or low all alike attain rebirth; hence it says, “dwell neither above nor below.” If one attains birth there, one's spiritual penetrations are thoroughly penetrating, without any boundary; hence it says, “penetrate to the boundless edge.” “Each of you should diligently advance, and strive to seek it” again urges the cultivation of the cause. From “you will surely pass beyond” onward, the benefit of cultivation is again made clear: “you will surely pass beyond” reveals what one leaves behind; “reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss” reveals where one arrives. “Cutting across the five evils, the evil destinies are closed of themselves” reveals what one leaves. The three evil paths and the human and heavenly paths are the five destinies. Distinguishing among these, the lower three evil paths are called evil destinies, and the two paths of humans and gods are called good destinies. Here, however, in relation to Amitabha's pure land, the five paths of the Saha world are all alike called evil destinies: hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals are what pure evil leads to, and are called evil destinies; the humans and gods of the Saha world are what mixed evil leads to, and are also called evil destinies. If one relies on cultivation in this land to sever and remove them, one first severs the delusions of view, leaving the causes of the three evil paths and extinguishing their fruits; afterward one severs the delusions of cultivation, leaving the causes of the human and heavenly paths and cutting off their fruits. This gradual removal is not called cutting across. If one attains rebirth in Amitabha's pure land, the five paths of the Saha world are all at once abandoned, and therefore it is called cutting across. “Cutting across the five evil destinies” is cutting across their fruits; “the evil destinies are closed of themselves” is closing their causes. This makes clear what is left behind. “You rise upon the Way that knows no end” reveals what is attained: the Way attained is deep and broad, and therefore has no end. The above is the first, properly urging rebirth. From here is the second, the Tathagata's lament, wishing to make people of the world strive with all their strength for rebirth. The opening words, “easy it is to go, and yet there are none who go,” are precisely the lament: to cultivate the cause is at once to go, and this is called easy to go; that none cultivate the cause and those reborn are few is why it says there are none. “That land turns none away” reveals the former, that it is easy to go; “drawn on by nature itself” reveals the latter, that there are none. The living beings of the Saha world, long habituated to the hindrances and fetters, are naturally bound and dragged away by them and do not go; hence there are none. From here is the third, again urging rebirth: “why not cast the world's affairs aside, and diligently seek the Way and its virtue” urges the cultivation of the cause; “thus may you attain the utmost of long life, with lifespan and bliss that have no end” makes clear that by cultivation one obtains the fruit.
The above is the first, setting forth the supremely blissful matters of Amitabha's land, to make people vow and seek it.

From here is the second, revealing that the Saha world is filled with filth and evil, to make people weary and renounce it. Within it there are four: first, it raises the faults of the three poisons and the afflictions; second, it urges people to cultivate renunciation; third, it raises the faults of the suffering of the five evils, five pains, and five burnings; fourth, it urges people to cultivate renunciation.

In the first part, first the fault of greed is made clear. From “the people of the world, fathers and sons” onward, the fault of hatred is made clear. From “such people of the world do not believe” onward, the fault of delusion is made clear.

Yet the people of the world are shallow and vulgar, contending together over matters that are not urgent. Amid such fierce evil and extreme suffering they labor body and mind in their affairs to supply and sustain themselves.
