There is no noble and no base, no poor and no rich: young and old, men and women, all alike worry over wealth; whether they have or have not, it is the same, and their anxious thoughts are exactly equal. Distressed and sorrowful, they pile up thoughts and accumulate cares, driven about by their minds, with never a moment of peace. Having fields, they worry over the fields; having houses, they worry over the houses; cattle and horses, the six kinds of livestock, servants and slaves, money and goods, clothing, food, and the various necessities — over these too they worry together. Thought upon thought, breath upon breath, they worry, brood, and fear. Unexpectedly they meet with fire and flood that are not of the ordinary course, with robbers and thieves, with enemies and creditors, who burn, drown, seize, and plunder them, so that all is scattered, dissolved, worn away, and destroyed. The poison of anxiety leaves them restless and fearful, with no time of release. Wrath knotted in the heart, they never part from care and affliction. Their minds are hard and their wills fixed, and they will not let go. At times they are crushed and broken, their bodies die and their lives end; they are cast off and go, and none follows them. The honored and the wealthy have this affliction too: a thousand kinds of worry and dread, toil and bitterness like this, binding up all manner of cold and heat, dwelling together with pain. The poor and lowly are oppressed and lacking, in constant want. Having no fields, they worry and wish to have fields; having no houses, they worry and wish to have houses; having no cattle, horses, the six kinds of livestock, servants and slaves, money and goods, clothing, food, and the various necessities, they likewise worry and wish to have them. Having just one, they are again short of one; with this and lacking that, they think only of having equal measure. Just as they wish to be fully supplied, all is again scattered and ruined. In such worry and suffering they must again go seeking; unable to obtain it in time, their thoughts bring no benefit. Body and mind are both wearied, and whether sitting or rising they are never at ease. Anxious thoughts follow one another; toil and bitterness like this bind up all manner of cold and heat, and they dwell together with pain. Sometimes because of this their lives are cut short. Unwilling to do good, to walk the Way, and to advance in virtue, when their lifespan ends and their bodies die they must go far away alone, toward some destination; whether the path be good or evil, none can know it.

[Commentary] Within greed there are three: first, taking worldly people generally to make clear the fault of greed; second, from “the honored” onward, taking the wealthy in particular to make clear the fault of greed; third, from “the poor” onward, taking the poor and lowly in particular to make clear the fault of greed. In the first part, “the people of the world are shallow and vulgar, contending over matters that are not urgent” makes clear that they have evil — that is, these people of the world are shallow in their customs and contend together over the world's matters that are not urgent. From “amid such fierce” onward, it reveals that they have suffering. Within suffering there are three: first, the suffering of seeking wealth; second, from “having fields” onward, it makes clear the suffering of guarding and protecting; third, from “unexpectedly” onward, it makes clear the suffering of loss and scattering. In the first, on the suffering of seeking: “amid such fierce suffering they labor body and mind in their affairs to supply and sustain themselves” is seeking for the sake of the body; “no noble, no base” and the rest is seeking for the sake of others — “no noble and no base, no poor and no rich” names those who are able to seek; “young and old, men” and the rest names those for whom they seek. Below it makes clear that there is suffering: “all alike worry over wealth” makes clear the suffering of mind; “driven about by their minds” makes clear the suffering of body. In the suffering of guarding and protecting, “having fields, they worry over the fields; having houses, they worry over the houses” and the like separately make clear their suffering; “thought upon thought” concludes it. In the suffering of loss and scattering, “unexpectedly they meet with fire and flood that are not of the ordinary course, with robbers” and the rest makes clear the suffering of losing wealth; “at times they are crushed” and the rest makes clear the suffering of losing the body. Next, taking the wealthy to make clear the fault of greed, the text is evident. In making clear the fault of greed with respect to the poor and lowly, the text has three parts: first, the suffering of seeking wealth; second, from “sometimes because of this” onward, the suffering of losing the body; third, from “unwilling” onward, future suffering. In the suffering of seeking wealth the text has five parts: first, when there is presently nothing, worrying about it gives rise to suffering; second, from “having just one” onward, when there is a little, it makes clear the suffering of insufficiency; third, from “just as they wish to be fully supplied” onward, when things have been obtained, it makes clear the suffering of scattering and loss; fourth, from “they must again go seeking” onward, it makes clear the suffering of not obtaining while pressing forward to seek; fifth, from “they bind up all manner of cold and heat” onward, it makes clear the suffering of cold and heat and the like while pursuing and seeking. These five together form the suffering of seeking wealth. The suffering of losing the body and the future suffering are evident in the text.

The people of the world — fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers, husbands and wives, household members, and relatives near and far — should mutually respect and love one another, and should not hate or envy one another. Whether they have or have not, they should communicate with one another, and must not be greedy and stingy. In speech and countenance they should always be harmonious, and must not oppose or go against one another. Sometimes, when the mind is calm, there may arise some anger; the resentment of this present life, with slight mutual hatred and envy, in later lives becomes more violent, until it grows into great enmity. Why is this? In the affairs of the world, people harm one another; though it is not immediate, one should urgently break it off and dissolve it. Yet they hold poison and store up wrath, knotting their resentment into the spirit, and naturally it is marked and recorded, so that they cannot be parted; each must be born facing the other, and they retaliate upon one another. A person in the world, amid love and desire, is born alone and dies alone, departs alone and comes alone. When he must go on to the places of suffering and pleasure, his body must bear them itself, and there is none to take his place. Good and evil transform, calamity and blessing lie in different places; prepared and waiting in advance, he must go alone into them, far off to another place, and none can see him. Good and evil come naturally, following the deeds of where one is born. Dark and obscure, separation is long; the roads are not the same, and the meeting has no appointed time. It is very hard, very hard — and now you have met one another. Why not cast aside the many affairs, each of you, while you are strong and hale, strive diligently to cultivate goodness, and with vigor vow to cross over the world? Then you may attain the utmost of long life. How is it that you do not seek the Way? What are you waiting for? What delight is there?

[Commentary] In making clear the fault of hatred, the text has three parts: first, teaching and exhorting by principle — they should mutually love and respect one another, not hate or envy one another; whether they have or have not, they should communicate with one another and must not be greedy and stingy; in speech and countenance always harmonious, not opposing one another. Second, from “or when the mind contends” onward, it broadly makes clear the fault of hatred. Third, from “why not cast aside” onward, it urges the cultivation of renunciation. In the second fault there are three kinds: first, it makes clear the fault of future enmity and harm; second, from “a person in the world” onward, it makes clear the fault of future evil destinies; third, from “what is born is dark and obscure” onward, it makes clear the fault of separation and the difficulty of reunion. In the third part, the urging to renounce is evident.

Such people of the world do not believe that by doing good one obtains good and by practicing the Way one attains the Way; they do not believe that people die and are born again, or that giving brings blessing. The matters of good and evil they do not believe at all; they say it is not so, that in the end there is no such thing. Merely because of this, they hold to their own views, and looking at one another, first and last alike, they transmit and receive them in turn, the leftover instructions of their fathers. Their forebears and grandfathers from the first did no good and did not know the Way or its virtue; their bodies were dull and their spirits dark, their minds blocked and their thoughts shut. The destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil, they could not see for themselves, and there was none to tell them. Good fortune and ill, calamity and blessing, they vied with one another in bringing about, and not one was astonished. The constant way of birth and death is passed on and established in turn: sometimes a father weeps for a son, sometimes a son weeps for a father; brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another in turn. Reversed and turned upside down, high and low, impermanence is the root of it all; all must pass away and cannot be permanently kept. Though one teaches and instructs and opens the way for them, few believe. Therefore birth and death flow on in ceaseless round, without rest. People such as these are benighted and obstinate; they do not believe the sutras or the Dharma, their minds hold no far-reaching consideration, and each wishes only to please himself. Deluded by desire, they do not penetrate the Way and its virtue; lost and drowned in anger, they are ravenous as wolves for wealth and lust. Because of this they do not attain the Way, and must again suffer in evil destinies; birth and death have no end. Alas, how grievous! Sometimes in a household, father and son, brothers, husbands and wives, one dies and one lives, and they pity one another; with loving thoughts they long and yearn, their cares and memories bound fast, their hearts pierced and attached, looking back to one another in love. Day after day, year after year, there is no release. Though one teaches them the Way and its virtue, their minds are not opened; they dwell on thoughts of affection and fondness and do not part from desire. Dull and darkened, blocked and shut, covered over by delusion, they cannot deeply consider and carefully plan, set their own minds upright, devote themselves single-mindedly to practicing the Way, and decisively cut off worldly affairs. Thus they spin on until the end, and when their years and lifespan are exhausted they cannot attain the Way, and there is no help for it. All in confusion and disorder, they covet love and desire; those deluded about the Way are many, those who awaken are few. In the world's hurrying there is nothing to rely on. Noble and base, high and low, rich and poor, honored and humble, toiling anxiously in their busy affairs, each harbors the poison of killing; evil airs darken, and they stir up false undertakings, opposing heaven and earth and not following the human heart. The nature of evil does not [strike] at once: first it accords and is granted to them, and they are left free to do as they please, until their offenses reach the extreme. Before their lifespan is ended, it is suddenly snatched away, and they fall into evil destinies, toiling bitterly through successive lives, turning and turning within them for thousands of millions of kalpas, with no time of escape. The pain is beyond words, and they are greatly to be pitied.

[Commentary] In making clear the fault of delusion, the text has two parts: first, it makes clear that there is delusion; second, from “the constant way of birth and death is passed on” onward, it makes clear the fault of delusion. The former has two parts: first, it makes clear that deluded people themselves have no right faith; second, from “looking at one another” onward, they wholly receive the words of others. In [the part on] having no faith themselves, the discussion is first made separately; from “merely because of this” onward, it concludes with a summary revealing the fault: because they do not believe, they obstinately grasp their own views — this is their fault. In [the part on] receiving the words of others, “looking at one another, first and last alike, they imitate and learn from others”; from “they transmit and receive them in turn” onward, they inherit and learn from their fathers and grandfathers. Within that, the opening words, “they transmit and receive them in turn, the leftover instructions of their fathers,” make clear that the son, being without knowledge, receives his father's false words. From “their forebears and grandfathers” onward, it raises the father's delusion and obstinacy, which forms the son's lack of knowledge. Within that there are four clauses. First, “their forebears and grandfathers from the first did no good” makes clear that they have no practice. Second, “they did not know the Way or its virtue” reveals that they have no understanding. Third, “their bodies were dull and their spirits dark, their minds blocked and their thoughts shut; the destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil, they could not see for themselves, and there was none to tell them” again makes clear that they have no understanding. The preceding clause's lack of understanding was not knowing the way out of delusion; this clause's lack of understanding is not knowing the causes and fruits of good and evil in the world. That they could not see the destinies of birth and death for themselves is not knowing the fruit; that they could not see the paths of good and evil for themselves is not knowing the cause. Toward these causes and fruits their own minds have no understanding, and there is none to tell them, and therefore they never understand. Fourth, “good fortune and ill, calamity and blessing, they vied with one another in bringing about, and not one was astonished” again makes clear that they have no practice. The preceding clause's lack of practice revealed that they did not do good; this clause's lack of practice makes clear that they create evil — they do evil themselves, and there is none to tell them, and therefore they never leave it. The above passage makes clear that there is delusion; below it makes clear the fault of delusion. Within that there are four: first, because of delusion fathers and sons weep for one another; second, from “people such as these” onward, it makes clear that because of delusion they create evil and suffer; third, from “sometimes in a household” onward, it makes clear that because of delusion relatives remember one another; fourth, from “all in confusion” onward, it makes clear that because of delusion they create evil and suffer. In the first, it first makes clear that fathers and sons weep for one another; from “though one teaches and instructs” onward, it makes clear the difficulty of opening and awakening them — this is why birth and death flow on without cease, and they turn about within it. In the second part there are five clauses: first, it makes clear that these deluded people are benighted and obstinate, do not believe the sutras or the Dharma, and each follows his own pleasure; second, they are deluded by love and desire and do not penetrate the Way and its virtue; third, they are lost in anger and ravenous for wealth and lust; fourth, because of the former three they do not attain the right Way but receive many sufferings — “must again [suffer in] evil destinies” reveals that they have heavy suffering, and “birth and death have no end” reveals that their suffering is deep; fifth, from “alas” onward, the Tathagata grieves and laments, making people weary and renounce it. The third passage has three clauses: first, because of delusion relatives remember one another and cannot be opened or released; second, from “they dwell on thoughts” onward, it makes clear that because of such remembering they cannot cultivate goodness; third, from “thus they spin on” onward, because they do not cultivate goodness they cannot attain the Way. In the fourth passage there are four clauses: first, because of delusion they give rise to greed, pursue worldly affairs, and are all in confusion and disorder — greed, desire, and love and the rest; second, from “each harbors the poison of killing” onward, because of delusion they give rise to hatred and harm one another — each harbors the poison of killing, evil airs darken, and they stir up false undertakings; third, from “naturally” onward, it makes clear that because of their former evil they receive suffering and find no way out: those who create offenses, by the power of their past offenses, naturally gather unlawful and evil conditions, which accord and are granted to them; they are left free to commit offenses until their offenses reach the extreme, when all is suddenly snatched away and they are about to enter evil destinies, to suffer without limit; fourth, from “the pain is beyond words” onward, the Tathagata grieves and laments, causing people to feel revulsion.

The above broadly raises the faults of the three poisons. From here is the second, urging people to strive to cultivate renunciation. Within it there are four: first, it properly urges the cultivation of renunciation; second, Maitreya understands and receives it; third, it again urges renunciation; fourth, Maitreya receives and practices it.

The Buddha told the bodhisattva Maitreya, the gods and humans, and all the rest: I now say to you: in the affairs of the world, it is by these that people are hindered and do not attain the Way. You should consider them carefully, keep far from all evils, choose what is good, and diligently practice it. Love and desire, glory and splendor cannot be permanently kept; all must be parted from, and there is nothing to delight in. Having met a Buddha in the world, you should diligently press forward. Those who have the utmost vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss can attain wisdom, clarity, and penetration, with merit and virtue supreme. Do not follow the desires of your own mind, failing and betraying the sutras and precepts and falling behind others. If perchance you have doubts and do not understand the sutra, you may ask the Buddha fully, and he will explain it for you.

[Commentary] The first has two parts: first, it urges people to cultivate practice; second, from “if perchance you have doubts” onward, it urges people to ask questions. The urging to cultivate has three parts: first, it raises the former faults and urges people to cultivate their severance — “the Buddha told Maitreya: in the affairs of the world, it is by these that people are hindered and do not attain the Way” raises the former faults. “The affairs of the world” takes up and raises the matters of the three poisons set forth above. “By” is “because of”; “hindered” is “owing to.” The people of the world, because of these matters of the three poisons, are hindered from attaining the Way. From “you should carefully” onward is the exhortation: “you should consider them carefully and keep far from all evils” urges people to renounce faults — that is, to keep far from the many evils of the three poisons set forth above; “choose what is good and practice it” urges the cultivation of the antidotes. Second, from “love and desire” onward, it raises the fault of the impermanence of the five desires of the world and urges people to cultivate renunciation. Third, from “having met a Buddha in the world” onward, it raises the Buddha's presence in the world and urges people to practice diligently. Within that, it first raises the Buddha's presence in the world and properly urges cultivation; from “those who have the vow” onward, it reveals the benefit and urges them on — “attain wisdom, clarity, and penetration” is attaining the supremacy of wisdom; “merit and virtue supreme” is attaining the supremacy of blessing. From “do not” onward, it raises the loss and admonishes and restrains. The above, urging practice and urging questioning, may be understood.

The bodhisattva Maitreya, kneeling long upon the ground, said: “The Buddha's majestic spirit is honored and weighty; what you have spoken is excellent and good. Hearing the Buddha's sutra words, I penetrate them with my mind and ponder them. The people of the world are truly so, as the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha, in his compassion, displays the great Way, so that ear and eye are opened and brightened, and we long attain deliverance. Hearing what the Buddha has spoken, none are other than joyful. The gods, the people, and the crawling creatures all receive the compassionate grace and are freed from care and suffering. The Buddha's words of teaching and admonition are very profound and very good; his wisdom clearly sees the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, of past, future, and present, and nothing is not thoroughly understood. That we, this assembly and others, have been able to receive deliverance is entirely owing to the Buddha's humility and hardship in former lives when he sought the Way. His grace and virtue cover all; his blessings are towering; the light shines everywhere, reaching the emptiness that has no limit, opening people to nirvana, teaching and gathering the scriptures, subduing and transforming by awe, moving the ten directions, without end or limit. The Buddha is the king of Dharma, honored beyond all sages, the teacher of all gods and humans everywhere, and according to the vows of their minds he causes them all to attain the Way. Now we have met the Buddha and again heard the name of Immeasurable Life; none are other than joyful, and our minds attain opening and clarity.”

[Commentary] The second, Maitreya's understanding and reception, has two parts: first, he properly understands and receives; second, from “now we have met” onward, he rejoices and congratulates himself. The former has four parts: first, he praises the Buddha's words as excellent — “I penetrate them with my mind and ponder them; the people of the world are truly so” completes the praise of the teaching as excellent. “Penetrate” means to pass through: passing through with the mind and pondering it, the people of the world truly follow the matters of the three poisons and are hindered from attaining the Way — this is called “truly so.” Second, from “the Buddha's words” onward, he receives the Buddha's compassionate transformation. Third, from “the Buddha's words of teaching” onward, he again praises the Buddha's teaching as profound and good; within that, it first praises the teaching as profound and good, and “his wisdom clearly sees” and the rest raises the wisdom that perfects the teaching. Fourth, from “that we, this assembly and others” onward, he again celebrates the Buddha's grace. That we, this assembly and others, have been able to receive deliverance is the reason; below it properly brings it forth: because the Buddha in former lives diligently and painfully cultivated the Way, he now has attained the Buddha fruit and transforms and guides us, and therefore we attain deliverance. “Entirely owing to the Buddha's humility and hardship in former lives when he sought the Way” raises the Buddha's cause; “his grace and virtue cover all” reveals the Buddha's fruit. “His grace and virtue cover all” raises the Buddha's virtue in general; “his blessings are towering” and the rest reveal it in particular; “the Buddha is the king of Dharma, honored beyond all sages” concludes and praises in summary. In the particular, the opening words, “his blessings are towering, and the light shines everywhere,” mean that his own blessing is supreme; “reaching the emptiness that has no limit” means his own wisdom is supreme; “opening people to nirvana, teaching and gathering the scriptures” is benefiting by wisdom — “opening people to nirvana” transforms people to realize cessation; “teaching and gathering the scriptures” teaches people to arouse the Way: training the world in the Dharma of the Way is called teaching; taking up the many meanings in these scriptures and causing people to study and learn them is called gathering. “Subduing and transforming by awe” and the rest is benefiting by blessing: for hard and stubborn living beings, by the power of majestic virtue he restrains and repels them, causing them to submit and yield and take refuge in the sacred transformation; therefore it is called subduing and transforming by awe. For gentle living beings, he gathers them in by the power of compassion, and this is called moving the ten directions: those with karmic affinity are gathered in — this is called without end or limit. The concluding praise may be understood. The above is understanding and reception; “now we have met the Buddha and again heard the name of Immeasurable Life; none are other than joyful, and our minds attain opening and clarity” is rejoicing and congratulating himself. This second passage is Maitreya's understanding and reception.

From here is the third, again urging the cultivation of renunciation. Within it there are four: first, it praises Maitreya's receiving and bearing the Buddha's grace; second, from “Maitreya, you should know that you, from countless kalpas past” onward, it congratulates Maitreya on having met the Buddha and heard the Dharma, and on having heard the name of Immeasurable Life; third, from “you may also now be weary of” onward, it properly urges cultivation; fourth, from “each of you should diligently advance” onward, it urges the renunciation of doubt.

The Buddha told Maitreya: What you have said is so. If there are those who are compassionate and reverent toward the Buddha, this is truly great goodness. Only after long ages does a Buddha again appear in the world. Now I have become a Buddha in this world, expounding the sutras and the Dharma, proclaiming the teaching of the Way, cutting off all nets of doubt, pulling up the root of love and desire, and blocking up the source of all evils. I walk through the three realms without any obstruction; I gather the essentials of wisdom and of all the paths; I hold fast the guiding principles, clear and distinct, opening and revealing the five destinies, delivering those not yet delivered, and decisively settling the Way of birth and death and of nirvana.

[Commentary] In the first, “the Buddha told Maitreya: what you have said is so” seals his former words: Maitreya had just praised the Buddha's teaching as excellent, very profound, and very good, and these words accord with principle, and therefore it says “is so.” From “if there are those who are compassionate” onward, it praises Maitreya's receiving and bearing the Buddha's grace: Maitreya had just taken pity on the Buddha's diligence and hardship for the sake of living beings in former lives, when he aspired to seek the Buddha Way — this is called being compassionate toward the Buddha; reverently bearing the Buddha's grace is called revering the Buddha. This is truly great goodness. From “only after long ages does a Buddha appear in the world” onward, it raises the Buddha's transforming benefit and recounts what was said above: that only after long ages does a Buddha again appear in the world reveals how hard it is to meet one. From “now I” onward, it makes clear his own transforming benefit. Within that there are four: first, it reveals that he himself has become a Buddha and transforms the world by the Dharma; second, from “cutting off all” onward, because the Buddha now appears and transforms, he teaches all living beings to cut off the cause of death — “cutting off all nets of doubt” and “pulling up the root of love and desire” cause them to leave affliction; “blocking up the source of all evils” causes them to leave evil karma. “Blocking” is “stopping”: evil karma is the root of the evil destinies, and is called the source of all evils; he teaches them to cut it off and stop it, and this is called blocking. Third, from “I walk” onward, it reveals that he himself has become a Buddha and transforms the world by the Dharma: “I walk through the three realms without any obstruction” is transformation by the karma of body — bodily transformation being at ease, there is no obstruction. “I gather the essentials of wisdom and of all the paths” is transformation by the karma of mind: understanding the scriptures well and gathering and knowing their many meanings is called gathering the essentials of wisdom; knowing well the essentials of the practice of the three vehicles is called the essentials of all the paths. “I hold fast the guiding principles, clear and distinct, opening and revealing the five destinies” is transformation by the karma of speech: holding the Dharma and upholding living beings is called holding fast the guiding principles; distinguishing the right and setting apart the false is called clear and distinct; using this to transform the multitudes is called opening the five destinies. Fourth, from “delivering those not yet delivered” onward, it is the Buddha's transformation of the world: he teaches all living beings to go forth from the fruit of birth and death. “Delivering those not yet delivered” and “decisively settling the Way of birth and death” cause them to go forth from birth and death; “the Way of nirvana” causes them to attain nirvana. Raising this transforming benefit recounts what Maitreya praised and received. This first passage is finished.

Maitreya, you should know that since countless kalpas past you have cultivated the bodhisattva practice, wishing to deliver living beings, and it has been long indeed. Those who have attained the Way from you, up to nirvana, cannot be numbered. You, and all the gods, humans, and the fourfold assembly of the ten directions, since everlasting kalpas have turned about in the five paths, in care, dread, toil, and suffering beyond full telling, and even in this present life your birth and death have not ceased. Now you have met the Buddha and heard and received the sutras and the Dharma, and again have heard of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. How joyful, how excellent! I rejoice with you.

[Commentary] The second congratulates Maitreya on having met the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and heard of the Immeasurable Life [Buddha]. Within it there are three: first, it reveals that Maitreya's cultivation reaches far back; second, from “even in this” onward, it makes clear that now he has met the Buddha and heard of Immeasurable Life; third, from “how joyful” onward, the Tathagata congratulates him. In the former, the opening words, “since countless kalpas past you have cultivated the bodhisattva practice, wishing to deliver living beings, and it has been long indeed,” mean his cultivation reaches far back; “those who have attained the Way from you, up to nirvana, cannot be numbered” means the noble ones who have come forth from him are far-reaching. “You, and all the gods, humans, and the fourfold assembly of the ten directions, since everlasting kalpas have been in care, dread, toil, and suffering beyond full telling” means their toil and suffering are many; “everlasting” means long. By relying on these many causes, they now meet the Buddha and hear of Immeasurable Life, and this is cause for congratulation. The latter two may be understood. This second [passage] is finished.

Now you should also yourselves be weary of birth and death, old age, sickness, and pain; of what is foul and impure, there is nothing to delight in. You should decisively resolve, make your bodies upright and your conduct correct, increasingly do all that is good, cultivate yourselves and purify your bodies, and wash away the defilement of the mind. Let your words and deeds be loyal and trustworthy, so that the outside and the inside correspond. A person can deliver himself and in turn rescue others. With keen clarity seek and vow, and accumulate the roots of goodness. Though for one life you toil and suffer, it is but a moment; afterward you will be born in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond limit. You will long be joined with the Way and its virtue in one brightness, forever uprooting the root of birth and death, and never again will you have the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, of care and suffering. If you wish for a lifespan of one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand million myriads of kalpas, freely and as you will, all can be obtained. By non-doing and spontaneity you will be next to the Way of nirvana.

[Commentary] The third properly urges cultivation. The words are addressed to Maitreya, but the meaning includes all. Within it, first it properly urges cultivation; from “though for one life” onward, it reveals the benefit and urges living beings on. The former has three parts: first, it urges the renunciation of faults; second, from “make your bodies upright” onward, it urges the cultivation of good dharmas; third, from “a person can deliver himself” onward, it urges benefiting living beings. In urging the renunciation of faults, “now you should also yourselves be weary of birth, old age, sickness,” and the rest urges the arising of a mind of revulsion: birth, old age, sickness, and death are the inner sufferings; the words “and pain” refer to outer sufferings; “of what is foul and impure there is nothing to delight in; you should decisively resolve” reveals the faults and causes them to be renounced. In urging the cultivation of good dharmas, “make your bodies upright and your conduct correct” is the goodness of cessation; “increasingly do all that is good” is the goodness of doing; “cultivate yourselves and purify your bodies, and wash away the defilement of the mind” urges the cultivation of mental conduct, in which cultivation is the doing of good and the rest is the cessation of evil; “let your words and deeds be loyal and trustworthy, so that the outside and the inside correspond” urges the cultivation of verbal conduct, in which loyalty and trustworthiness in words and deeds is the doing of good, and the correspondence of outside and inside is the cessation of evil — the outside being the expression and the inside the mind, one's speech does not go against one's mind, and therefore they correspond. In urging the benefiting of living beings, “a person can deliver himself” takes up the former virtue of self; “in turn rescue” and the rest properly urges benefiting living beings: “in turn rescue others” transforms others to leave faults; “with keen clarity seek and vow, and accumulate the roots of goodness” transforms people to accomplish goodness — keen clarity in seeking and vowing transforms them to arouse the vow, and accumulating the roots of goodness transforms them to arouse practice. The above urges cultivation; below it raises and makes clear the benefit, causing people to cultivate and study. “Though for one life you toil and suffer, it is but a moment” means the time of cultivation is brief. From “afterward you will be born” onward is the benefit gained. Within that, first it makes clear that the benefit gained is long-lasting; “by non-doing and spontaneity you will be next to the Way of nirvana” means the benefit gained is supreme. In the long-lasting benefit there are four clauses: first, “afterward you will be born in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss beyond limit” means love and bliss are long; second, “you will long be joined with the Way and its virtue in one brightness” means accomplished virtue is long — the body joined with blessing is called union with the Way and its virtue, and the mind joined with wisdom is called union in brightness; third, “forever uprooting” and the rest means freedom from faults is long — within it, “forever uprooting the root of birth and death” is long freedom from the cause of karma; “never again will you have greed” and the rest is long freedom from affliction; “and the afflictions of care and suffering” is long freedom from the retribution of suffering; fourth, “if you wish for a lifespan” and the rest means the lifespan is long. This third [passage] is finished.

Each of you should diligently advance and seek what your mind desires. Do not fall into doubt and midway regret, bringing fault upon yourselves, so that you are born in the border land, in seven-jeweled palaces, and for five hundred years undergo all manner of hardship.

[Commentary] The fourth urges the renunciation of doubt. “Each of you should diligently seek what you desire” urges them to cultivate single-mindedly. “Do not fall into doubt” and the rest urges the renunciation of doubt. From “born in the border land” onward, it reveals the fault and urges renunciation.
The above is the third, again urging the cultivation of renunciation.
Maitreya said: I receive the Buddha's weighty instruction; single-mindedly and intently I shall cultivate and learn, and practice as taught, not daring to harbor doubt.

[Commentary] The fourth, Maitreya's receiving and practicing: within it, the opening words, “I receive the Buddha's weighty instruction; single-mindedly and intently I shall cultivate and learn, and practice as taught,” receive the Buddha's former words urging cultivation and reveal that he himself will practice them. “Not daring to harbor doubt” receives the Buddha's former words urging the renunciation of doubt and reveals that he himself is free of doubt.
End of fascicle five of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha.

blocks.text: Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha, Fascicle Six

inline.s: From here is the third, broadly raising the faults of the karma and suffering of the five evils, five pains, and five burnings, to make people weary and renounce them. Within it, first a general statement; from “what are” onward the divisions; from “the Buddha told Maitreya: I say to you” onward, it again makes a general explanation.

The Buddha told Maitreya: That you are able, in this world, to make your minds upright and your thoughts correct and to do no evil is the highest virtue; among the worlds of the ten directions there is none to compare with it. Why is this? In the Buddha-lands, the classes of gods and humans naturally do good and do not greatly do evil, and are easy to open and transform. Now I have become a Buddha in this world, amid the five evils, five pains, and five burnings, in the most fierce suffering, teaching and transforming the multitudes, causing them to renounce the five evils, to put away the five pains, and to leave the five burnings; subduing and transforming their minds, causing them to uphold the five goods and obtain their blessing and virtue, and the Way of deliverance from the world, long life, and nirvana.

[Commentary] In the first general statement, the text has two parts: first, it praises the former and introduces the latter — it praises Maitreya's former understanding, reception, and practice; second, from “now I” onward, it reveals his own intent in transforming: to transform living beings, causing them to leave the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, and causing them to uphold the five goods and obtain the five blessings. In the former, the opening words, “in this evil world, to make the mind upright and the thoughts correct and to do no evil is the highest virtue,” are the direct praise; “among the worlds of the ten directions there is none to compare with it” relies on a contrast to reveal its supremacy. From “why is this” onward is the explanation: first the question, then the answer — “in the Buddha-lands they naturally do good, do not greatly do evil, and are easy to open and transform” raises what is easy in order to reveal what is difficult, and so establishes this as supreme. In the latter passage, “now I have become a Buddha in this world” reveals that he himself has attained buddhahood; “amid the five evils” and the rest reveals the place of his transformation; “causing them to renounce the five” and the rest makes clear his intent in transforming, that he transforms living beings so that they may have something to go forth from and something to obtain. That from which he causes them to go forth is the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings. What the five precepts guard against — killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking alcohol — are the five evils. Creating these five evils, in the present life one is punished by the king's law and the body meets with calamity: this is called the five pains. By these five evils, in future lives one receives retribution in the three evil paths: this is spoken of as the five burnings. From all of these he causes them to go forth. Among what he causes them to obtain, “subduing and transforming their minds” tames them so that they follow the Dharma; “causing them to uphold the five goods” means the so-called five precepts, which reverse the former five evils; “obtaining their blessing” means that by upholding the five precepts, in the present life the body is at peace and free of suffering, reversing the former five pains; “the Way of deliverance from the world, long life, and nirvana” means that afterward one is born with Amitabha and in the end attains nirvana, reversing the former five burnings.

The Buddha said: What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What are the five burnings? What is the subduing and transforming of the five evils, so that one upholds the five goods and obtains their blessing and virtue, and the Way of deliverance from the world, long life, and nirvana?

[Commentary] In the second, the divisions: “what are the five evils, five pains, and five burnings” asks about the former and brings on the latter, and below it answers and distinguishes them. In each gate, first the evil is made clear, and afterward the good is revealed in contrast.

The first evil is this: the gods, humans, and crawling creatures all alike wish to do every evil. The strong subdue the weak, and they rob and harm one another in turn; they maim and kill and devour one another. They do not know to cultivate goodness; they are evil, rebellious, and without the Way. Afterward they receive calamity and punishment, and naturally tend toward it; the spirits record and mark it, and the offender is not pardoned. Hence there are the poor and lowly, beggars and the solitary, the deaf, the blind, and the mute, the foolish, the deluded, and the vile, and even the crippled, the insane, and the deficient. And again there are the honored and wealthy, the highly talented and clearly wise — all owing to compassion and filial piety in former lives, to the cultivation of goodness and the accumulation of virtue. In the world there are the constant laws, the king's law and the prisons; yet they are unwilling to fear and be careful. Doing evil they fall into crime and receive its calamity and punishment; they seek and hope for release, but it is hard to struggle free. In the world such present things are seen before the eyes; but when the lifespan ends and the next life comes, it is deeper still and fiercer still. Entering that darkness, they are reborn and receive a body; as with the king's law, there is painful and extreme punishment. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction and suffering. They trade one body for another, change their form and alter their path, and the lifespan they receive is sometimes long, sometimes short. The spirit and the subtle consciousness naturally tend toward it, and each must go alone to meet it, following on to be born together, retaliating upon one another without cease. Until the calamity and evil are exhausted they cannot be parted, and turning and turning within it there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. Between heaven and earth this is naturally so: though it does not come at once with sudden violence, the path of good and evil will in the end bring them to it. This is the first great evil, the first pain, and the first burning. Toil and suffering are like this — like a great fire burning a person's body. If a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind, make his body upright and his conduct correct, and alone do all that is good and do no evil, then he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing and virtue, the Way of deliverance from the world, of rebirth in heaven, and of nirvana. This is the first great good.

[Commentary] In the first gate, first the evil is made clear, and below the good is revealed in contrast. In the evil, the opening words, “the first evil is this,” raise it in general; next the divisions; afterward the Dharma [of punishment]; below, similes reveal the fault. In the divisions, first the evil of killing is made clear. From “in the world there are the constant laws, the king's law” onward, it makes clear the pain with respect to killing. From “when the lifespan ends” onward, it makes clear the burning with respect to killing. In the former, the making clear of evil: “the gods, humans” and the rest makes clear those who create evil; “wish to do every evil” and the rest properly makes clear the creating of evil; from “they do not know to cultivate” onward, it makes clear the fault of creating evil, and within that it first properly makes clear the fault, and from “and again the honored” onward it raises what they obtained to reveal what they lost. The pain and burning may be understood. From “this is” onward is the conclusion; from “like” onward, similes reveal the marks of the burning. In the making clear of good, first the divisions and then the conclusion; in the divisions, the opening words, “if a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind,” properly make clear the doing of good, contrasting with the former evil; “he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing” contrasts with the former pain and the former burning. From “this is” onward is the conclusion.

The Buddha said: The second evil is this: the people of the world — fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers, household members, husbands and wives — are wholly without principle and do not accord with the Dharma and its measure. They are extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and self-indulgent, each wishing to please himself, giving free rein to his mind and indulging his own will. They deceive and mislead one another; their minds and mouths are at variance, and their words and thoughts are without truth. They are flattering and fawning, disloyal, with artful speech and adulation; they envy the worthy and slander the good, and plunge people into grievance and wrong. The ruler above is not clear-sighted and employs his ministers; the ministers do as they please, full of schemes and falsehoods, trampling the measures and doing as they can, knowing the circumstances of the situation. Those in office are not upright and are deceived by them, recklessly injuring the loyal and good, not matching the heart of heaven. Ministers deceive their lords, sons deceive their fathers, brothers, husbands and wives, and acquaintances near and far deceive and cheat one another. Each harbors greed, hatred, and delusion, wishing to enrich himself and coveting much. Noble and base, high and low, their minds are all alike. They ruin their families and destroy their bodies, giving no thought to what comes before or after. Relatives within and without are brought by this to the extinction of their clans. Sometimes household members and acquaintances, the people of the villages, towns, and markets, ignorant folk and rustics, join together in undertakings and set profit and harm against one another, until anger becomes enmity knotted tight. The rich are stingy and grudging and will not give in charity; loving and guarding and greedily prizing their goods, their minds are wearied and their bodies suffer. Thus to the very end they have nothing to rely on; they come alone and go alone, and not one follows them. Good and evil, calamity and blessing, follow the life where one is born; sometimes in a place of bliss, sometimes entering bitter poison — and only then do they repent. What use is that? The people of the world are foolish in mind and scant in wisdom; seeing the good they hate and slander it, and do not think to admire and emulate it. They only wish to do evil and recklessly commit what is unlawful. They constantly harbor a thievish mind and hope for others' profit; when it is scattered and worn away, they seek for it again. Their crooked minds are not upright, and they fear others' looks. They do not consider and plan beforehand, and when the matter comes they only then repent. In this present life there are the king's law and the prisons, and following their offenses they go to receive their calamity and punishment. Because in former lives they did not believe in the Way and its virtue and did not cultivate the roots of goodness, and now again do evil, the gods fully record it and set apart their names in the registers. When the lifespan ends the spirit departs and goes down into the evil paths. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction and suffering. Turning and turning within them, through life after life and kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. This is the second great evil, the second pain, and the second burning. Toil and suffering are like this — like a great fire burning a person's body. If a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind, make his body upright and his conduct correct, and alone do all that is good and do no evil, then he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing and virtue, the Way of deliverance from the world, of rebirth in heaven, and of nirvana. This is the second great good.

[Commentary] In the second gate, first the evil and afterward the good. In the evil, first it raises it, next the divisions, afterward the Dharma [of punishment], and below similes reveal it. In the divisions, first the evil. From “in this present life there are the king's law” onward is the second, making clear the pain. From “because in former lives they did not believe” onward is the third, making clear the burning. In the evil, again first it makes clear those who create evil; from “wholly without principle” onward, it properly makes clear the creating of evil; from “they ruin their families” onward, it makes clear the fault of creating evil. In the proper making clear of creating evil, “wholly without principle and not according with the Dharma and its measure” makes clear that they have no goodness; “extravagant, licentious, arrogant” and the rest makes clear that they create evil — extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and self-indulgent, each wishing to please himself; engaging in theft and doing as one will, giving free rein to the mind and indulging the will; “deceive one another” and the rest properly makes clear robbery and theft. The remaining text may be understood.

The Buddha said: The third evil is this: the people of the world live leaning on one another, dwelling together between heaven and earth; the years of their lifespan are not much. Above there are the worthy and wise elders, the honored and wealthy; below there are the poor and menial, the crippled and inferior, and foolish men; in between there are unwholesome people who constantly harbor evil and wrong. They think only of lust and indulgence; their breasts are full of vexation, and love and desire tangle and disorder them, so that sitting or rising they are never at ease. Greedy in mind, they hoard and begrudge, wishing only to get things for nothing. They cast sidelong glances at fine beauty, and their lewd manners show abroad. They loathe and hate their own wives, and privately go in and out wantonly, wasting and damaging the family wealth, doing what is unlawful. They form ties and gather in companies, raise troops and attack one another, assault, plunder, and kill, seizing by force without the Way. With evil minds set on the outside, they do not cultivate their own affairs, but steal and snatch whatever they can get, wishing to strike and carry the matter through; and by fear and force and coercion they bring it home to wife and children, indulging their minds and pleasing themselves, exhausting their bodies in pleasure. Sometimes toward their own relatives they do not avoid noble or base, and the household within and without is afflicted and suffers by it. Nor do they fear the king's law and prohibitions. Evils such as these are manifest to men and ghosts; the sun and moon shine upon them, and the gods record and mark them. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction and suffering. Turning and turning within them, through life after life and kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. This is the third great evil, the third pain, and the third burning. Toil and suffering are like this — like a great fire burning a person's body. If a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind, make his body upright and his conduct correct, and alone do all that is good and do no evil, then he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing and virtue, the Way of deliverance from the world, of rebirth in heaven, and of nirvana. This is the third great good.

[Commentary] In the third gate, first the evil and afterward the good. In the evil, first it raises it, next the divisions, afterward the Dharma [of punishment], and below similes reveal it. In the divisions, first the evil. From “nor do they fear the king's law” onward is the pain. From “evils such as these are manifest” onward is the burning. In the evil, first it makes clear those who create evil; from “constantly harbor evil” onward, it properly makes clear the creating of the evil of sexual misconduct; from “they form ties and gather in companies” onward, it makes clear the fault of creating evil — that for the sake of lust they commit killing, stealing, and the like is their fault. The remaining text may be understood.

The Buddha said: The fourth evil is this: the people of the world do not think of cultivating goodness; they teach and command one another and together do every evil — divisive speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech. They slander and harm and stir up strife; they hate and envy good people and ruin the worthy and wise, taking pleasure at their side. They are unfilial to their two parents, slight and scorn their teachers and elders, are faithless toward friends, and are seldom honest. The honored and noble are proud and great, claiming that they themselves possess the Way, running rampant in power and might, encroaching upon and slighting others, unable to know themselves, shameless in doing evil, considering themselves strong and hale and wishing to be feared and revered. They do not fear heaven and earth, the gods, the sun, and the moon, and are unwilling to do good. They are hard to subdue and transform, self-willed and arrogant, thinking that it can always be so, with no care or dread, constantly harboring pride. Evils such as these the gods record and mark. Relying on the little merit and virtue they made in former lives, small goodnesses uphold and connect them and protect and help them; but now in this life, doing evil, their merit and virtue are utterly extinguished, and the good gods and spirits each depart and leave them. Their bodies stand alone and empty, with nothing more to rely on. When the lifespan is utterly ended, they are where all evils return; naturally they are pressed and hurried, and together they rush to snatch them away. Moreover, their names are recorded in the registers of the gods, and calamity and fault draw and pull them; they must go toward it. The retribution of their offenses is natural, and there is no way to be parted from it; they can only go forward and enter the cauldron of fire, where body and mind are crushed and broken, and spirit and consciousness suffer pain. At such a time, what use is repentance? The Way of heaven is bright and clear; there is no stumbling. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction and suffering. Turning and turning within them, through life after life and kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fourth great evil, the fourth pain, and the fourth burning. Toil and suffering are like this — like a great fire burning a person's body. If a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind, make his body upright and his conduct correct, and alone do all that is good and do no evil, then he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing and virtue, the Way of deliverance from the world, of rebirth in heaven, and of nirvana. This is the fourth great good.

[Commentary] In the fourth gate, first the evil and afterward the good. In the evil, first it raises it, next the divisions, afterward the conclusion, and below it is revealed by similes. In the divisions, first the evil. From “evils such as these the gods record” onward is the making clear of the pain. From “when the lifespan is ended” onward is the making clear of the burning. In the evil, first it makes clear those who create evil; from “do not think of cultivating” onward, it properly makes clear the creating of the evil of false speech: the four verbal faults, because they do not accord with the Dharma, are all alike called false speech; from “they hate and envy the good” onward, it makes clear the fault of creating evil. In the pain, it makes clear that their former goodness is utterly extinguished, the good gods abandon and leave them far, their bodies have nothing to rely on, and they meet with many calamities — this is their pain. In the burning, it makes clear that they are dragged by their evil karma, seized and recorded by the ghosts and gods, and led into the evil paths, where they suffer being scorched and burned — this is called burning. The remaining text may be understood.

The Buddha said: The fifth evil is this: the people of the world loiter and are lazy and indolent; they are unwilling to do good, to cultivate themselves, or to attend to their work. Their households and dependents suffer hunger and cold and hardship. When their parents teach and instruct them, they glare and answer in anger, and their words are not harmonious; they are contrary, rebellious, and defiant, like enemies, and better it would be to have no son at all. In giving and taking they have no measure, and all alike are afflicted and disgusted by them. They betray grace and violate righteousness, with no thought of repaying. Poor and destitute, unable to obtain more, they plunder and seize by force and fraud, giving themselves up to idleness and dissipation, accustomed to getting things for nothing to relieve and supply themselves. They are addicted to wine and crave delicacies, eating and drinking without measure; they give free rein to their minds and wander at ease, rude and overbearing and defiant, not knowing human feeling. By force they wish to suppress others; seeing others have good, they envy and hate them. Without righteousness or propriety, they have no scruples; self-willed and self-approving, they cannot be admonished or enlightened. Toward the needs and possessions of their six kinds of kin and dependents they cannot take thought or care. They do not consider the grace of their parents, nor keep the righteousness of teachers and friends. Their minds constantly think evil, their mouths constantly speak evil, their bodies constantly do evil, and never once do they do a single good. They do not believe in the sutras and Dharma of the former sages and Buddhas; they do not believe that by practicing the Way one may be delivered from the world; they do not believe that after death the spirit is born again; they do not believe that doing good brings good and doing evil brings evil. They wish to kill true people and to throw the sangha into strife; they wish to harm their parents, brothers, and dependents; the six kinds of kin hate and loathe them and wish them dead. People such as these, their minds and thoughts all alike, are foolish and benighted, yet consider themselves wise. They do not know from where they have come in birth, nor to where they go in death. Unkind and unfilial, they are evil and defy heaven and earth; and amid all this they hope for luck and chance, wishing to seek long life — yet they will surely come to death. Though with a compassionate heart one teaches and instructs them, causing them to think on the good, and opens and reveals to them birth and death and the destinies of good and evil, that it is naturally so, yet they are unwilling to believe. With heartfelt effort one speaks to them, and it profits them nothing; their minds are blocked and shut, and their thoughts are not opened or understood. When the great life is about to end, repentance and fear come together. They did not beforehand cultivate goodness, and at the extremity they only then repent. Repenting afterward — what use will it be? Between heaven and earth the five paths are clearly divided, vast and dark, wide and boundless. The retribution of good and evil and the succession of calamity and blessing are borne by oneself, and there is none to take one's place. The reckoning is natural and answers to what one has done; calamity and fault follow the life, and there is no letting go. The good person doing good passes from joy to joy and from light to light; the evil person doing evil passes from suffering to suffering and from darkness to darkness. Who can know this? Only the Buddha knows. Though one teaches and speaks and opens and reveals it, few believe and accept. Birth and death do not rest, and the evil paths are not emptied. People of the world such as these are hard to tell of fully. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable affliction and suffering. Turning and turning within them, through life after life and kalpa after kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to obtain, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fifth great evil, the fifth pain, and the fifth burning. Toil and suffering are like this — like a great fire burning a person's body. If a person can, amid all this, single-mindedly control his mind, make his body upright and his mindfulness correct, so that words and deeds match each other, all that he does is utterly sincere, what he speaks is as it is, and his mind and mouth do not turn from one another, and alone do all that is good and do no evil, then he alone will be delivered, and will obtain that blessing and virtue, the Way of deliverance from the world, of rebirth in heaven, and of nirvana. This is the fifth great good.

[Commentary] In the fifth gate, first the evil and afterward the good. In the evil, first it raises it, next the divisions, afterward the Dharma [of punishment], and below similes reveal it. In the divisions, first the evil. From “people such as these, their minds and thoughts” onward is the pain. From “when the great life is about to end, repentance and fear” onward is the burning. In the evil, first it makes clear those who create evil; from “loiter and are lazy and indolent, unwilling” onward, it properly makes clear the creating of the evil of drinking alcohol. Those who drink wine do not cultivate good practices and do not attend to their family's work; they oppose teachings, and in anger cause delight in quarreling; they turn their backs on grace and begrudge righteousness, bullying and resisting. To speak of them all together, from “give free rein to their minds and wander at ease, rude and overbearing and defiant” onward, it makes clear the fault of creating evil; the marks of the fault are many, and are fully revealed in the text. In the pain, it makes clear that in the present they are foolish and deluded, with the obstruction of darkness covering their minds, knowing and understanding nothing — this is taken as their pain. There should also be punishment by the king's law, but the text omits it and does not speak of it. The burning and the rest may be understood.
The above is the separate discussion.

The Buddha told Maitreya: I say to you: these five evils of the world, with toil and suffering such as this, and the five pains and five burnings, give rise to one another in turn. Simply doing all evils and not cultivating the roots of goodness, all naturally enter the evil destinies. Or in this present life they first meet with calamity and sickness, unable to die and unable to live, drawn by their offenses, shown to the multitude to be seen. When the body dies, following their deeds they enter the three evil paths, with suffering and poison beyond measure, scorching and burning one another. In the long time afterward they together form enmity knotted tight; from the smallest beginnings it grows into great evil. All this is because they are greedy and attached to wealth and lust and cannot give in charity; pressed by deluded desire, they follow the thoughts of their minds, and the afflictions bind and fetter them with no release. They enrich themselves and contend for profit, taking no account of anything. Wealth, honor, glory, and splendor give pleasure for the moment; unable to endure insult and not attending to cultivating goodness, their power and might are but brief, and they are worn away along with it. Their bodies sit in toil and suffering, and after long time it becomes greatly fierce. The Way of heaven is relaxed and drawn tight, and naturally it investigates and seizes them; the guiding net and snare respond above and below. Lonely and fearful, the rich enter into it. From ancient times to now this has been so; how painful, how grievous! The Buddha said to Maitreya: The world being thus, the Buddha pities them all. By the power of majestic spirit he crushes and extinguishes all evils and causes all to incline to goodness, casting off what they think on, receiving and upholding the sutras and precepts, accepting and practicing the Dharma of the Way, without any transgression or loss, so that in the end they attain the Way of deliverance from the world and nirvana.

[Commentary] This again makes a general explanation. Within it, first the five evils are made clear; from “the Buddha said to Maitreya: the world being thus, the Buddha pities them all” onward, the good is revealed in contrast to the evil. In the evil, first it makes clear in general that the five evils, five pains, and five burnings give rise to one another; from “simply doing” onward, it reveals them in particular. In the particular there are two rounds: first it makes clear that from evil, pain and burning arise; from “when the body dies, following” onward, it makes clear that from burning, evil and pain arise. In the former, the opening words, “simply doing all evils and not cultivating the roots of goodness,” make clear the evil; “all naturally enter the evil destinies” makes clear the arising of burning; “or in this present life they first meet with calamity” makes clear the arising of pain. In the latter, the opening words, “when the body dies, following their deeds they enter the three evil [paths],” make clear the burning; from “in the long time” onward, evil arises from burning — “in the long time afterward they together form enmity knotted tight; from the smallest beginnings it grows into great enmity” is the arising of the evil of killing; “all this is because they are greedy and attached and cannot give in charity” is the arising of the evil of robbery and theft; “pressed by deluded desire, they follow the thoughts of their minds” is the arising of the evil of sexual misconduct; “they enrich themselves and contend for profit, taking no account of anything” is the arising of the evil of false speech; “wealth, honor, glory, and splendor give pleasure for the moment, unable to endure” is the arising of the evil of drinking alcohol. These give rise to evil. From “their bodies sit” onward, pain arises from evil: sitting in the former five evils, their bodies receive toil and suffering, and the suffering increases without cease, and this is called “after long time it becomes greatly fierce.” Below the marks of the fierceness are revealed. Whatever is in the world, the principle of heaven and earth is naturally established and set up, and therefore it is called the Way of heaven relaxed and drawn tight. Those who do evil must be exposed, and this is called investigating and seizing themselves; their bodies meet the net of the law, and therefore it is called the guiding net and snare. Noble and base, high and low, none fail to follow the law, and therefore it is called responding above and below. The offender returns to it, and no one is his companion or match, and therefore it says, lonely and fearful, he must enter into it. From “from ancient times to now” onward, it concludes to reveal the fault. The above makes clear the evil; below the good is revealed in contrast. “The Buddha said to Maitreya: the world being thus” takes up and raises the former evil; “the Buddha pities them all” reveals his own compassion. From “by the power of majestic spirit” onward, it teaches the extinction of the former evil and transforms them to follow goodness: “he crushes and extinguishes all evils and causes all to incline to goodness” teaches the cultivation of worldly goodness; “casting off what they think on, receiving and upholding the sutras” and the rest teaches them to practice supramundane goodness — from the beginning to “without any transgression” makes clear the cause of going beyond the world, and from “in the end they attain” onward accomplishes the fruit of going beyond the world.
The above is the third, making clear the faults of the karma and suffering of the five evils and the rest.

The Buddha said: You gods and humans now, and people of later ages, who obtain the Buddha's sutra words, should ponder them carefully. If you can, amid them, make your minds upright and your conduct correct; let rulers above do good and lead and transform those below, instructing one another in turn, each keeping himself upright and watchful, honoring the sages and revering the good, being kind, compassionate, and widely loving. Toward the Buddha's words of teaching and instruction, let none dare fail or betray them. Seek deliverance from the world and pull up and cut off the root of the many evils of birth and death; keep far from the way of the three evil paths with its immeasurable care, dread, suffering, and pain. In this [world] you should broadly plant the roots of virtue, bestow grace and give charity, not transgress the prohibitions of the Way, endure insult, press forward with vigor, and be single-minded in wisdom, teaching and transforming one another, establishing virtue and setting up goodness. With mind upright and thoughts correct, pure in the fasts and precepts, for one day and one night, you surpass a hundred years of doing good in the land of Immeasurable Life. Why is this? In that Buddha-land all is non-doing and spontaneous; all accumulate manifold goodness, and there is not the slightest hair of evil. In this [world], cultivating goodness for ten days and ten nights surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is this? In the Buddha-lands of other directions there are many who do good and few who do evil; blessing and virtue come naturally, and there is no place for creating evil. Only here is there much evil, and nothing comes naturally; with toil and suffering they seek their desires, deceiving and cheating one another in turn, their minds wearied and their bodies exhausted, drinking bitterness and eating poison. In such evil pursuits they are never at peace. I pity you, the classes of gods and humans, and with heartfelt effort teach and instruct you, causing you to cultivate goodness, opening and guiding you according to what is fitting, granting you the sutras and the Dharma, and none fail to receive and use them; according to the vows of your minds, I cause you all to attain the Way. Wherever the Buddha walks, in countries, towns, and villages, none fail to receive his transformation: the world is harmonious and compliant, sun and moon are clear and bright, wind and rain come in season, calamity and pestilence do not arise, the country is rich and the people at peace, weapons are of no use, virtue is honored and benevolence promoted, and all attend to cultivating propriety and yielding. The Buddha said: I pity you gods and humans more than parents think of their children. Now I have become a Buddha in this world, subduing and transforming the five evils, dissolving the five pains, cutting off and extinguishing the five burnings, attacking evil with good, pulling up the suffering of birth and death, causing you to obtain the five virtues and rise to the peace of non-doing. After I pass away, the sutras and the Way will gradually be extinguished; the people will be flattering and false and will again do every evil, and the five burnings and five pains will be as before. After long time they will become more fierce, beyond full telling; I have but spoken of them to you in brief. The Buddha said to Maitreya: Each of you should ponder this well, teach and admonish one another, and according to the Buddha's sutras and Dharma, let none transgress. Thereupon the bodhisattva Maitreya, with palms joined, said: What the Buddha has spoken is very good; the people of the world are truly so. The Tathagata, in universal compassion, pities those who resent, and causes them all to attain deliverance. We receive the Buddha's weighty instruction, and dare not transgress or lose it.

[Commentary] The fourth urges people to cultivate renunciation. Within it there are two: first, the Tathagata urges cultivation; second, Maitreya understands and receives. The former has three parts: first, it properly urges by principle; second, from “I pity you” onward, it raises his own present transforming benefit in order to urge them; third, from “after I pass away” onward, it raises the decline and loss after his extinction in order to urge them. The first has two parts: first, it properly urges by principle; second, from “in this [world] you should broadly plant the roots of virtue” onward, it reveals the supremacy of this cultivation, increasing people's intention to learn. In the former, proper urging, first it urges one's own practice — “obtaining the Buddha's sutra words, you should ponder them carefully, make your minds upright and your conduct correct”; from “let rulers above” onward, it urges them to transform others: “let rulers above do good and lead and transform those below” and the rest transforms others to cultivate goodness; “seek deliverance from the world and pull up birth and death” and the rest transforms others to leave evil. In revealing this supremacy, first it makes clear that in this world one day of cultivating goodness surpasses a hundred years of doing good in [the land of] Immeasurable Life; from “why is this” onward is the explanation. Below it makes clear that in this world ten days of cultivating goodness surpass a thousand years of doing good in other Buddha-lands; from “why is this” onward is the explanation. In the first passage, “in this [world] you should broadly plant the roots of virtue” raises it in general; “bestow grace” and the rest are the particulars. In the particulars, first it raises the six perfections, which are the practice of self-benefit: bestowing grace is the perfection of giving; not transgressing is the perfection of precepts; enduring insult is the perfection of patience; pressing forward with vigor is the perfection of vigor; single-mindedness is the perfection of meditation; wisdom is the perfection of wisdom. “Teaching and transforming one another” is the practice of benefiting others. “Establishing virtue and setting up goodness” concludes them in summary. The former doing of good, and “with mind upright and thoughts correct, pure in the fasts and precepts,” is the goodness of cessation. Because this cultivation is difficult, one day surpasses a hundred years of doing good in [the land of] Immeasurable Life. In the second, raising his own present transforming benefit to urge them, first it makes clear that those he transforms cultivate goodness and obtain bliss; from “the Buddha said” onward, it makes clear that those he transforms extinguish evil and leave suffering. In the third, raising the decline and loss after his extinction to urge them, first it raises the matters of decline and loss after his extinction; from “said to Maitreya” onward, it urges people to cultivate and sever. The above is the Buddha's urging; from here is Maitreya's understanding, reception, and practice. “Maitreya said to the Buddha: what the Buddha has spoken is very good; the people of the world are truly so” is his understanding and reception; “the Tathagata, in compassion” and the rest reveals that he himself will practice it.
The above four sections together form the second, broadly raising the matters of the Saha world's filth and evil, to make people weary and renounce them.

From here is the third, taking the gain and loss of the land of Immeasurable Life and distinguishing both, to make people cultivate and renounce. Within it there are five: first, the Buddha urges Ānanda to bow to the Immeasurable Life [Buddha]; second, Ānanda receives the command and reverently bows to that Buddha and vows to seek to see him; third, in response to the former request, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sends forth radiance that universally illumines; fourth, by the Buddha's radiance each sees the other; fifth, through this mutual seeing, the matters of that land's gain and loss are fully revealed, making people cultivate and renounce.

The Buddha told Ānanda: Rise, and adjust your robes again; join your palms in reverence and bow to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. The Buddhas and Tathagatas of the lands of the ten directions constantly praise together that Buddha as unattached and unobstructed.
[Commentary] In the first passage, first it tells Ānanda to bow to that Buddha; from “the ten directions' lands” onward, it raises the Buddhas' common praise, completing his bowing in reverence.

Thereupon Ānanda rose and adjusted his robes, faced the west with body upright, reverently joined his palms, and prostrated himself with his whole body, bowing to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and said: World-Honored One, I wish to see that Buddha, the Land of Peace and Bliss, and the assembly of bodhisattvas, hearers, and multitudes.
